💡 Key Takeaways
  • Artificial intelligence tooling startup Epochal AI Inc.
  • In a recent development, the capital was provided by Chief Executive Officer Guodong Zhang, a machine learning researcher who earlier co-founded xAI Corp.
  • Epochal’s first offering is a cloud service called the Epochal Time Portal.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

UPDATED 20:30 EST / NOVEMBER 24 2026.

Artificial intelligence tooling startup Epochal AI Inc. released today with $100 million in funding.

In a recent development, the capital was provided by Chief Executive Officer Guodong Zhang, a machine learning researcher who earlier co-founded xAI Corp. He established Epochal earlier this year with two other xAI co-founders, Zihang Dai and Manuel Kroiss. The manufacturer’s staff also includes former researchers from Anthropic PBC, OpenAI Group PBC and Google DeepMind.

Epochal’s first offering is a cloud service called the Epochal Time Portal. According to the company, it enables developers to train AI models that can predict future events. The service does so by providing models with access to historical web data from the past 30 years.

If a bank wishes to train an AI that can predict quarterly earnings, it could use the service to fetch financial results from the first three quarters of 2025. It could then ask the AI to estimate fourth quarter results from the same year. After the model generates its predictions, developers can compare them against real fourth quarter earnings to check the model’s accuracy. They can make adjustments if necessary and then repeat the training workflow until the model starts generating accurate forecasts.

The Epochal Time Portal features more than 1 trillion historical web pages on launch. Each entry includes a timestamp that indicates when it was created. According to the firm, its timestamps make it possible to track how a webpage changed over time.

Sources indicate that AI models access the content through a purpose-built search engine. It enables them to specify the time periods from which they wish to retrieve webpages. According to Epochal, its platform provides one-minute granularity for the most frequently updated pages.

It has been revealed that like consumer search engines, the Epochal Time Portal prioritizes the webpages that are most relevant to each given query. The difference is that it considers webpages’ creation date when evaluating relevance. If a query contains the term “Meta” but asks for pages created before 2021, the year Facebook Inc. rebranded, the Epochal Time Portal will not bring up pages that relate to the social networking giant.

Industry observers note that today’s frontier models can determine that they’re being trained on historical data rather than up-to-date information. For example, a model might compare the creation date of a webpage to the virtual clock of the operating system on which it deployed. Such discrepancies can decrease the effectiveness of training runs.

According to Epochal, its service mitigates the issue by deploying AI models in sandboxes synced to their training data. If a tech giant is training a model on webpages from 2025, the Epochal Time Portal will run it on a Linux version from that year. It applies the same precautions to the software tools and programming language versions that models use.

Industry observers note that the Epochal Time Portal is initially available in a single free tier with low usage limits. Epochal aims to follow up the launch by sharing the results of several AI experiments that its researchers have carried out using the service.

Google acquires Seattle startup Howie and its AI scheduling assistant

💡 Key Takeaways
  • by Kurt Schlosser on Nov 18, 2026 at 2:03 pmNovember 18, 2026 at 2:03 pm.
  • Google is bringing Seattle-based Howie, maker of an AI scheduling assistant that works from your inbox, into its Google Labs division.
  • Terms of the deal were not disclosed this week.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

by Kurt Schlosser on Nov 18, 2026 at 2:03 pmNovember 18, 2026 at 2:03 pm.

Google is bringing Seattle-based Howie, maker of an AI scheduling assistant that works from your inbox, into its Google Labs division.

Terms of the deal were not disclosed this week. Google Labs, the company’s experimental arm, unveiled the acquisition in a post on X, saying it “can’t wait to learn from them as we build the next generation of intuitive AI tools together for small businesses.”.

According to recent reports, howie CEO and co-founder Austin Petersmith noted on LinkedIn that the team will continue building Howie at Google. “Howie has always been built on top of Gmail and Google Calendar, so Google Labs is the perfect place for us to take this product to the next level,” he wrote.

According to recent reports, petersmith co-founded Howie around 2023 with CTO Dave Newman. The two first worked together in 2013 at Assembly, which Newman co-founded, and prototyped an AI assistant in 2015 before deciding the market wasn’t ready.

Industry observers note that we’re excited to welcome Howie to Google Labs! The @Howie_ai team has spent years figuring out scheduling and calendar management. We can’t wait to learn from them as we build the next generation of intuitive AI tools together for small businesses 🤝 https://t.co/8bzjebeGdD.

Users cc Howie on an email thread, and it coordinates meeting times, adds events to calendars, follows up as needed and flags scheduling conflicts. Customers set their own rules in an open-ended preferences document, such as “if it’s a pitch call, set it to 25 minutes and use Zoom.”.

Behind the scenes, Howie ran tasks through fine-tuned language models and looped in human scheduling experts when the AI wasn’t confident.

According to recent reports, howie raised a $6 million seed round led by True Ventures in September 2025, when it launched publicly out of private beta. At the time, it had more than 1,000 paying customers, including startup founders, venture capitalists, recruiters, consultants and journalists, and was scheduling more than 5,000 meetings a week.

The deal comes as Google and rivals including OpenAI, Anthropic and Meta race to build AI agents that complete tasks on behalf of users. Google Labs acquired music generation platform ProducerAI earlier this year.

#190632. Industry News: 8 of the biggest MLB contracts for Japanese players, from $700 million to $34 million

📅 24 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 15m • 📚 Deep Dive (2941 w)
📖 Baca
Business & Policy ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Qz ↗ Open Full Page

Industry News: 8 of the biggest MLB contracts for Japanese players, from $700 million to $34 million

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 15 min read (2941 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Qz

⏱️ ~15 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Eight of the largest MLB deals for Japanese players, from Ohtani's $700 million to Murakami's $34 million, and what each total leaves out.
  • Shohei Ohtani signed the richest contract a Japanese player has ever received, and the Dodgers paid it for a star they had already watched in the majors.
  • The Dodgers will pay most of Ohtani's money long after he signed, and they will spread it across a decade.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Eight of the largest MLB deals for Japanese players, from Ohtani's $700 million to Murakami's $34 million, and what each total leaves out.

Shohei Ohtani signed the richest contract a Japanese player has ever received, and the Dodgers paid it for a star they had already watched in the majors. Los Angeles committed $700 million over 10 years to a player who had spent six seasons across town with the Angels, according to ESPN. Nobody had to guess whether his game would carry over from Japan, so the hard question about the deal is how the Dodgers built it. The Associated Press reports that 97% of the money was deferred without interest when he signed in 2023. Almost all of the record total is a promise to pay later, and the question that matters is when the Dodgers actually hand the money over.

The Dodgers will pay most of Ohtani's money long after he signed, and they will spread it across a decade. The deferred payments arrive each July 1 from 2034 through 2043, according to The Associated Press. A dollar paid that far in the future, with no interest added, is worth less than a dollar paid today, and the Dodgers' real cost is below $700 million. Nobody needs to settle on an exact figure for that gap to matter. Ohtani's total can't be compared directly with a contract that pays a player during the seasons he plays.

Recent findings suggest that the Dodgers committed more money to Yoshinobu Yamamoto than any team had committed to a player moving straight from Japan to the majors, and they did it before he had thrown a major league pitch. His $325 million contract is the largest for a player arriving directly from Japan, according to ESPN. The Los Angeles Times reports that he was 25 when he signed in 2023, and that before bidding opened, he was expected to command at least $200 million. Clubs judged him on his pitching in Japan, where he won the Pacific League's MVP award in three consecutive seasons. Teams kept raising their offers well past that early estimate, and his final price measures how hard clubs competed for him as much as how good he was.

The Chicago Cubs paid one of the highest prices ever for a hitter coming from Japan, and they paid it for the best batting season any player there had put together in years. ESPN reports that Sato agreed to $120 million over six years with the Cubs, the third-largest deal for a player from Japan's league. Sato became the first Triple Crown winner in Japan since Munetaka Murakami's 2022 season, according to CBS Sports. The Cubs are paying for the one skill Sato highlighted best, his power. They are not paying for a hitter without flaws.

Sato misses the ball far more often than a typical major league hitter, and the Cubs signed him anyway. He made contact on 66% of his swings, against a major league average of 77%, according to . That gap means he will likely strike out more than most hitters once he faces major league pitching. Chicago is betting that his home runs will outweigh the empty swings, and the six-year term shows the team expects that power to last for years. "Like Murakami, Sato carries risk, and like Murakami, his power makes that risk worth the dice roll," CBS Sports writer Dayn Perry wrote.

Toronto paid Kazuma Okamoto a solid price rather than a superstar's price. The Blue Jays gave him a four-year, $60 million contract, which tops the $54 million deal Tatsuya Imai signed, according to ESPN. Bringing him to Toronto cost the team more than his contract. Toronto must also send $10,875,000 to the Yomiuri Giants, the club he played for in Japan, according to CBC. A contender spent that much on a hitter who isn't a headline star because it needed a third baseman.

Toronto finished last season without a regular third baseman. Addison Barger and Ernie Clement split the starts at the position almost evenly, CBC reports, and neither player held the job. With this contract, the team bought a full-time answer at a position it had been filling day to day.

According to recent reports, the Blue Jays are betting that Okamoto's power will carry over to the majors. He arrives directly from Japan's league with 248 career home runs, according to CBC, and he hit every one of them in Japan. Toronto paid for a proven record that major league pitching has yet to test. It did not pay for star power.

The White Sox may have paid too little for Munetaka Murakami rather than too much. Chicago signed him to a two-year, $34 million contract, according to ESPN, the smallest of the biggest deals Japanese players have signed with MLB teams. For that price, the team got power that only one other Japanese-born hitter has shown in the majors. Murakami and Shohei Ohtani are the only Japanese-born players with 35 or more home runs in a season, according to the Chicago Sun-Times. Murakami's contract is the smallest in this group, but his power puts him in the same company as the most celebrated Japanese hitter in the game.

Major league teams now compete to sign the best players from Nippon Professional Baseball, Japan's top league, and fans tend to judge each of those signings by the total written on the contract. That total leaves out a second payment, because a team that signs a posted Japanese star pays the player and also pays the Japanese club that let him go. MLB.com reports that the Yankees paid Masahiro Tanaka's Japanese club a posting fee separate from his contract. The Blue Jays owed the same kind of fee to Kazuma Okamoto's club under MLB's agreement with NPB, with that money kept outside his contract, according to CBC. The second bill is a standing part of the price of Japanese talent. It keeps rising on deals past $50 million, with the Japanese club taking 15% of any value above that mark, according to CBS Sports. None of that money appears in the headline figure, so the total fans quote covers only part of what a team spends.

Deadlines also shape the price, and they favor the team most willing to spend. Once his club posts him, a Japanese player has 45 days to negotiate with MLB teams, according to MLB.com. Every interested team has to make its best offer within the same few weeks. The final number reflects how many teams wanted the player and how badly they needed him, as much as his record in Japan. The years and dollars on paper can also differ from what a team actually pays and how long the player stays. Money deferred for years costs a team less than money paid now, and an opt-out can end a deal well before its last season. Fans who compare totals learn less than it seems about who is the better player, and the smallest deal can turn out to be the best one.

ESPN set out to rank the largest MLB deals that Japanese players have signed, including the Yankees' 2014 contract for Masahiro Tanaka, the Cubs' deal for Teruaki Sato and the White Sox's deal for Munetaka Murakami. Each of those totals is the money a team promised, and it is best read as a starting point. Behind a total can sit a fee owed to a club in Japan, pay that arrives years later, an exit the player controls or a team in a hurry to fill a hole. Read that way, the order of these deals says more about what each team promised than about what each player turned out to be worth.

Sources indicate that the 10 years are also less certain than they look, because Ohtani can leave for reasons that have nothing to do with how he plays. The Associated Press reports that the 2023 contract lets him opt out if Mark Walter stops being the controlling owner or if Andrew Friedman leaves as president of baseball operations. A change in the front office, rather than a slump, could end the decade early.

The record contract puts off most of its payments for a decade and leaves its length in the hands of the team's owner and its top baseball executive.

It has been revealed that the Dodgers bid the highest because signing Yamamoto served a strategy built around Shohei Ohtani. Ohtani helped recruit him, taking part with teammates Betts and Freeman in the meeting the Dodgers held with Yamamoto at their ballpark, according to the Los Angeles Times. "It was crucial to Shohei that this wasn't the one move we were gonna make, and I think anyone who has watched us operate over the years, we're trying to add really good players at every turn," Andrew Friedman, the Dodgers' president of baseball operations, told the Los Angeles Times in 2023. A team that had made that promise to its biggest star had little reason to stop bidding at the early estimate. When several teams compete for one player, the team with the most pressing plan usually decides the final price.

It has been revealed that so far, Yamamoto has pitched well enough to justify the Dodgers' spending. He earned the World Series MVP award in 2025, according to MLB.com. Paying well above the early estimate looks less like a mistake when the player is judged the most valuable performer in the World Series. The competition among teams raised what the Dodgers spent, but it did not make the deal a bad one.

The Dodgers paid extra to sign him, and so far he has pitched like the player they were bidding for.

The Yankees offered Masahiro Tanaka a sum that few pitchers of any background had received. Newly introduced York signed him for $155 million over seven years in 2014, according to ESPN. MLB.com reports that it was then the fifth-highest contract ever given to a pitcher, and only Kershaw, Verlander, Hernandez and Sabathia had been paid more. The Yankees put a pitcher who came directly from Nippon Professional Baseball, and who had never thrown a major league inning, in the same pay bracket as those four.

According to recent reports, newly introduced York spent more to get Tanaka than the figure that ranks him. The Yankees also paid Rakuten, the Japanese club that posted him, $20 million for the right to sign him, according to MLB.com. That payment bought permission alone, and none of it went to Tanaka. The Yankees' real bet on him was larger than his ranked total.

The Yankees made their case for Tanaka entirely on what he had done in Japan. In 2013, his last season with Rakuten, he went 24-0 with a 1.27 ERA, according to MLB.com. No team had seen him face major league hitters, so that season highlighted promise rather than proof. The Yankees still bid as if they would never get another chance. "That was our one shot, and we took it very seriously," Yankees general manager Brian Cashman said in 2014.

The Yankees paid to find out what Tanaka could do against major league hitters, not to buy a record he had already set there.

The Cubs took that risk because the departure of two regulars left them short of a bat. Ian Happ and Seiya Suzuki both left in free agency, according to CBS Sports, and together they were worth 7.8 wins above a replacement player in 2026. Sato is being asked to replace a large share of that production by himself. Chicago looks to use him in left or right field, even though he is known mainly as a first or third baseman, and his biggest adjustment will be the better pitching he faces. Sato's price reflects how badly Chicago needed a bat as much as it reflects the quality of his bat.

According to recent reports, toronto turned to Kaima Taira after several other starting pitchers it pursued signed elsewhere. The Blue Jays agreed to pay him $80 million over five years, with a $5 million bonus and an opt-out, according to ESPN. Tarik Skubal chose the Latest York Mets even though Toronto had reportedly offered him nine years and $420 million, according to USA TODAY. Two more starters the team went after also landed with other clubs, with Trevor Rogers joining the Chicago Cubs and Freddy Peralta joining the Baltimore Orioles. MLB's labor deal expires Dec. 1, and Toronto chose to fill its rotation before that deadline rather than keep searching. The team paid Taira's price out of need and failed pursuits as much as for anything he did on the mound.

Toronto is paying mostly for Taira's return to starting. After working strictly in relief as a closer in 2025, he moved back into a rotation in 2026 and led every qualified starter in Japan with a 1.36 ERA, according to USA TODAY. He has never thrown more than 150 innings in a season, yet Toronto will likely slot him third in its rotation in 2027. The Blue Jays are betting less on the ERA than on whether his arm can last through a full season of starts.

The opt-out puts much of the reward in Taira's hands. If he holds up as a starter, he can leave and look for a better deal before the five years run out. If his arm wears down, the choice to stay is his as well, and Toronto keeps the cost.

Need brought Taira to Toronto, and his own success could take him away.

Okamoto settles one position in an infield that is otherwise uncertain. Bo Bichette is a free agent who has not re-signed, CBC reports, so Toronto may still have a hole elsewhere in the infield. The team put its largest money that winter into pitching. In the same winter it committed $60 million to Okamoto, Toronto gave Dylan Cease a seven-year, $210 million deal. That made Okamoto a supporting piece for a team spending heavily to win now.

Toronto paid Okamoto's price as a team in a hurry to fill a gap, and the figure is no measure of how good he will turn out to be.

Recent findings suggest that tatsuya Imai earned a place among the largest MLB contracts signed by Japanese players, though near the low end of that group, when the Astros gave him three years and $54 million, according to ESPN. Those three years look like a firm commitment from Houston. But Imai can opt out after the 2026 season, MLB.com reports, and he can opt out again after 2027, which means he could become a free agent after one or two seasons. The $54 million shows what the Astros promised him. How long he stays is Imai's decision.

In a recent development, imai could take a short deal because his results have held up for years. He has posted a 2.18 ERA since 2023, according to MLB.com. That mark covers several seasons of work, so his success does not rest on a single strong year. His camp put him on the same level as Yoshinobu Yamamoto. "Certainly, he's done everything that Yamamoto's done in NPB," Scott Boras, Imai's agent, said. Even with that standing, Imai signed for three years instead of locking in his prime at a fixed rate. He kept the right to ask for a latest price soon. The short term reads as Imai's wager on himself rather than a sign that teams doubted him.

The Astros accepted a deal that could end early because they needed starting pitchers right away. Three Astros pitchers had Tommy John surgery in 2025, according to MLB.com. Pitchers usually miss more than a season after that operation, so the Astros faced the coming year with holes in their rotation. They also expect to lose Framber Valdez, a mainstay of that rotation, in free agency. A team that short of starters now gains more from one or two excellent seasons than from waiting for a longer commitment.

The Astros are guaranteed to pay Imai $54 million, but they carry the risk that his success will take him to another team before the three years are up.

According to recent reports, chicago has already received a full slugger's season from the first year of a short deal. By Sept. 25 of his rookie season, Murakami had hit 35 home runs, the Chicago Sun-Times reports, and only Jose Abreu and Ron Kittle had reached that mark as White Sox rookies. Murakami does most of his damage by pulling the ball toward right field, but 29% of his home runs have gone to center field or the left side. His power reaches more than one part of the park. One season of that production already makes a $34 million price look low.

Murakami came to Chicago straight from Japan's Nippon Professional Baseball, and one season later he is an vital hitter for a White Sox team chasing the Cleveland Guardians in the AL Central. His value is being tested in games that matter now, and the bargain depends on him staying at this level. "We know how impactful he can be when he's right and feeling good," White Sox manager Will Venable said, as reported by the Chicago Sun-Times. Chicago signed Murakami for only two seasons, and half of that time is nearly over. One poor season could erase the bargain.

Chicago got a historic return in the first year of the smallest of these deals, and only Murakami's second season can show whether he can repeat it.

Crypto exchange Binance has issued a "one-letter" security warning to crypto owners, urging them to carefully check website addresses before logging into their accounts. According to Binance, a fake site can be just one letter off.

A post on X by the crypto exchange pointed out that a small difference in a website URL, sometimes just one letter, can lead owners to visit fake websites impersonating legitimate platforms.

"Sometimes the biggest red flag is just one letter," Binance wrote.

The exchange advised users to double-check URLs before entering their login credentials. It also encouraged anyone uncertain about a website's authenticity to use Binance's official verification tool to confirm whether the URL belongs to the platform.

The Binance Verify platform allows crypto owners to stay safe from scammers, as they can enter a URL, email address, phone number, Telegram account, or social media account to check if the source is verified and officially from Binance.

Sources indicate that impersonation scams are quietly growing across the crypto space, with one of the most troubling tactics seen being the deepfake: lifelike, AI-generated impersonations of crypto executives and employees soliciting money on video calls that look and sound real enough to make anyone hesitate. The personas are fabricated, but the sophistication is genuine.

Every day, people are contacted by impersonators using the names, likenesses, and even job titles of crypto personnel, including Binance staff, to solicit investments or financial transactions via WhatsApp, Telegram, and other channels.

Binance stated that scammers prey on people's growing interest in investing and digital finance and on their trust, often masquerading as its employees or executives to exploit its credibility.

Sources indicate that with advances in AI and deepfake technology, they can create personas that look and sound real. Crypto owners are therefore urged to beware of unsolicited advice or "special opportunities" and to refrain from clicking on unknown links or URLs.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, XRP’s return below the psychologically notable $1 level hasn’t convinced every investor that it is time to buy the dip. Despite believing the payments-based token could eventually climb to a staggering $10, one trader is holding back. His cautious stance raises an interesting question: if XRP has such massive upside potential, why is he waiting on the sidelines?

  • It has been revealed that the startup remarked today that it successfully demonstrated an electrically heated Stirling generator in a controlled maritime setting in Washington state.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

by Alan Boyle on Nov 19, 2026 at 7:00 amNovember 19, 2026 at 8:01 am.

Zeno Power has hit a major milestone in its push to build nuclear batteries for underwater use.

It has been revealed that the startup remarked today that it successfully demonstrated an electrically heated Stirling generator in a controlled maritime setting in Washington state. The two-week demonstration produced electrical power outputs in excess of 20 watts, said Lindsey Boles, Zeno’s chief product officer.

“It’s a really massive step for us — just solidifying our expertise in how to design these, and then confirming our ability to translate that into operational hardware that meets or exceeds what our customers need,” Boles told GeekWire.

Zeno is developing the power system with support from the Department of Defense as a follow-up to an initial $7.5 million contract awarded in 2023. The generator uses a Stirling engine to convert heat into electricity by cycling gas through heating and cooling phases in a closed cylinder.

For the recent demonstration, the prototype device relied on an electric heating element. Future devices will instead rely on heat generated by the radioactive decay of strontium-90, a radioisotope that can be extracted from spent nuclear fuel.

Nuclear batteries have been in use for decades, primarily for space missions ranging from the Apollo moon shots to NASA’s Voyager spacecraft and Mars rovers. But the batteries being developed by Zeno Power promise to be at least four times more efficient than traditional radioisotope thermoelectric generators, Boles said.

Boles mentioned the non-radiological test exceeded expectations. “There’s a difference between a design that works on paper and hardware that works in the field,” she said in a news release. “This is the moment our team has been building toward: proof that this technology works outside the lab.”.

Long-lasting nuclear batteries could be used to power undersea sensor networks or recharge autonomous underwater vehicles. “There are a lot of applications, especially on the maritime front, that we really want electricity for,” Boles said. “And we really don’t need a ton of it. But we need it to be really reliable, and we need it to be long endurance, and we need it to be self-managed. … I think of it like a slow Tesla supercharger on the seabed.”.

Retired Navy Adm. John Richardson, former chief of naval operations and a member of Zeno’s board of directors, called the recent test an “notable step toward undersea superiority.”.

Sources indicate that “Protecting maritime infrastructure and powering distributed systems at sea requires energy; energy that lasts for years, not days or months,” Richardson said in a written statement. “As competition intensifies in contested domains, powered subsea systems will help keep us ahead. Zeno Power has steadily reduced risk, proven its technology, built a supply chain, and prepared to scale production.”.

Industry observers note that next year, Zeno Power plans to install a radioisotope heat source in its generator and test the system in a water tank under controlled laboratory conditions. If those tests are successful, Zeno will move forward with the first operational seabed deployment of its radioisotope-fueled maritime system later in 2027.

Recent findings suggest that the maritime battery isn’t Zeno’s only product. The company is also working on a nuclear-powered heater system for spacecraft, with a demonstration on the lunar surface planned as early as 2028. Zeno’s broader vision is to provide long-lasting, reliable power on the moon and Mars, and in extreme environments on Earth.

According to recent reports, since its founding in 2018, Zeno has secured $105 million in private capital and has brought in $60 million in contracts with the Pentagon and NASA. The organization has more than 95 employees at locations in Seattle, California and Washington, D.C., with the largest contingent working at its engineering headquarters in Seattle’s South Lake Union district.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • “I’m a long-term optimist, and I’ve been doing this for 30 years, but I see activity in the capital markets that reminds me of 2021,” stated Mina Faltas, founder and CEO of Washington Harbour Partners.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

When it comes to defense tech, it’s a FOMO-YOLO market, two prominent investors in the sector mentioned onstage this week at the Fortune 500 Innovation Forum in Detroit.

“I’m a long-term optimist, and I’ve been doing this for 30 years, but I see activity in the capital markets that reminds me of 2021,” stated Mina Faltas, founder and CEO of Washington Harbour Partners.

In a recent development, “There are a lot of latest entrants into the space. The death of SaaS and the disruption from AI has shifted capital into areas of deep tech, space, robotics, energy, and defense,” he said. “There’s folks deploying capital who aren’t experts in any one of those sectors. So, consequently, we can talk about a bubble.”.

In a recent development, the money has arrived fast. Venture capitalists put a record $37.9 billion into defense tech across 269 deals in the third quarter of 2026, up 117.5% from the prior quarter, according to PitchBook data cited by Fortune in its coverage of defense tech CEOs at the forum. Valuations have climbed with it: Early-stage defense startups have fetched 17 to 50 times revenue, Fortune reported this summer.

In a recent development, even the sector’s biggest winners are uneasy. Anduril cofounder Trae Stephens told Fortune in June that mid-stage defense startups trade at multiples that are “completely disconnected from reality.”.

Aidan Madigan-Curtis, a partner at venture firm Eclipse, described the mood bluntly.

Recent findings suggest that “There is a pretty big YOLO sentiment happening right now, essentially in physical tech investing,” Madigan-Curtis mentioned. “There are a lot of tourist investors who are excited about a person, a background, a theme … [and] maybe they’re most excited about who invested in the last round and the signal that that gives, versus a hardcore underwriting of a real set of capabilities that can truly pierce into a market.”.

That froth now meets a broader shock. Jensen Huang’s abrupt resignation as Nvidia CEO on Nov. 12, under pressure from the chipmaker’s board, has left the startup ecosystem primed for change and possible disruption.

AI startups are most exposed, but private capital markets more broadly are in flux, including the deep-tech bets now crowding into defense.

For startups, the harder test is selling to the government. It has long been a difficult market to crack, and the Pentagon, which has used the name Department of War as a secondary title since a 2025 executive order, is among the hardest. Part of the trouble is that government isn’t a monolithic customer, even if it looks like one.

“There’s a misconception that the Pentagon is this all-or-nothing type of customer,” mentioned Faltas. “It’s actually not. The building itself is … called the Pentagon. It’s got five corners, and each of those five corners needs to be engaged with, and educated with, and listened to … That requires a very focused ground game.”.

Georgia has promised more than any other school to keep its coach, and Smart is the one who decides whether the deal holds.

Shibburn’s page reveals that just $1 worth of SHIB has been burned over the past 24 hours, indicating a decrease in Shiba Inu’s token-burning activity.

The daily burn rate has dropped by 37.21% due to a burn of 303,294 SHIB worth just $1 over the last day.

The latest figure suggests that very little SHIB was destroyed during the reported period, although an increase in burn rate was seen on a weekly time frame.

157.31 million SHIB were burned in the last seven days, with the burn rate increasing by 113%; a different scenario presents itself on a 30-day basis, when the monthly burn rate fell 48.87% with 343.11 million SHIB burned.

Burns involve sending tokens to inaccessible wallet addresses, effectively taking them out of the available supply, with Shiba Inu advancing this course as 41.08% of its initial supply has now been erased.

A total of 410,845,365,512,059 SHIB has been burned in 21,978 transactions, according to Shibburn.

Shiba Inu fell to a fresh low of $0.00000337 as widespread selling picked up across the crypto market.

According to recent reports, at the time of writing, SHIB remains down 5.73% over the last 24 hours to $0.00000362. Just below SHIB's current price, a large buy wall has emerged, with Binance's spot order book revealing 17.92 trillion SHIB positioned at $0.00000361.

SHIB is exhibiting a strong accumulation of buy orders, which could signal a key support level as traders monitor buyers’ ability to soak up selling pressure.

A buy wall occurs when a lot of limit buy orders are stacked up around some price level and can show strong buying interest, providing temporary support if market participants are willing to fill those orders.

In a recent development, now, if the price of Shiba Inu goes lower, then the 17.92 trillion SHIB order concentration that was reported could be an important area to watch. If the orders get filled and remain there, they could help absorb some of the selling pressure.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • by Todd Bishop on Nov 19, 2026 at 9:54 amNovember 19, 2026 at 10:10 am.
  • Anthropic made its Nasdaq debut today in a record $81.3 billion initial public offering, with significant financial stakes for the Seattle area’s two tech giants.
  • For Amazon, the IPO is a paper windfall.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

by Todd Bishop on Nov 19, 2026 at 9:54 amNovember 19, 2026 at 10:10 am.

Anthropic made its Nasdaq debut today in a record $81.3 billion initial public offering, with significant financial stakes for the Seattle area’s two tech giants.

For Amazon, the IPO is a paper windfall. The company started putting money into Anthropic in 2023, about $18 billion in all. At the $83 IPO price, its stake was worth about $161 billion. With Anthropic opening at $111.50 a share, that number was closer to $216 billion. The stock has since dropped below $100, which put Amazon’s stake under $200 billion.

Beyond the value of the investment, Anthropic is a major customer for Amazon’s cloud platform. The Claude maker has committed to spend at least $110 billion on Amazon Web Services through 2036.

For Microsoft, it’s more complicated. The Redmond manufacturer agreed in late 2025 to invest up to $5 billion but hasn’t disclosed the size of its stake. Microsoft is buying $1 billion of Anthropic stock alongside the IPO, one of seven tech companies buying a combined $26 billion. Anthropic has committed to spend at least $47 billion on Microsoft’s Azure cloud through 2033.

But Microsoft is also pitching its own AI models against Anthropic’s, and it has been working to replace Anthropic’s models with OpenAI’s in some Copilot features, The Information reported this week.

Listing Anthropic’s compute partners on CNBC this morning, co-founder Daniela Amodei named Nvidia, Amazon, Google and Broadcom, but not Microsoft. Whether it was a slip or something more significant, it was an interesting omission.

A historic debut: The offering tops SpaceX’s $75 billion IPO in June, and it makes Anthropic the first standalone AI lab to go public, ahead of OpenAI.

The five-year-old firm was valued at about $1.5 trillion at the $83 IPO price, on a fully diluted basis that counts employee stock and other shares not yet issued. The stock opened at $111.50, valuing Anthropic at about $2 trillion on the same basis. It has since traded as low as about $95.

Speaking before the opening bell, CEO Dario Amodei mentioned Anthropic will slow the training and release of its AI models for as long as it takes to be confident they’re safe, and that going public only strengthens that resolve.

“We will not bend to either business nor political pressure,” he said.

In an interview with CNBC’s Andrew Ross Sorkin afterward, Amodei called the push and pull between growth and that kind of restraint “one of the central tensions at the heart of the company.”.

Anthropic is also a public benefit corporation, a structure that legally requires the manufacturer to balance shareholders’ interests with the public good.

What’s next: Both Seattle-area giants have hedged their bets. Microsoft owns about 24% of OpenAI, and Amazon put $50 billion into OpenAI earlier this year.

OpenAI, which confidentially filed for its own IPO in June, is still aiming to go public in 2027.

Anthropic’s co-founders and some of its biggest shareholders are barred from selling for up to a year under the IPO’s lock-up rules, and Amazon has said it expects a customary lock-up period.

Amazon will update the value of its Anthropic holdings in its fourth-quarter results, much of it through earnings, which means the paper windfall is likely to boost Amazon’s fourth-quarter profit even though it hasn’t sold a share.

Tech Report: Base Switches Off Flashblocks as Denim Goes Live: The Migration Risks Behind 200ms Blocks

📅 06 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1246 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Nulltx

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Base's Denim upgrade replaced Flashblocks with five canonical blocks per second.
  • Sources indicate that for about sixteen months, Base's fastest blocks were only promises.
  • Denim went live on Base mainnet on November 5, after activating on Sepolia on October 21.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

AI-assisted summary, reviewed by NullTX editors.

Base's Denim upgrade replaced Flashblocks with five canonical blocks per second. What that means for sequencers, RPC providers and smart contract developers is where the real story sits.

Sources indicate that for about sixteen months, Base's fastest blocks were only promises. Since November 5, they are the ledger itself.

Denim went live on Base mainnet on November 5, after activating on Sepolia on October 21.

According to the upgrade page, the chain now produces five complete canonical blocks every second instead of one every two seconds. Flashblocks, the preconfirmation layer that ran alongside the two-second blocks since July 2025, is retired.

According to recent reports, most coverage stopped at the speed figure. The sharper question is what separates a canonical block from a preconfirmation, because that gap decides what breaks and what improves for anyone building on the chain.

Those updates were the sequencer's early word on what the next block would contain. They were previews of pending state, and nothing in them had its own hash, state root or receipts until the two-second block was sealed. Developers therefore had to keep an early execution result mentally separate from a settled transaction.

According to recent reports, denim turns the 200ms unit into the real thing. Under Base's 200ms Native Blocks specification, every block carries its own number, hash, state root, receipts and forkchoice updates, and moves through the unsafe, safe and finalized stages like any other block.

It has been revealed that the sequencer's job gets heavier and stricter. Instead of streaming fragments of a larger block, it has to build and execute a full block for every 200ms slot. The header keeps its timestamp in whole seconds, so Denim adds a metadata transaction, the BaseTime deposit, placed second in every block. It supplies the sub-second portion: 0, 200, 400, 600 or 800 milliseconds.

According to recent reports, timing rules are tight. Slots can't be skipped, and each block's full timestamp must land exactly 200ms after its parent's. That timestamp comes from a schedule tied to the Denim activation and the block number, not from the sequencer's clock, so wall-clock time only determines when a build begins. Once execution finishes, the client rejects any block that breaks the 200ms progression.

This removes a layer of ambiguity. A preconfirmation was only as strong as the sequencer's word, while a canonical block can be validated, replayed and challenged by any node running the same derivation rules.

App developers face the biggest practical shift. Flashblocks streams ended at activation, so anything built on newFlashblocks, pendingLogs or the pending block tag has to move to canonical subscriptions like newHeads and logs. The migration guide lists the API changes required.

Recent findings suggest that the seconds-based timestamp field stays as it was for compatibility. Block, header, transaction, log and receipt responses now include optional millisecond fields, timestampMs and blockTimestampMs, derived from authenticated BaseTime data. They are left out when that data has been pruned or is unavailable. One tooling detail deserves attention: the spec warns that the plain Alloy AnyRpcHeader type drops unknown fields, so anyone who needs millisecond timestamps must use a different type.

Node providers will see heavier traffic too. Dwellir's analysis notes that any service doing work on every block now does it ten times as often. Five fetches a second replace one every two seconds. Denim improves latency without adding capacity, so infrastructure bills are likely to climb.

It has been revealed that finality hasn't gone away either. Faster production doesn't erase the confirmation policy an application picks, and each 200ms block still passes through the same unsafe, safe and finalized stages. Bridges and exchanges that wait for a specific stage before crediting funds may need to rethink how many blocks they wait for, since a block count no longer equals the same stretch of time.

In a recent development, this is the area that deserves the most urgent attention. Base's spec warns that block.number now advances ten times faster in real time, while block.timestamp still ticks in whole seconds. A contract that treats a block count as a duration will see that duration collapse to a tenth of what its authors intended.

In a recent development, the affected patterns are common ones. Timelocks and cooldowns measured in blocks expire in a tenth of the time. Vesting and emission schedules run ten times faster. Per-block rate limits reset five times a second instead of once every two seconds, which lifts the effective per-second limit tenfold. Governance voting windows set in blocks shrink the same way. Uniswap V3-style TWAP oracles stay accurate, but a fixed observation cardinality now covers less wall-clock history, so long lookbacks can revert sooner.

Recent findings suggest that contracts built on block.timestamp are unaffected. Where a block count can be adjusted through governance, teams initiative to divide it by ten. Where it is hardcoded into an immutable contract, the spec says it can't be retuned after activation, which leaves migration as the only fix. Denim also tightens transfer rules for Base's B20 token standard, and transfers to a token's own address now revert.

The coming weeks will show how much of this stays theoretical. Three things are worth tracking: whether any immutable contract with block-count logic misbehaves, how providers cope with the jump in per-block requests, and whether apps built around Flashblocks have fully moved over.

Recent findings suggest that denim looks like a cleaner design than the layer it replaced. A preview mechanism gives way to a block anyone can verify, and developers pay for it with a real migration. Speed grabbed the headlines, but the lasting change is that Base's sub-second confirmations now stand on the same footing as the chain's ordinary blocks.

‘Voluntary, revocable’: The fine print behind Anthropic founders’ $112 billion giving pledge

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (873 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Fortune

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Anthropic’s record-setting IPO may have created one of the largest pools of charitable capital ever assembled.
  • The Claude maker priced 980 million shares at $83 on Nov.
  • Sources indicate that on Monday, as the Nasdaq jumped roughly 6% on Jensen Huang’s reinstatement as Nvidia CEO, Anthropic went the other way.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Anthropic’s record-setting IPO may have created one of the largest pools of charitable capital ever assembled. Its size depends on a stock that has swung more than $30 a share in its first three sessions.

The Claude maker priced 980 million shares at $83 on Nov. 18, above its marketed range of $70 to $78, raising a record $81.3 billion and valuing the company at about $1.5 trillion on a fully diluted basis. The stock opened at $111.50 on Nov. 19, closed its first day at $97.17, then fell 8.5% to $88.91 on Friday.

Sources indicate that on Monday, as the Nasdaq jumped roughly 6% on Jensen Huang’s reinstatement as Nvidia CEO, Anthropic went the other way. Shares closed down 1.4% at $87.64, about 5.6% above the IPO price.

TechCrunch estimated Thursday that Anthropic’s charitable commitments could be worth about $156 billion at roughly $95 a share, where the stock traded early in its debut. The figure combines the firm’s Public Benefit Fund, employees’ pledged shares, and Anthropic’s match on those pledges.

According to recent reports, because all three are paid in stock, the total moves with the share price. At Monday’s close, the same math yields about $144 billion, down $12 billion from Thursday. At the $83 IPO price, it would be roughly $136 billion.

Recent findings suggest that even the lower figures are enormous. By TechCrunch’s count, Americans gave $617 billion to charity in all of 2025, so Monday’s value equals nearly a quarter of a year of U.S. giving.

Recent findings suggest that the largest piece is the Anthropic Public Benefit Fund, a wholly owned LLC the organization announced in October. Anthropic’s S-1 filing shows it contributed 846.8 million shares to the fund, 5% of fully diluted shares as of June 30, a stake worth about $74 billion at Monday’s close.

The fund can grow. Anthropic notes its board may add another 2% of the organization for every 50% increase in value above a set baseline; TechCrunch reported that baseline is the $83 IPO price, which would put the next trigger near $124.50 a share. The company mentioned it will disclose more about the fund’s governance and valuation milestones in the coming months, and it has not declared a distribution timetable.

The second channel is employees. About half of Anthropic’s staff take part in its equity donation program, and the company matches pledged shares 3-for-1 for longer-tenured employees and 1-for-1 for newer ones, according to strategy documents filed with the S-1. TechCrunch estimated employees have pledged about $23 billion in stock, which would draw roughly $53 billion in matches at $95 a share.

It has been revealed that that money is closer to moving, but not yet. Most holders face a lockup of up to 180 days, which could end sooner after first-quarter 2027 results, and many employees cannot sell or gift most of their shares until next spring, the Associated Press reported. Shares parked in donor-advised funds, which have no annual payout requirement, may take even longer to reach working charities.

According to recent reports, the third channel is the least certain. Anthropic’s seven cofounders have pledged to give away 80% of their personal equity, a commitment the AP valued at $112 billion at the IPO price. But the S-1 describes the pledges as “voluntary, revocable expressions” of intent that are not legally binding, and timing, amounts, and recipients remain undecided. TechCrunch’s $156 billion estimate excludes them.

Recent findings suggest that the cofounders also face the longest lockup: up to 365 days from the Nov. 18 prospectus, or earlier after third-quarter 2027 results, with a portion of their shares eligible for release around the 180-day mark.

It has been revealed that some money is already committed. Earlier this month, Anthropic pledged $50 million to a donor-advised fund at the San Francisco Foundation for Bay Area nonprofits through 2027. The first $500,000 went to the SF-Marin Food Bank, GLIDE, the Interfaith Winter Shelter, and the San Francisco Firefighters Local 798 Toy Program, and a organization spokesperson told TechCrunch the gift did not come from the Public Benefit Fund.

Anthropic has also committed $200 million to study and address AI’s effects on the labor market. In June, it pledged $150 million to Claude Corps, a fellowship that places early-career workers at nonprofits to help them use AI.

It has been revealed that separately, Anthropic has given $40 million this year to Public First Action, a bipartisan group that advocates for AI safeguards. That is policy spending, not charity, and Anthropic states it will not use equity held by the Public Benefit Fund for lobbying or political giving.

According to recent reports, the next test for the share price comes Dec. 15, when up to 303 million shares can become eligible for sale under the prospectus’s lockup schedule, followed by another 303 million on Jan. 5. For charities, the date that matters more is spring 2027, when employee pledges and the firm’s matches can start to move.

In a recent development, until then, Anthropic’s philanthropic promise is marked to market every trading day. A return to the $115 debut high would lift TechCrunch’s measure to nearly $190 billion; a slide below $83 would take it under $136 billion.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • by Lisa Stiffler on Nov 19, 2026 at 10:07 amNovember 24, 2026 at 9:53 am.
  • Editor’s note: This series profiles five Seattle-area “Uncommon Thinkers,” who will be recognized Dec.
  • Andrew Redd‘s career path creates a tidy narrative: grow up in Seattle steeped in aviation and maritime culture, study mechanical engineering and aerospace, work at SpaceX, then launch an offshore geothermal energy startup.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

by Lisa Stiffler on Nov 19, 2026 at 10:07 amNovember 24, 2026 at 9:53 am.

Editor’s note: This series profiles five Seattle-area “Uncommon Thinkers,” who will be recognized Dec. 10 at the GeekWire Gala in partnership with Greater Seattle Partners.

Andrew Redd‘s career path creates a tidy narrative: grow up in Seattle steeped in aviation and maritime culture, study mechanical engineering and aerospace, work at SpaceX, then launch an offshore geothermal energy startup.

The dots connect, but the picture they form is anything but ordinary: bold in vision, fast in execution and enormous in potential.

Redd has next-level ambition, and he’s directing it at solving one of the world’s biggest and most urgent problems — adding renewable, massively scalable energy that can outcompete fossil fuels and reach the grid quickly enough to make a difference in the race against climate change.

Recent findings suggest that underwater geothermal energy has never been tapped in a significant way, but to Redd, the idea was irresistible. “It checks all of the boxes for our perfect future energy source,” he said.

According to recent reports, he founded Endurance Energy on the north shore of Seattle’s Lake Union in January 2025, and this September the team oversaw its fifth deep-sea deployment. At a site 300 miles off the Oregon coast, its prototype system generated more electricity than it consumed. The startup has raised $63 million from investors and has roughly three dozen employees.

Nate Bek, a principal at Ascend, praised Redd’s ability to attract “brilliant” talent in pursuit of his goal. The Seattle venture firm is one of the startup’s early backers.

“I’ve been deeply inspired by what [Redd]’s building at Endurance and haven’t shut up about it since the day we met,” Bek remarked. “He somehow makes powering the world from the bottom of the ocean feel inevitable, all while remaining remarkably measured and transparent about the progress.”.

Sources indicate that for Redd, studying engineering and aerospace in college was so clear-cut that it wasn’t a choice at all. Growing up around Boeing, seaplanes, the Museum of Flight and the Pacific Northwest’s rich maritime industry naturally pointed him toward those sectors. He wanted a degree as expansive as his influences.

Sources indicate that “I didn’t really want to have to choose whether it was going to be boats or space travel or airplanes,” he mentioned. “I just wanted to be able to do anything — keep the world as wide open as possible.”.

It has been revealed that after graduating from Princeton University, Redd worked at Neuralink, an Elon Musk company developing technology that lets the brain communicate directly with computers. A year later, in 2021, he moved to Musk’s rocket company, SpaceX.

That was another no-duh decision, as Redd viewed it.

“I saw SpaceX as really the place to be, where early-career people are given the most amount of resources and responsibility, and that felt like the fastest way to learn and the most engaging possible scenario to be in,” Redd said. “I wanted to be tossed into something that was a little bit crazy.”.

According to recent reports, redd joined as SpaceX was starting to build its first orbital Starship rockets. The program brought together passionate young people and experienced SpaceX engineers who served as mentors. Wild ideas were entertained and explored. Everyone was committed to the mission. It was just the experience Redd wanted, and he planned to stick around for seven to 10 years.

Then artificial intelligence started booming.

In a recent development, in 2024, the build-out of sprawling, energy-hungry data centers for AI was accelerating with no end in sight. At the same time, efforts to electrify transportation, heating and cooling were driving up demand for power. Redd saw these trends sparking a surge in new natural gas generation, locking in decades of carbon emissions.

According to recent reports, he wanted to find a better way. He went into engineering mode, focusing on all the essential criteria for an energy source: it had to be clean, not dependent on intermittent sun or wind, capable of producing massive amounts of energy, readily deployable, subject to fewer regulatory hurdles than something like nuclear, economically competitive, and scalable.

Redd recognized the tremendous heat contained under Earth’s surface as a terrific source for renewable energy and realized that most of the world’s active volcanoes are offshore. The unknown was whether the rocky ocean floor would be suitable for geothermal wells, so he did some research and found publications from geology experts who mentioned the conditions would be “perfect.”.

“You can tell,” he said, “when there’s a moment in time that you need to go and reach out and grab something, and that was really my impression — if I didn’t start this now, this would never come into existence, or wouldn’t come into existence soon enough to make a meaningful impact.”.

In launching Endurance, Redd was intentional about the culture he wanted to create. He was aiming for a multidisciplinary group of mission-driven employees eager to collaborate and learn from each other: top talent that would attract more of the same and make Endurance a place people were excited to work.

“The hardest part of an early-stage startup is recruiting,” Redd remarked, “especially if you’re a first-time founder.”.

The startup employs about a dozen SpaceX alumni, plus employees from the fusion tech giant Helion Energy and the aerospace venture Blue Origin.

Industry observers note that A strong team is key to Endurance’s success. That’s because, enthusiasm and passion aside, the startup faces steep engineering and economic challenges. The technology must withstand high pressure, corrosive conditions and mineral scaling inside devices, and seafloor machinery could be costly to repair. The systems will need expensive subsea cables to carry power to shore over potentially long distances. It’s a heavy lift.

While the September sea trial didn’t go perfectly, Redd is happy with the results. The company landed its 3-ton power plant on the seafloor near a natural vent and produced net energy from it — albeit for only 8.7 seconds. Technical difficulties and a power-cable failure cut the dive short.

Sources indicate that team members successfully operated the system remotely from Seattle through a fiber-optic network running along the seabed. Redd noted he’s grateful for access to the network, which is part of the National Science Foundation’s Regional Cabled Array and operated by the University of Washington.

Endurance engineers also drilled what they called the world’s first subsea geothermal well at a site about 5,000 feet below the ocean’s surface. The 2-inch-wide, 52-foot-deep well delivered hydrothermal fluid, but the flow was too restricted to run the power plant, sending the team to the natural vent.

Redd said there’s a lot of work ahead, but the team “made huge strides” in learning and in reducing the project’s risks.

Recent findings suggest that the tech giant now is developing Leopard, its 2-megawatt generator. After testing the technology at the research site off the Oregon coast, Endurance aims to deliver power from a Leopard system in Tonga next year as its first commercial project. Subsea geothermal energy could ultimately reduce the island nation’s reliance on imported diesel and put the startup one step closer to its objective of generating terawatts of planet-friendly energy.

Industry observers note that “This was always the end goal,” Redd noted. “Create something that is highly meaningful for the world.”.

Editor’s Note: Nate Bek of Ascend is a former GeekWire reporter.

A buy wall occurs when a large volume of buy orders is concentrated around a particular price level on an exchange's order book. Such an order cluster can indicate that traders are prepared to purchase an asset at that price, potentially slowing further declines if selling pressure meets sufficient demand.

Industry observers note that in Cardano's case, the 3.96 million ADA order cluster that occurred below the $0.14 level revealed a notable level of buying interest. 💡 Key Takeaways

  • In a recent development, since then, interest in women’s football has grown significantly.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that the 1999 FIFA Women’s World Cup final was a watershed moment for women’s football, with record-breaking attendance and viewership numbers. More than 40 million people in North America tuned in to watch the U.S. beat China 5–4 on penalties in the final. Among them was ­ Canadian Nikki Doucet, then a student and college basketball player at St. Francis Xavier University. “That was the first time I’d seen women’s team sports on TV, and I remember feeling so excited,” she indicates.

In a recent development, since then, interest in women’s football has grown significantly. Its global fan base is projected to surpass 800 million by 2030, according to Nielsen Sports, while Fifpro expects the sport to be a $1 billion industry by 2027—a 72% increase from 2024.

Now CEO of Women’s Super League Football, the firm responsible for operating the top two English women’s leagues (WSL and WSL2), Doucet is at the sharp end of that opportunity. England has become a commercial force in women’s football: Eight of the world’s 15 highest-revenue clubs are in the WSL, according to Deloitte, and Doucet believes the league is well-positioned to capture a “significant portion” of the potential $1 billion the sport is predicted to generate.

According to recent reports, american entrepreneurs and investment groups are taking note. The success of the Women’s National Basketball Association—now an $850 million franchise—and the soaring valuations of teams in the National Women’s Soccer League (league leaders Gotham FC were recently valued at $350 million) underlines the potential. And many see an opportunity to buy in at an early stage in the commercial development of the sport in Europe.

Recent findings suggest that U.S. businesswoman Michele Kang bought the London City Lionesses in 2023, leading the club to its 2025 WSL promotion. Other notable investors include Reddit cofounder Alexis Ohanian, who holds a minority stake in Chelsea FC Women, and U.S. financier Marc Zahr, an investor in Aston Villa Women.U.S. businesswoman Michele Kang bought the London City Lionesses in 2023, leading the club to its 2025 WSL promotion. Other notable investors include Reddit cofounder Alexis Ohanian, who holds a minority stake in Chelsea FC Women, and U.S. financier Marc Zahr, an investor in Aston Villa Women.

Speaking at the WSL’s Latest Playbook ­ summit earlier this year, one investor argued that European women’s football represented the “best opportunity in sport,” on a risk-adjusted basis.

It has been revealed that “I think of my career as if I’m still an athlete. I practice for every board meeting in the same way that I used to train for a game. Your practice should be so hard, the game is easy.”.

In a recent development, “The enterprise value of these clubs is 100% going up,” Doucet, a former investment banker at Citi, indicates. “The question is, do you have owners that want to participate in this asset class of women’s football? There are different tradeoffs versus men’s football and different risk factors because we’re in a different stage of development.”.

Doucet’s challenge is turning rising global interest in the women’s game into regular paying customers. There was a surge in interest following the England Lionesses’ UEFA Women’s Euro 2022 victory: Average attendance at WSL matches tripled to 5,616 the following season. But last year, median attendance was 3,236—and it remains heavily concentrated in a few clubs.

In a recent development, “This isn’t a manufacturing challenge. This is a marketing and revenue challenge,” Doucet says. The league invested in a rebrand of both the WSL and WSL2 ahead of the newly expanded league this season, and clubs are also investing more. In April, WSL team Brighton revealed intends to build Europe’s first purpose- built women’s football stadium at an estimated cost of more than £75 million ($99 million).

“You have to invest in building the foundations that will generate long- term returns, but they might take time until you actually see the results,” Doucet says. “That’s the constant tradeoff.”.

Industry observers note that the underlying economics also remain fragile. Despite the high revenues, only four of the 14 clubs in the WSL recorded a profit (two clubs did not publish detailed financial data). The league itself, which is co-owned by the participating clubs, posted an operating loss of £8.2 million ($10.8 million) for the year ending July 2025.

According to recent reports, doucet attributes much of the loss to one-off costs associated with becoming an independent business, including establishing its own HR, finance, legal, and regulatory teams. The WSL and WSL2 formally split from the Football Association (FA) in 2024, shortly after Doucet joined the organization. She notes the league is now profitable, although declined to share the financial details.

“We’re in a transition phase, which is probably a little bit messy. The challenge is going from big structural moments, like a World Cup, to building a weekly fan habit around women’s professional football,” Doucet states.

The majority of the league’s revenues so far have come from broadcast rights and commercial partnerships. The league generated £8.7 million ($11.5 million) from Sky and the BBC in 2025, and the league counts Doucet’s former employer Nike, in addition to Airbnb, Apple, and ­ Barclays, among its growing list of sponsors.

It has been revealed that the opportunities for commercial sponsors are different from those in the men’s sport, Doucet notes. “We have a different audience that really values companies that are investing in women’s football,” she says. “They’re very brand loyal, and they show much deeper engagement.”.

Doucet’s current priority is improving the spectacle on the pitch. “The fans want to watch the best players, and they want to watch a competition that’s exciting and has jeopardy,” she says. Good progress has been made in this area, too. The London City Lionesses signed three-time Ballon d’Or winner Alexia Putellas from Barcelona this summer, and the WSL had the highest representation of players at last year’s Women’s Euro tournament of any league.

In a recent development, ensuring the WSL’s longevity is a responsibility Doucet is acutely aware of. “This isn’t a five-year business,” she says. “This is a generational asset.” She remains optimistic about what lies ahead. Doucet adds: “We’re in an early stage, so the potential is almost completely untapped—you don’t know how big it could be.”.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • by Nikesh Parekh on Nov 19, 2026 at 12:41 pmNovember 19, 2026 at 12:41 pm.
  • It has been revealed that nikesh (Niki) Parekh is a former Microsoft GM who is now CEO of Seattle-based AI talent recruiting startup Provn.
  • Tens of thousands of Microsoft employees have a massive decision to make in the next few weeks: take the company’s offer to leave, or stay and take their chances.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

by Nikesh Parekh on Nov 19, 2026 at 12:41 pmNovember 19, 2026 at 12:41 pm.

It has been revealed that nikesh (Niki) Parekh is a former Microsoft GM who is now CEO of Seattle-based AI talent recruiting startup Provn. This is the fourth post in his series on “Life after Big Tech,” including the Seattle startup guide, laid off at 50 and VC funding is changing dramatically.

Tens of thousands of Microsoft employees have a massive decision to make in the next few weeks: take the company’s offer to leave, or stay and take their chances.

According to recent reports, microsoft chief people officer Amy Coleman revealed the initiative in a memo on Oct. 26: a Voluntary Exit Offer (VEO) for about 60,000 employees at level 70 and below, which includes general managers and some vice presidents, in the U.S., Canada, the U.K. and India. That’s roughly 27% of Microsoft’s 223,000 people. The firm expects 3,000 or fewer of them to accept.

Microsoft states the terms match its standard severance: base pay tied to level and tenure, continued stock vesting, a period of health coverage and career transition help. The severance package varies greatly based on the seniority or level of the employee and the number of years of service. Employees have until early December to decide and would leave by the end of the year.

The offer follows the Voluntary Retirement Program (VRP) that Microsoft extended to about 8,750 U.S. employees in April. About 30% of them, or roughly 2,600 people, took that offer.

Industry observers note that all of this comes as Microsoft cuts jobs and changes the kinds of roles it hires for, while pouring money into AI infrastructure and data centers. At the same time, AI is reshaping the broader workforce, flattening management layers and changing what employers look for in new hires.

The worry I hear most is whether more layoffs are waiting on the other side. So the real choice is whether you leave on your own terms or let the tech giant decide for you.

I hear two questions from Microsoft employees thinking about the VEO: How easily can I get another job, and how hard is it to start a company right now?

Harder than you think, and it depends a lot on who you are. We are in the “low hire, low fire” economy.

There is MASSIVE demand for AI-native builders — product managers, data scientists and engineers — as companies adapt products to deal with AI. Companies are also in the process of adopting AI.

One of the fastest-growing tech roles is the “Forward Deployed Engineer,” who implements AI solutions at customers. Security is also job #1 as models and agents get smarter and better at hacking legacy systems.

According to recent reports, but it is very hard to be seen by recruiters and hiring managers right now. Candidates are using AI to customize their resumes to each job and using AI agents to apply, sending out 100 to 200 job applications per day. Recruiters are inundated with resumes and job applications, many of which are fake or inappropriate for the role.

It is critical to leverage your network in the job search, which can be hard if you have spent your entire career within one tech giant.

Hiring managers have changed what they look for, too. AI fluency is becoming table stakes. The “process” of how you build/sell/market with AI is more crucial than what you build. Candidates are expected to show prototypes and proof of how they use AI tools every day.

Sources indicate that the jobs themselves are changing. A friend told me last month that he wanted an engineering manager role. There are fewer manager roles in the market now.

AI has driven a reduction in management layers and a general flattening of organizations. The engineering team at a small AI organization today is a CTO and a group of strong individual contributors. It is normal for managers to have 10 to 30 direct reports now, versus five to 10 in the pre-AI era.

Product management, program management and design teams are shrinking, as well, as AI automates certain jobs.

Hiring managers may view spending your whole career at Microsoft as a yellow flag. Microsoft is an iconic but unusual firm. Almost no one else sells to and services customers the way Microsoft does, with an account executive inside nearly every large enterprise in the world.

The skills that get you promoted in Redmond don’t always carry over to a 500- to 5,000-person software tech giant.

It has never been easier to build a product, and it has rarely been harder to fund a manufacturer.

Industry observers note that software is cheap to build now. A product leader and an engineer using AI tools can ship in weeks what used to take a team a year.

It has been revealed that this cuts both ways for startups. Every good idea attracts a dozen competitors within months, and the big platforms will copy anything that works.

The true strength of a startup today is the ability to grow revenue quickly and establish leadership in a beachhead market. The sales, marketing, product-led growth and distribution strategies are becoming the most critical parts of the business.

The bar for venture funding is extremely high. Jason Lemkin of SaaStr recently shared data from ICONIQ showing that top “AI forward” startups under $10 million in annual recurring revenue are growing 900% a year at the median.

One venture investor told me they advise their portfolio companies that if they aren’t on track for a $10 million run rate within two years, they won’t raise another round. Last week I spoke with an investor who owns part of a business with $4 million in revenue, growing 100% a year and losing $1 million, and it can’t raise.

There are three fundraising paths.

1) Think VERY significant, raise a lot and grow fast enough to justify it. Build an incredible team pursuing an ambitious idea. Raise a large round based on the promise of becoming the next Anthropic, OpenAI or legal AI startup Harvey. Many of the most interesting companies are not software or AI-related, but are “deep tech” companies in defense, robotics, energy and biotech.

It has been revealed that 2) Raise a moderate amount of money from angels, family offices and nontraditional funds to build a business that has the ability to be profitable on one round of financing. You can control your destiny by building a manufacturer that doesn’t rely on the venture capital funding market.

Sources indicate that 3) Bootstrap and build a business that you own. Fund it yourself, grow it with revenue and get to profitability.

The question that most people are NOT asking is: What do I really want?

Before December, block out an afternoon and think about the last time you were happy at work.

There are many frameworks for figuring out what you want in your career and life in general. I’m a fan of the Four Elements exercise. Write down three times in your career when you felt energized and effective. From those, work out what gives you energy, where you have the most impact, what culture you do best in and what your constraints are: money, kids, aging parents and how many more years you want to work.

On LinkedIn, I have seen examples of Microsoft employees taking the VEO to start their own businesses in property management, buy car washes, take time to recharge, spend time with family and travel.

Industry observers note that other employees are starting the job search in earnest but not taking the VEO. Many others are just getting back to work and doubling down on Microsoft.

In a recent development, whichever way you go, start now. Start by aligning on your priorities and what you want from your career. If you stay, use the next year to build your skills with AI and to grow a network outside Redmond. If you leave to build something, decide early which of the three funding paths you’re on, because that choice shapes everything that follows.

The people I’ve watched land well after Substantial Tech had one thing in common: they knew what they wanted before they walked out the door, whether that was a newly introduced role, a firm of their own or a year with their family.

#190612. Loopscale Pauses Protocol After kySOL Collateral Was Priced as zBTC in a 4,597 SOL Loan

📅 07 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1311 w)
