#190590. Breaking: Public Markets Are Frequently Wrong. The SaaSpocalypse Demonstrates Us Why

📅 19 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (965 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Crunchbase ↗ Open Full Page

Breaking: Public Markets Are Frequently Wrong. The SaaSpocalypse Demonstrates Us Why

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (965 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Crunchbase

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Panics and pile-ons are a familiar pattern in the public markets, with a herd mentality wiping value from companies in an instant.
  • According to recent reports, we have seen this play out with AI’s impact on software companies and the supposed end of the Software as a Service business model.
  • The SaaSpocalypse didn’t reveal the end of software.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Panics and pile-ons are a familiar pattern in the public markets, with a herd mentality wiping value from companies in an instant. Trading can swiftly become a barometer of emotions, rather than a well-informed gauge of value.

According to recent reports, we have seen this play out with AI’s impact on software companies and the supposed end of the Software as a Service business model. The doom-laden talk of the SaaSpocalypse was noise, with little signal, and most traders were initially unable to distinguish between a manufacturer that will thrive in the AI age and one that will be decimated by it.

The SaaSpocalypse didn’t reveal the end of software. It revealed the limits of public markets in judging its value.

This pattern erodes trust in the public markets. For companies, being publicly owned may no longer be appealing, and founders considering an exit may not view an initial public offering as the ultimate goal.

In a recent development, the markets have struggled to keep up with the tech advances of the AI era and judge their impact on incumbent companies. Sometimes they underreacted and ignored these developments, and other times they overreacted and panicked.

According to recent reports, when OpenAI rolled out ChatGPT to the public in November 2022, Alphabet stock was punished even though later Google emerged as a clear winner with generative AI. And with SaaS, the markets were slow to respond to the advent of generative and agentic AI through to the end of 2025.

The market capitalization of enterprise software companies continued to rise through this period, until January 2026 when all hell broke loose. The launch of Claude Cowork triggered a panic, especially when additional plug-ins were announced later that month that targeted specific workflows for enterprise support functions such as HR and legal.

According to recent reports, from there, valuations went into a tailspin, with traders treating software companies indiscriminately. Over two days, an estimated $285 billion of market capitalization was wiped from software, data analytics and financial tech companies, and by April the benchmark cloud software index — the BVP Nasdaq Emerging Cloud Index —  had dropped by 31% since the start of the year.

As an investor in software over many decades, I have seen this pattern many times before. AI does not mean the end of software companies. Rather, AI has driven a shift in how software is built, where user growth will come from — primarily agents rather than humans — and in the sources of defensible competitive advantage. This was always going to benefit some companies, like those deeply embedded into their customers’ core business processes, and harm others.

Sources indicate that there were predictions of the death of SaaS, but this is the hype cycle pattern that always plays out when newly introduced technology emerges: a surge of excitement, then a correction, then productivity. In the short term, the markets overestimated the harm AI would inflict on the software sector as a whole.

That is now being corrected as the markets start to realize which companies benefit from AI and which are threatened by it. At the end of October, the cloud software index was up by 26% since the start of the year and by a massive 83% since its nadir in April.

At my firm, Oxx, we never believed in the SaaSpocalypse, and the markets have recovered from this turmoil. The recovery is bifurcated with some sub sectors, like cybersecurity and data and analytics, faring well while others, like workflow management, have fallen back.

In cybersecurity, a great example is CrowdStrike, whose share price dropped by 27% in early 2026 but was up 114% between the start of the year and the end of October.

The knee-jerk reactions to the latest developments with AI, however, are not just temporary market sentiment. They are part of a broader shift that has occurred since the late 1990s and accelerated in 2002 when the Sarbanes-Oxley Act was introduced to improve investor protections in the wake of the dot com crash.

It produced the unintended consequence of driving firm ownership from public to private markets. While the number of public companies in the U.S. has halved, private markets have grown dramatically in recent years. This is where much of the smart money can be found, along with a more accurate, and patient, assessment of software companies’ value.

The panic over the SaaSpocalypse has shown that the public markets aren’t an accurate reflection of the intrinsic value of many software companies. This disconnect may be causing a systematic mispricing of private firm transactions — multiple transactions which had been in process early this year fell away in the wake of the false signals which came from public markets. This needs to be addressed. At the moment, few people recognize there’s a problem with the pricing function of public markets, and the first step to solving this issue is to recognize there is actually a problem.

Richard Anton is the co-founder and general partner of Oxx, a specialist software investor backing European founders on a mission to transform their industries with AI at the moment they’re readying to scale.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • According to recent reports, it’s happened hundreds of times.
  • Then I have to explain that none of those documents will reduce their tax bill or protect their assets from future lawsuits or creditors.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Opinions expressed by Entrepreneur contributors are their own.

According to recent reports, it’s happened hundreds of times. A business owner shows up at my office, in the middle of selling their company, and tells me, “Don’t worry, my estate strategy is all done: I have a revocable living trust, will, powers of attorney, and health care directives, and my lawyer told me years ago that I was all set.”.

Then I have to explain that none of those documents will reduce their tax bill or protect their assets from future lawsuits or creditors. A revocable trust avoids probate. That is all it does.

The planning that actually changes the outcome of an exit lives primarily in three strategies that have been authorized by the Tax Code for decades, and every one of them should be considered well in advance of marketing the tech giant for sale.

The Tax Code imposes a federal estate tax at death equal to 40% to the extent your reported net worth — including your business, real estate and other illiquid assets — exceeds the federal estate tax exemption (right now $15 million per person for 2026).

In addition, some states impose their own inheritance tax or estate tax, which can result in a combined rate ranging from 40-75%. States oftentimes have very low and costly exemption limits, many starting at $1-2M.

Recent findings suggest that the government expects a cash payment within nine months after death. Although some estates heavily concentrated in businesses or illiquid assets can qualify for installment payments, the IRS requires liens and reporting — so you are effectively putting your spouse and children in business with the IRS as their de facto partner.

The easy fix is to take action before your manufacturer jumps in value. Specifically, you should transfer all or a portion of your business shares to an irrevocable gift trust for your spouse and/or children while the company is still private and appraisable at a defensibly low discounted value (allowing you to transfer the shares within the $15 million gift tax limit).

Properly done, every dollar of appreciation on your business shares happens outside your estate. In addition, the assets inside the trust are protected from future personal lawsuits. These benefits can continue indefinitely for the benefit of your heirs.

It has been revealed that most business owners balk at the word “irrevocable” when considering this planning. However, so-called “optimized” irrevocable gift trusts can let you keep far more control than you might expect. For example, you can:.

Sources indicate that suppose you own a company and expect to sell the company for $30 million in 18 months. Moving 40% of the shares into a trust today removes roughly $12 million from your estate, plus whatever that 40% position grows to before (and after) the sale. If the deal falls through and the business doubles to $60M in three years, you have just removed $24 million of value from the 40% estate tax ($60M x 40%).

For the seller of a company, a charitable lead annuity trust (CLAT) is the most underused financial tool that I am aware of.

With a CLAT, you transfer assets into a trust account before December 31 of the year of the sale. The CLAT pays a fixed annual amount to the charities that you choose for a term of years (typically 20-30 years — the longer, the greater the benefits), and whatever investments remain in the CLAT account are returned to you (or your heirs).

Sources indicate that for example, an optimized CLAT (zeroed-out grantor trust with maximum IRS-approved charitable backloading) gives you an income tax deduction in the year of the sale equal to nearly 100% of your contribution to the CLAT, and returns a significant amount back to you (assuming a reasonable 7-8% rate of return). The payments to charity are set using the IRS interest rate in effect when you fund the CLAT, and these rates are reasonably low.

Since the charitable payments are back-loaded, most of the donations from the CLAT happen in the final years … after the assets have presumably compounded to a very large amount. After all donations are made, everything left in the CLAT account passes to your heirs, without any gift tax (and without consuming any of your lifetime $15 million gift tax exemption).

Suppose you sell your company for a $20 million gain and fund a 30-year optimized CLAT with $4 million. You would receive a tax deduction equal to approximately $4 million, the CLAT would donate approximately $14 million over the 30-year period, and your children could expect to receive back approximately $10 million (assuming 7% rate of return), free of the 40% federal gift tax. The caveat, however, is that the CLAT funds cannot be spent during the 30-year term, and this strategy only makes sense if you are charitably inclined.

Section 1202 of the Tax Code lets a founder exclude up to $10 million of gain on the sale of qualified small business stock (QSBS) — and for shares issued after July 4, 2025, that figure rises to $15 million with partial benefits starting at year three instead of year five.

A married couple can multiply that exclusion by placing shares in special non-grantor trusts (each of which counts as its own taxpayer).

Here is the catch that disqualifies many of the founders that I talk to: QSBS only exists for C corporations, and the holding period starts when the C corporation issues the stock. If you have run your company as an S corporation or LLC for 15 years, you have zero qualifying years. Converting the month before the sale accomplishes nothing.

There are three things to do now:.

It has been revealed that check your state, too. For example, California does not conform to the federal QSBS exclusion, which means a founder who is a California tax resident saves federal tax only.

Every one of the moves above is irrevocable, and requires a team (including a trust attorney, CPA and appraiser) with unique technical expertise and experience.

In a recent development, but all three share a single feature: They only work if you plan ahead. The owner who calls the attorney after the term sheet is signed has drastically limited their options — and increased their tax bill.

If a sale is possible in the next two to three years, put an estate planning meeting on your calendar today. You spent a decade building the business. Spend one quarter planning so your business is “built to sell” in the event of an exit.

It’s happened hundreds of times. A business owner shows up at my office, in the middle of selling their tech giant, and tells me, “Don’t worry, my estate plan is all done: I have a revocable living trust, will, powers of attorney, and health care directives, and my lawyer told me years ago that I was all set.”.

Recent findings suggest that then I have to explain that none of those documents will reduce their tax bill or protect their assets from future lawsuits or creditors. A revocable trust avoids probate. That is all it does.

#190588. How the surge in AI-discovered bugs is straining Microsoft security and threatening tech stability

📅 20 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 9m • 📚 Deep Dive (1893 w)
📖 Baca
AI & Tech 📈 Bullish 🌐 Geekwire ↗ Open Full Page

How the surge in AI-discovered bugs is straining Microsoft security and threatening tech stability

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1893 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Geekwire

⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • by Angela Gunn on Nov 20, 2026 at 9:25 amNovember 20, 2026 at 9:25 am.
  • According to recent reports, it has come to the attention of the general public this month that adversaries successfully adopt technology a lot faster than defenders do.
  • It has been revealed that now multiply “every time” and “occasionally” by AI.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

by Angela Gunn on Nov 20, 2026 at 9:25 amNovember 20, 2026 at 9:25 am.

According to recent reports, it has come to the attention of the general public this month that adversaries successfully adopt technology a lot faster than defenders do. This has nothing to do with the willingness of defenders to try. It has everything to do with the ancient truth that to succeed, defenders have to get it right every time but adversaries only have to get it right occasionally.

It has been revealed that now multiply “every time” and “occasionally” by AI. Do you like that math? Does anyone?

Recent findings suggest that the disastrous enhancement that broke Teams, Outlook, SharePoint and other packages was not a direct attack by AI-wielding bad guys. Nor was the FAA outage. Nor were most of the outage events of the past few weeks, though who can say what’s up with those European Union refrigerators.

According to recent reports, no. The true AI-driven mayhem has been predicated for several months now not on powerful latest AI-honed attacks, but on an absolute deluge of bugs of relatively low severity that Microsoft and other defenders with a formal patch process aren’t built to process.

It has been revealed that the question is whether traditional patch programs can adapt their processes to handle the deluge. Microsoft’s is MAPP (Microsoft Active Protections Program), to which the company has been committed for nearly two decades. If the industry-spanning events of the past few weeks are any indication, these programs can’t.

Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella said Wednesday at the New York Times DealBook Summit that last week’s Microsoft 365 outage came from a latent bug and wasn’t directly tied to AI, but he warned that AI-driven patching could bring more instability.

He elaborated in a separate appearance on CNBC the same day, saying the flood of patches being applied to older infrastructure is making systems less stable.

AI has “allowed us to find these bugs and fix these bugs, but that means you’ve got to then patch them, and that creates instability,” Nadella stated, when asked by Jim Cramer about a string of recent outages at United, Schwab, Chase and other organizations.

Recent findings suggest that some context: MAPP turned 18 this year. The program, run by the MSRC (Microsoft Security Response Center), handles outreach to partner companies that gain early access to information on the bugs in advance of each month’s Patch Tuesday release. In-house, it coordinates the patch release process, just as the larger MSRC organization helps coordinate the handling of bug reports from external finders.

Industry observers note that MSRC also runs point on prioritizing patches of the worst bugs through its SSIRP (Software and Services Incident Response Strategy) program, itself dating to 2004. In its time, it was an industry leader in how companies can efficiently get their arms around bad bugs.

Recent findings suggest that MAPP in its own way is similarly remarkable. It has undergone a few traumas over the years, usually when a partner breaks confidence and leaks the advance details it receives. In 2025, after attacks on SharePoint raised suspicions of a leak from the program, Microsoft stopped giving Chinese companies early access. But MAPP continues to tick along in a way that would make any program manager proud. Other companies have their own version of MAPP / MSRC, as do community efforts such as those supporting Linux.

Sources indicate that full disclosure: I’m a former MSRC employee who learned about MAPP at the knee of the program’s principals. I subsequently tracked patch releases at a company partnered with MAPP at its highest (Validate) level, which means I was privy to the 14-day multi-stage run-up to each month’s release. I admire and respect the program… and I’m afraid that in the AI-finder era, it’s in major, big trouble.

Let’s look at the numbers for Microsoft.

Since January 2021, Microsoft has issued patches for an estimated 10,319 CVEs. (I use estimated numbers throughout this analysis because there are various ways of counting such things, including whether or not the patch accrues to an application such as Edge, which actually relies on the Chromium project for its fixes. Other analysts arrive at larger or smaller counts.).

Over half of those — 5,383 CVEs — are 2026 releases, 5,128 of which were addressed since April. In comparison, 2025’s full-year CVE total was 1,180.

Sources indicate that what happened in April? As nearly as analysis can determine, the floodgates opened and finders (security researchers) started barraging the manufacturer with reports.

The first quarter of 2026 saw 255 CVEs addressed over three months. April had 163, May 132; in June the number jumped to 209. In July it was off to the races with 575 CVEs. In October, the monthly count topped 1,400.

It has been revealed that most of these bugs aren’t coming from the usual security stalwarts. They’re coming from latest finders, they’re coming in with multiple simultaneous finders not believed to be working together, and they’re coming in relatively weak.

Though the overall volume has skyrocketed, the number per month of bugs under active exploit in the wild — the notorious “zero-days” — hasn’t increased proportionally.

Moreover, average bug severity has in fact decreased. Until 2026, the average CVSS severity score for all bugs tended to hover around 7.8 (out of 10) each month. In 2026, that’s dropped to approximately 7.4 as of September — not garbage finds, but the sort of thing that doesn’t scramble the jets.

No surge in zero-days and a drop in severity — that’s good news. The problem is the volume.

Once bugs are received by Microsoft, each goes through a MAPP-helmed, multi-team process of investigation and patch development.

According to recent reports, since many products have several versions still in support, that often means that multiple teams within each product group are asked to ingest a bug report, replicate the problem, devise and test a fix, ensure the fix doesn’t trigger other problems or inadvertently point to a similar bug elsewhere in the product and ready it for mass consumption. Even AI slop has to be taken seriously, just in case.

Meanwhile, MAPP is the traffic cop for the entire release, working with each team to ascertain patches are ready, understand the nature of the bugs and what can be safely communicated to partners and the public, and ready the processes that make the second Tuesday of each month a festival of downloads and reboots. From where we stand right now, it’s all fairly… hand-crafted.

In theory the process is automatable to some extent, though the success of that effort so far in light of recent events is debatable. But high volume also leads to other problems, such as exposing information on incomplete patching.

For instance, Microsoft has recently patched Office bugs that apply to both Windows and Mac, but patches have initially only been available for Windows versions.

Microsoft’s release-day information about such bugs — patching Windows versions while asking Apple users to monitor Microsoft communications for news of their own patch — alerts the world, including eager adversaries, that the flaw exists. Apple customers just have to hope no adversaries exploit it while their patch is pending.

According to recent reports, more broadly, many of the steps in the current patching process involve judgment calls, not processes that scale well or that can reliably be handled by existing AI-driven systems. In Microsoft’s case, MAPP is a remarkably small team of humans and, being security folk at Microsoft, they’re not always the loudest or most popular voice in Redmond.

Add the mercurial nature of finders, who may or may not provide full details on their bugs (ask any MSRC person how often they receive a crash dump and a demand for payment) and may or may not disclose their finds publicly if they don’t feel they’re getting sufficient response.

Do not add the kind of defender staffing needed to handle a massive increase in volume — either in MAPP or in the individual product groups building the actual patches — because in the AI era, it’s likely the companies won’t add it either.

The cracks are showing. Microsoft has been compelled to issue OOB (out-of-band) releases and servicing updates monthly since July, often within just a few days of the original release.

Recent findings suggest that OOBs are vital enough to merit release outside the usual patch cadence, often because there’s a security issue involved, but they’re tough on administrators already wading through a slew of regularly scheduled patching. With volumes high, patch testers may rush or elide certain steps, such as checking that a fix doesn’t break something deeper in the system.

Nadella told the DealBook audience this week that a patch for a critical bank system might once have been tested for a week. Now, he remarked, the patch “needs to go instantly from being available to being patched in production because it’s being exploited in the wild. So that’s going to create instability.”.

It has been revealed that think of MAPP as Mariners catcher Dan Wilson in 2001: a pro handling a staff of skilled human pitchers, one pitch at a time. Now it’s 2026, and the pitchers have been swapped for a bank of mediocre pitching machines all slinging fastballs at … 2026-era Dan Wilson.

Here, again, AI can’t fix a system that requires defenders to catch every pitch. Secondary lines of defense that have worked in the past — for instance, the requirement by various regulatory programs that enterprises ascertain that patches are safe for their own systems — rely heavily on companies sending out the soundest possible patches.

Managed service providers might at least make sure that patches are flagged to customers as available, relevant and urgent. But they’re in no position to do much more than trust that what’s shipped is safe to deploy and react when things go wrong.

Even that gets harder when a bug kneecaps the security tools they depend on. Last week’s Microsoft 365 outage affected parts of Microsoft Defender that interact with Exchange Online.

It’s not just Microsoft, of course. The Linux community is seriously suffering, and both Apple and (especially) Google have struggled with patch-release quality in 2026 as evidenced by their own emergency updates and post-release device instability reports. Industry-wide, ecosystems built around reliable, transparent patch cadences and patch-development processes have never seemed more in danger of being overwhelmed.

Sources indicate that what needs to happen? Sure, build those AI systems; the marketing people will be pleased. It’ll speed up some parts of the process. But a system capable of replicating, every time, the human judgment calls that go into the patch-release process isn’t going to magically create itself; people have to create it.

Is there some chance that the deluge will ebb — that researchers and their tools will at some point finally find all the bugs in all the world’s products?

It’s a pretty thought, and some relief may eventually come. When more and more unrelated finders turn up the same bug, it gives one hope that the set is finite. But no one knows when relief will come, and most folk in tech suspect that really, no, there is no bottom to the bug barrel. Nor, for the foreseeable future, any rest for the weary.

FinCEN Bars US Institutions From Transmitting Funds to MEXC: What Changes and What Doesn't

📅 07 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1600 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Nulltx

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, finCEN's November 6 order cuts US financial institutions off from MEXC Global, barring any transmittal of funds to or from the exchange.
  • In a recent development, MEXC notes user assets remain secure.
  • On November 6, the Financial Crimes Enforcement Network issued a final order under Section 9714(a) of the Combating Russian Money Laundering Act.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

AI-assisted summary, reviewed by NullTX editors.

According to recent reports, finCEN's November 6 order cuts US financial institutions off from MEXC Global, barring any transmittal of funds to or from the exchange. The order spells out what is banned, what MEXC is accused of, and how the exchange has answered.

In a recent development, MEXC notes user assets remain secure. The FinCEN order never suggested otherwise, and the gap between the exchange's reassurance and the order's actual target is the key to this story.

On November 6, the Financial Crimes Enforcement Network issued a final order under Section 9714(a) of the Combating Russian Money Laundering Act. It names MEXC Global a financial institution of primary money laundering concern in connection with Russian illicit finance. From there, it bars "covered financial institutions," a category that includes banks, broker-dealers and money transmitters, from any transmittal of funds to or from MEXC Global. Transmittals, as defined, include convertible virtual currency.

In a recent development, on the MEXC side, the reach is wide. The order covers the exchange's subsidiaries, branches and offices outside the United States: MEXC Global Ltd and MX Global Ltd in Seychelles, MEXC Estonia OÜ, GIDA Technology AG in Switzerland and MXC Global Ltd in the United Kingdom. Former Singapore entities and any successors are included as well. US-based affiliates, by contrast, are expressly excluded.

The ban won't bite right away. It takes effect 30 days after publication in the Federal Register, which had not happened as of the announcement, and it carries no end date. FinCEN keeps the authority to attach conditions and grant exemptions, and willful violations can lead to civil and criminal penalties under 31 U.S.C. 5321 and 5322.

MEXC's statement is short and carefully built. The exchange claims it is aware of the order and is reviewing it with its legal and compliance teams. It describes itself as operating normally, with user assets secure. It also says it takes the concerns seriously, plans to engage constructively with FinCEN and other regulators, and has started an independent review of its AML and sanctions controls.

Two points stand out. For one, the reassurance lines up with the order's text. Nothing in it freezes balances or halts trading, so "operating normally" is plausible. The threat is to MEXC's access to US financial counterparties, not to the exchange's wallets.

The other point is what the statement skips. It disputes none of the allegations, and the independent review it promises targets AML and sanctions controls, the very area where FinCEN indicates the exchange failed. The order also invites anyone with relevant information to submit it to FinCEN, so MEXC already has a formal channel for the constructive engagement it describes.

It has been revealed that the charges are specific. FinCEN assesses that MEXC facilitated at least $16.7 billion in likely illicit activity between May 2021 and May 2026, a figure Treasury's announcement rounded to $16 billion. The order splits that total across several categories.

It has been revealed that on Russia, FinCEN cites nearly $1.5 billion in direct and indirect exposure to sanctions-evasion transactions, including $232 million in direct dealings with entities sanctioned by the US, EU or UK. According to the order, MEXC processed about $129 million with Garantex and $4.1 million with its successor Grinex after both were designated, with activity continuing as recently as June 2026. It also points to at least $26 million benefiting the A7 Network and nearly $200 million tied to the ruble-backed A7A5 token. Beyond that, FinCEN indicates MEXC handled more than $13 billion with four UK-sanctioned exchanges between May 2018 and July 2026.

It has been revealed that iran features just as heavily. The order cites nearly $2 billion tied to Iranian actors or terrorist groups, including about $1.87 billion in exposure to Iran and over $1 billion in direct transactions with more than 40 Iranian exchanges. About $22 million is linked to the Central Bank of Iran and the IRGC Quds Force. For North Korea, the order describes roughly $350,000 received by a sanctioned money launderer between June and September 2025. On cybercrime, it cites $1.99 billion in flows linked to illicit cyber actors and $37.9 million in suspected ransomware payments between January 2022 and July 2024.

The order then turns to MEXC's own rulebook. Its stated KYC and AML policies prohibit accounts in certain jurisdictions, yet FinCEN says the exchange facilitated transactions involving them. The order also notes that MEXC has operated without a license in Seychelles, Hong Kong and Japan, and it points to the Seychelles Financial Services Authority's May 2026 enforcement action against MX Global Ltd. All of this reflects FinCEN's assessments, drawn from public and non-public information, and MEXC has not answered them point by point.

The order is not an OFAC sanctions designation, and the difference matters. A funds-transmittal ban limits what US-covered institutions can do with MEXC. It does not make it illegal for ordinary users anywhere in the world to hold an account there. The order also states that it leaves existing Bank Secrecy Act and OFAC obligations untouched.

Section 9714 gives Treasury two routes: the special measures of Section 311 of the USA PATRIOT Act, or a ban on certain transmittals of funds. FinCEN took the second and explained its reasoning. Recordkeeping requirements would still let transfers continue, and a correspondent-account restriction would miss funds moving outside a strict correspondent relationship. FinCEN also went with an order rather than a rulemaking, citing imminent threats and ongoing transactions.

One provision stands out for its practicality. FinCEN acknowledges that a covered institution often can't reject incoming crypto before it arrives, so the order allows discretion in cases such as funds that sat in an unhosted wallet for an extended period. The carve-out underlines how difficult enforcement will be in practice.

For most MEXC customers outside the US, nothing changes on day one. Counterparties face a tougher picture. Once the order takes effect, US banks, regulated exchanges and money transmitters will have to block transmittals to and from MEXC, and global institutions with US exposure have strong reasons to follow suit. FinCEN states plainly that the order puts US and foreign financial institutions and regulators on notice.

Recent findings suggest that before issuance, the draft went to the Justice Department, State, the Federal Reserve, the FDIC, the SEC, the CFTC, the OCC and the NCUA, and none objected. The order also fits into a wider Treasury campaign. It cites the October 1 Operation Economic Outcast action against the A7 Network, and a separate FinCEN proposal on A7 sub-agents followed days later.

Industry observers note that predicting how users or markets will react would be guesswork. What users can do is track the dates, know which institutions they depend on, and watch for official updates from MEXC.

Industry observers note that finCEN used the same Section 9714 authority against the exchange Bitzlato in January 2023. This time, though, the target is by FinCEN's own account among the 20 largest exchanges by trading volume, with roughly 9% of centralized exchange market share as of December 2025 and about $5 billion in reserve assets as of June 2026. Applying a transmittal ban to an exchange of that size signals a more aggressive posture.

In a recent development, three things will show what comes next. The first is the Federal Register publication date, which starts the 30-day clock. The second is whether FinCEN grants any exemptions or conditions. The third is what MEXC's independent review turns up, and whether the exchange shares the results. For now, the statement buys MEXC time without answering the order. The real answer will come from changes to its controls, and from whether its banking and liquidity partners are satisfied with them.

Meet the Indigenous Founder and Investor Teaching People How to Manifest Their Dream Businesses: ‘The Folks Who Are Winning Are Thinking Differently’

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways

  • In a recent development, “It was like, If you can dream it, you can build it,” Fore recalls.
  • Fore has spent the past two decades as an inventor, CEO, serial entrepreneur and investor.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Betsy Fore was raised in rural Illinois, but she often made the 17-hour drive to the Turtle Mountain Reservation in North Dakota, where her mother grew up. To this day, Fore’s uncle owns an auto body shop there; as a child, she helped him, and her father, tinker in the garage.

In a recent development, “It was like, If you can dream it, you can build it,” Fore recalls. “So I believed that. That was really my start as an entrepreneur because I believed I could kind of do anything.”.

Fore has spent the past two decades as an inventor, CEO, serial entrepreneur and investor.

Sources indicate that she rolled out WonderWoof, one of the first dog activity monitors, in 2014. She was the co-founder and CEO of Tiny Organics, a organization delivering organic, nutrient-rich meals for babies and toddlers. Her nonprofit career accelerator, Natives Rising, empowers indigenous communities with technology, entrepreneurship and wellness.

Recent findings suggest that currently, she’s the founder and managing director of Velveteen Ventures, investing in solutions for children and the planet for the next seven generations. “Velveteen was built on my deep inner why. Before you build anything externally, you have to excavate why you’re building it at the level of your soul — not just your resume.”.

In a recent development, what’s more, Fore just revealed the launch of Velveteen Labs, a first-of-its-kind studio model that allows children to be shareholders in incubated companies. Shares are placed into a trust, and when the children turn 18, they give a majority of them to a cause of their choice.

In a recent development, “She’s showing that investing in Indigenous and Gen Alpha-focused founders isn’t a trade-off between impact and returns,” Roy Swan, director of mission investments at Ford Foundation and author of Positive Sum: How Zero-sum Thinking Broke Capitalism—and How We Can Fix It, states. “It’s simply good investing, done with the next seven generations in mind.”.

In a recent development, needless to say, Fore has accomplished a lot over the course of her career, and she’s met many entrepreneurs along the way. There’s one thing that always gets her very excited within the first five minutes of a conversation: when the person has a unique insight, based on lived experience, into the problem they set out to solve.

“You can just see when someone is speaking from their authentic self,” Fore explains. “It’s not really a sales pitch at that point. They’re literally saying, ‘I’ve tried everything. This is what worked for me. This is how I’m going to try to bring it to market.’”.

Entrepreneur sat down with Fore to learn exactly how founders can reach that authentic place and accomplish the goals they set for themselves.

Fore’s book, Built on Purpose: Discover Your Deep Inner Why and Manifest the Business of Your Dreams, “breaks down how to go from idea to making something real through a values-driven approach,” Michael Acton Smith, co-founder of meditation space company Calm, shared in a statement.

Uncovering that deep inner why, and bringing the idea to life, starts with lessening the focus on external relationships — with customers, investors, and board and team members — and looking inward, Fore says.

It has been revealed that fore highlights the centuries-old practice of anchoring as an example of how to kick off the process. “ When yogis put their index finger and thumb together in meditation, it’s not just a pose,” she explains. “That gesture is a signal through your nervous system. It’s connecting your individual consciousness to something larger than yourself.”.

Fore encourages founders to build their own version of that practice, and it begins with identifying your values. For instance, in her own life, Fore draws on the seven grandfather teachings that guide her Turtle Mountain Chippewa tribe: love, respect, bravery, truth, honesty, humility and wisdom.

Whatever your individual values are, the next step is to physically anchor and embody those values day to day, Fore notes.

“Lean into them with a gesture, a breath, a word, so that when you walk into a fundraising meeting or have a hard call, you’re not operating from the scarcity mindset, but instead one of abundance,” Fore says. “You’re operating from who you actually are.”.

Manifesting the results you want to see also plays a key role in success, Fore claims.

A study conducted by Dr. Gail Matthews, a psychology professor at Dominican University of California, showed that people are 42% more likely to achieve their goals if they write them down every day.

Fore recommends opening your laptop each morning and starting with a simple sentence.

“Write it in the ‘I am’ present moment,” Fore explains. “I am building this for. I am building this because. So it’s not the pitch. It’s the real reason. The act alone changes your follow-through at a neurological level, if you’re able to live as if it’s already happening.”.

Additionally, Fore notes a therapeutic model called Internal Family Systems (IFS), developed by Dr. Richard Schwartz in the 1980s, can support in taking the next step toward a desired future.

The idea is that we’re not one unified self; we’re a whole system of parts, and each one has a job to do, Fore says.

It has been revealed that “ Some of them are what IFS calls exiles, and those are the wounded or the younger versions of us that formed in hard moments in our life, the ones that carry the shame or the fear, the grief,” she explains. “Essentially, embodying that sort of scarcity mindset. And then there are the protectors, the parts that showed up to keep those exiles safe. For instance, your inner critic, that’s a protector.”.

A lot of leadership advice tells people to push past fear, silence their inner critic and be more confident to get what they want. However, while Fore acknowledges there can be some value in that, she also believes that being afraid can only get you so far. Instead of simply fighting fear, she encourages founders to engage with it.

“Literally, out loud or in your head, identify it and ask what that part wants — the answer incorporates parts you love about yourself and want to bring to the forefront,” she notes.

Fore points to difficult conversations with a team as an example. Instead of asking why an issue wasn’t flagged sooner, she can admit that part of her feels frustrated, then express gratitude it was caught.

Industry observers note that “ This is a leader who’s not being hijacked by these exiles in the middle of a critical moment,” she states. “The folks who are winning are thinking differently.”.

When founders do look outward and consider their relationship to customers, they might be using a transactional lens — Fore admits she made the same mistake in the beginning.

Instead, Fore suggests flipping the traditional fundraising model on its head and asking, What if the foundation of every product was built with the customer in mind, and every bit of capital was leveraged to return exponential value to them?

“ That shift from extraction to service is the difference between founders who build loyal communities and founders who churn customers,” Fore says. “So if you can ask yourself every single day, Who isn’t being served right now? That question is where your next great idea lives.”.

Fore put that idea into practice when she launched Tiny Organics, which scaled to more than $13 million in sales in 24 months.

It has been revealed that fore sent an email to a local parent group in Park Slope, asking if other people were also interested in getting their babies to eat real fruits and vegetables that didn’t come from a pouch. She received hundreds of messages in response and had to cap the project at 100 families within two hours.

Those 100 founding families helped develop Tiny Organics’ first hero product and led to a series of supper clubs introducing kids to their first 100 flavors; those ultimately expanded to Boston, Atlanta and Chicago.

Fore’s customer-first approach that continues to resonate with the companies Velveteen Ventures invests in today.

Industry observers note that “We wanted partners who see caring for families as one of the most important economies of our time,” Emily Greenberg, president and co-founder of AI family assistant Joy Parenting Club, says. “Velveteen leads in the care economy, and Betsy gets it in a way few investors do as a previous founder in this category. She knows that when you support parents, you’re investing in the next generation.”.

These days, in the age of AI, the soft skills have become the hard skills, Fore says, noting they’re the foundation of everything she’s seen actually work in business — and she looks forward to leaning on them now and in the years to come.

In a recent development, “ I have so much hope,” Fore claims. “You can probably tell I’m an eternal optimist. I’m going to turn everything into a victory in life. Then, inevitably it happens, where you’re able to figure it out and find a way. I know that’s been true for me, and for so many of the founders that we funded.”.

It has been revealed that betsy Fore was raised in rural Illinois, but she often made the 17-hour drive to the Turtle Mountain Reservation in North Dakota, where her mother grew up. To this day, Fore’s uncle owns an auto body shop there; as a child, she helped him, and her father, tinker in the garage.

“It was like, If you can dream it, you can build it,” Fore recalls. “So I believed that. That was really my start as an entrepreneur because I believed I could kind of do anything.”.

Fore has spent the past two decades as an inventor, CEO, serial entrepreneur and investor.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

by Lisa Stiffler on Nov 20, 2026 at 9:41 amNovember 20, 2026 at 9:41 am.

According to recent reports, A fresh baby can be the ultimate anxiety trigger: When will she sleep through the night? What if nursing is a challenge. What is that rash?! Given the countless unknowns, the last thing a parent needs are worries about the quality of the baby’s crib or the chemicals in a pacifier.

But when Karthik Gangiredla was preparing for the birth of his first daughter, he and his wife spent hours trying to figure out which baby products were trustworthy.

“We struggled a lot,” Gangiredla noted. “We did a lot of research on what was safe, what’s not.”.

An engineer with roughly 20 years of experience in supply chains and logistics, including roles at Amazon, Flexport and TikTok, Gangiredla found himself on the consumer side of the retail equation, scrutinizing strollers and bottles.

To spare other parents the same headache, he turned that research into Birch, an online marketplace that offers baby product buying guides and assigns each item a TrustScore. Its scoring system draws on certifications, lab reports and recall databases to help parents assess goods ranging from baby wipes to teething toys.

The site provides information on more than 10,000 items across 110 brands, including manufacturing locations, suppliers, certificate numbers and test reports.

Birch has contracts with brands it has checked out, and serves as their merchant of record, meaning if a customer has challenges with a product or wants to return it, Birch handles those steps. It operates fulfillment centers in Los Angeles and New Jersey.

Gangiredla noted the startup flips the e-commerce approach of retail giants, focusing on the shoppers’ needs, not those of the merchant. It does not accept ads or sponsored rankings.

Sources indicate that if you took away the ad revenue for Amazon or TikTok, “the business wouldn’t exist,” Gangiredla said. “So it’s very difficult for them to approach the problem in a different way.”.

The platform also offers a gift registry and tools for tracking fetal development during pregnancy, an infant’s nursing and sleep schedules, and other developmental steps. The tools are free for people.

We caught up with Gangiredla, Birch’s CEO and founder, for this edition of GeekWire’s Startup Spotlight.

In 50 words or less, give us your startup’s elevator pitch.

Sources indicate that birch is the trust-first platform for baby and kids products and parenting resources. We research and score products across 50+ safety and quality signals before listing — and stock only what clears the bar — so parents skip the endless research and buy with confidence, from pregnancy through the toddler years.

What problem are you obsessed with solving?

According to recent reports, the impossible research burden on fresh parents. Every purchase feels like a safety decision, the information is scattered and often unverified, and the stakes feel enormous. We’re obsessed with moving the work of figuring out what’s trustworthy off the parent and onto a system that does it rigorously — and then showing our work.

What surprised you after talking to customers?

How universal the trust problem is. We assumed it would track with income or with first-time parents, but our customers span all 50 states and every kind of household — massive metros to small towns. And what they consistently want isn’t more options or a lower price; it’s someone to tell them, credibly, what’s actually worth buying.

How has AI changed the way you build your manufacturer?

It’s core, not a feature. Our TrustScore engine evaluates thousands of products across dozens of safety and quality signals in ways a human team our size never could, and the same intelligence powers discovery and personalization. It also lets a very lean team operate like a much larger one — and we now license that engine to other baby and kids brands as a product called Juno.

What’s one thing people misunderstand about your startup?

That “curated” means limited or expensive. Curation isn’t about carrying less for its own sake, or about selling premium — it’s about removing the untrustworthy. In our own data, price and trustworthiness barely correlate; some of the highest-scoring products are among the most affordable. Fewer and better, not fewer and pricier.

What’s the toughest decision you’ve made in the past year?

Industry observers note that turning away brands and revenue. When you’re early, every dollar is tempting — but our entire promise is that everything on Birch has earned its place. Saying no to products and partners that didn’t clear the bar, even when the revenue was real, was hard. It’s also the decision that defines what we are.

What’s the one piece of advice you give to other entrepreneurs?

Earn trust before you try to scale it. It’s slower and less glamorous than chasing growth, but trust compounds and shortcuts don’t. And talk to your customers far earlier, and far more often, than feels comfortable.

We’ll know our manufacturer has made it when….

…a parent’s first instinct, the moment they find out they’re expecting, is to come to Birch — and “did you check the TrustScore?” is just how families talk about buying for their kids.

Recent findings suggest that ethereum developers want to change the gas accounting for validator deposits. The strategy is to measure the request bytes that these deposit events create.

In a recent development, the gas calculation already accounts for executing a deposit. However, after the deposit is finished, a 192-byte request is passed along with the block. Those 192 bytes are excluded from the minimum gas charge, so the same gas limit might allow more data than the initial calculation accounts for.

Industry observers note that under Gloas, there is no fixed cap on the number of deposit requests per block. The execution layer has not capped this either. Gas is the only limiting factor.

Neither EIP-8131 nor EIP-8279 accounts for those request bytes. This means that deposits could become another way to bypass the gas floor once EIP-8279 closes the loophole involving cold storage reads.

Industry observers note that A relay contract can call the deposit contract repeatedly, costing around 26,000 gas per deposit. In the author's example, that execution cost is below the point where the gas floor for zero-byte calldata would start to increase the total charge.

This results in a payload of about 1.44 times the block gas limit divided by 64, compared with about 1.15 times the same baseline.

The main issue is the data size, so the proposal directly addresses the data.

A log from the deposit contract with the deposit event topic counts as 192 bytes before the log entry is added. This is the same condition EIP-6110 uses to turn logs into requests.

The cost of this would be another check that client developers would have to implement and test.

According to recent reports, people are not expected to pay more for regular deposits. The cost of executing a regular deposit is already above the proposed minimum, so the extra 12,288 gas only raises the minimum charge.

The proposal has yet to be scheduled for a network upgrade.

Not Every Client Is Worth Taking On. The Wrong Ones Could Cost You More Than You Think.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • Recent findings suggest that we once worked with a student whose college application included, among several supplemental essay prompts, a question about a time they’d disagreed with someone.
  • The student’s father, however, insisted his child had never disagreed with anyone.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Opinions expressed by Entrepreneur contributors are their own.

Recent findings suggest that we once worked with a student whose college application included, among several supplemental essay prompts, a question about a time they’d disagreed with someone. Such prompts became especially prominent in the wake of Hamas’ October 7, 2023 terrorist attacks on Israel, the ensuing Israel-Hamas war, and the campus encampments and protests that swept American universities. Amid growing polarization on college campuses, universities increasingly emphasized the importance of students engaging respectfully with opposing viewpoints, challenging their own assumptions, and learning across difference.

The student’s father, however, insisted his child had never disagreed with anyone. His child simply wasn’t disagreeable! Surely, every teenager has disagreed with someone. But rather than help his child identify a meaningful disagreement, the father challenged the very premise of the essay. The irony, of course, wasn’t lost on us. Here was a father being disagreeable simply for the sake of being disagreeable, all while insisting his child had never disagreed with anyone.

Recent findings suggest that these are the kinds of interactions that can consume an extraordinary amount of a college admissions counselor’s time. And they illustrate a lesson every entrepreneur should understand. Sometimes, your most expensive clients aren’t the ones who pay the least. They’re the ones who question everything.

Industry observers note that most entrepreneurs know the Pareto principle, commonly called the 80/20 rule. Roughly 80% of results often come from 20% of efforts. But there’s another side to that equation. A relatively small percentage of clients can consume a disproportionately large share of your team’s time and energy. At Ivy Coach, our college admissions consulting firm, we’ve seen this firsthand.

Industry observers note that in another case, a family consulted their student’s school counselor about a Personal Statement we’d helped develop. The counselor recommended scrapping it in favor of an essay about what we call a third-rail topic, one so clichéd in college admissions essays that it can significantly undermine an otherwise compelling application.

Sources indicate that when we had the student ask the school counselor to explain the reasoning behind the ill-advised recommendation, the response came back in prose that appeared to have been generated by artificial intelligence. Our AI detection software flagged it as AI-generated, too. Here was a family paying for specialized college admissions expertise, only to ask our team to defend its recommendations against generic advice that apparently hadn’t even been written by a human. It’s madness!

There’s, of course, nothing wrong with seeking a second opinion. But there’s a difference between asking thoughtful questions and questioning everything simply because someone else has offered a different opinion, especially when that opinion may have come from a chatbot. For Ivy Coach’s college counselors, every hour spent defending sound advice is an hour that can’t be spent helping another student.

Ivy Coach has been in the college admissions consulting business for 35 years, and over the past decade, we’ve noticed a troubling trend. We track exclusions from our college admissions statistics: students who choose not to follow our recommendations. Or, more often than not, whose parents choose not to follow them. And while these families remain a small minority of our clients, their numbers have increased over the last 10 years. In other words, more families are paying for our expertise only to disregard it.

Sources indicate that I sometimes wonder whether our increasingly polarized political climate has something to do with it. We’ve grown accustomed to questioning expertise, seeking validation for our existing beliefs, asking AI chatbots to tell us precisely what we want to hear and treating disagreements as contests to be won rather than opportunities to learn. Has that mentality spilled over into relationships between clients and professional advisers, including college counselors? Maybe.

Recent findings suggest that our experience alone can’t establish the cause, but we’ve increasingly encountered families more interested in challenging our recommendations than understanding them. And that raises a question every entrepreneur should consider: What happens when clients pay for your judgment but refuse to heed your advice?

In a recent development, ivy Coach has grown considerably over the years, adding former admissions officers from many of America’s most selective universities. But we’ve remained boutique by design. We deliberately limit enrollment because helping students build compelling applications requires extraordinary individual attention. We can’t provide that attention if a handful of families consume a disproportionate share of our counselors’ time.

Recent findings suggest that that’s why our initial Complimentary Consultation isn’t simply an opportunity for prospective clients to evaluate us. It’s an opportunity for us to evaluate them. Are they seeking expert guidance or validation? Are they willing to hear advice that contradicts what they’ve read online? Do they understand that college admissions is inherently uncertain?

Industry observers note that these warning signs often emerge during that initial consultation. One is the word “guarantee.” No ethical college counselor can guarantee admission to Harvard, Stanford or any other highly selective university. Another is a parent who questions just about every recommendation without showing any willingness to consider the answers. We welcome thoughtful disagreement. We don’t welcome endless arguments for their own sake.

And when we spot these warning signs during that first conversation, as we so often do, we’d rather turn away the business than invite months or years of unnecessary headache.

Entrepreneurs are conditioned to chase growth, but revenue isn’t profitability, and growth isn’t always progress. A difficult client can consume so much of your team’s time that the relationship becomes far less profitable than it appears. Worse, that client can diminish the quality of service everyone else receives.

For businesses built on specialized expertise, protecting your team’s time isn’t just good management. Rather, it’s a critical responsibility to your other clients. The best college admissions counselors don’t tell parents what they want to hear. They tell them what they need to hear. And the best entrepreneurs recognize that not every prospective client is worth accepting. After all, the most expensive client may be the one you should never have taken on in the first place.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

by Todd Bishop on Nov 20, 2026 at 2:06 pmNovember 20, 2026 at 2:07 pm.

According to recent reports, microsoft acquired the popular Wunderlist app in 2015, shut it down in 2020 and told its loyal users that Microsoft To Do would be their latest home. Now they’re being asked to pack up again.

Microsoft looks to retire the To Do apps on June 30, 2027, moving personal task management for work and school accounts into Planner, its team project-management app. Microsoft disclosed the change Wednesday in a long Planner blog post amid the firm’s Ignite announcements, and Windows Latest flagged the change later that day.

The reaction was swift and mostly unhappy. Tom Warren of The Verge summed it up on X: “Microsoft is killing its great tasks app in favor of its worse tasks app.”.

That’s not entirely fair to Planner, which is built for a different job. But it captures the gripe: To Do was simple, free and worked across Windows, Mac, iOS, Android and the web, and nothing Microsoft is offering replaces all of that.

For work and school accounts, Microsoft indicates Planner “will be the destination for managing personal work tasks,” but “existing To Do tasks and lists will not migrate to Planner.” It says it will offer a way to export To Do data before the app shuts down.

Tony Redmond of Office365itpros, who tracks Microsoft 365 closely, cataloged the gaps: no file attachments on private Planner tasks, no equivalent for To Do’s list groups, no transfer of shared-list membership, assignments or permissions, and no native Planner apps for Windows or Mac.

He also noted the irony that Outlook’s old Exchange-based tasks will outlive To Do.

Why Microsoft is doing it: The manufacturer remarked putting individual and shared work on the same foundation lets it deliver more consistent features, and lets people connect their own tasks to Copilot and other AI agents. A new Planner agent, available with a Copilot add-on license, can take on tasks and generate status reports.

The Register’s Richard Speed put it less charitably, saying Microsoft had slipped the news into “this week’s Ignite AI puffery.”.

Customers weigh in: Brad Silverberg, the former Microsoft executive who led Windows 95 development and later became a Seattle venture investor, posted on X that he has used To Do daily, and Wunderlist before it.

“Very disappointed now,” he wrote, adding that he’s looking at TickTick and Todoist.

Similar posts piled up on LinkedIn from Microsoft 365 consultants and everyday owners, some of them describing Planner as clunky by comparison.

Patrick Husting, a Seattle-area entrepreneur and software developer whose Ghostwriter add-in brought AI to Microsoft Office before Microsoft unveiled Microsoft 365 Copilot, offered on LinkedIn to maintain To Do for Microsoft for free.

Rivals smell an opportunity: Competitors wasted no time. TickTick posted a migration guide for To Do refugees. Todoist CEO Amir Salihefendic wrote on LinkedIn that the shutdown was “pretty unexpected” and pointed out that his app has outlasted competitors for 20 years.

Recent findings suggest that the most pointed pitch came from Superlist, which called itself “the natural successor” and stated it already has a tool for importing To Do lists. Wunderlist founder Christian Reber started the manufacturer in 2020.

Reber and his co-founders sold Wunderlist’s parent company, 6Wunderkinder, to Microsoft in 2015 for a reported $100 million to $200 million. In 2019, as Microsoft prepared to shut the app down, he publicly asked Satya Nadella to sell it back. Microsoft kept it, then retired it in favor of To Do.

Now some of those former Wunderlist owners may end up back with the people who built it.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • AI agents and humanoid robots may dominate the funding headlines.
  • It has been revealed that so far this year, venture backers have poured close to $4 billion into an assortment of global companies focused on recruiting, finding jobs and streamlining processes associated with HR and payroll management, Crunchbase data shows.
  • To get a sense where capital is flowing, we used Crunchbase data to analyze investment to employment-related categories for the past few years.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

AI agents and humanoid robots may dominate the funding headlines. But even so, investors haven’t lost interest in startups focused on finding, filling and managing jobs for actual humans.

It has been revealed that so far this year, venture backers have poured close to $4 billion into an assortment of global companies focused on recruiting, finding jobs and streamlining processes associated with HR and payroll management, Crunchbase data shows. Not surprisingly, the vast majority are also incorporating a heavy dose of AI.

To get a sense where capital is flowing, we used Crunchbase data to analyze investment to employment-related categories for the past few years. Broadly, findings show 2026 funding on track to meet or slightly exceed year-ago levels, albeit with reduced deal count.

Much of this year’s investment has gone to a small group of companies. To illustrate, below we put together a list of 14 of the largest fundraisers.

As you can see, it’s a varied list, with a commonly shared theme of bringing more automation to hiring, HR and payroll tasks.

In a recent development, by far the largest funding recipient is Mercor, a startup that pairs human experts with developers of AI models and tools. The 4-year-old company raised $750 million in a Series D round this month at a whopping $20 billion valuation.

San Francisco-based Mercor is betting that as companies build AI agents to take on more work tasks, demand for subject matter experts to guide these efforts will grow. While frontier labs have been its primary buyers for the past few years, Mercor says it expects enterprises will soon be its major customers.

In a recent development, the next two largest fundraisers on our list for this year are focused on automating more employer tasks. Paris-based Skello secured $220 million this summer for its AI-enabled software platform for HR teams. And HiBob, a New York-based platform for HR and payroll, picked up $166 million in a Salesforce1-led financing.

Of course, investors aren’t only looking at startups automating work tasks or training AI agents to do so. They’re also backing companies focused on the old-fashioned business of matching workers and employers.

In this sector, one of the larger rounds this year went to San Francisco-based Juicebox, an AI tool for recruiters to find talented candidates. The 4-year-old firm picked up an $80 million Series B at an $850 million valuation.

Sources indicate that agentic hiring is also a thing. Metaview, a San Francisco-based startup that offers an agentic recruiting platform optimized, in its words, to “get the right butts in seats,” secured $60 million in a September Series C financing. Around the same time, London’s Jack & Jill AI, which offers AI agents for finding careers and for hiring, closed on $40 million in Series A funding.

Another agentic hiring platform, San Francisco’s Paraform, revealed a $40 million round this spring, pitching itself as an offering for an age in which employers are making fewer hires overall but still need highly skilled people for highly paid jobs.

So what kind of employment future do startup funding trends paint for human jobseekers?

Industry observers note that not a good one. As a human who has spent decades writing about sector-specific startup funding, this is probably the most depressing data dive into investment trends for an industry that I have ever done.

Overall, the bulk of massive rounds are going to one of three categories: using humans to help train their potential AI replacements, automating work tasks around supporting people in the workplace, and getting AI to help hire the right people for the dwindling pool of available positions.

Typically, I’m rooting for startups to succeed. And honestly, there’s not an individual company highlighted here that I’m specifically hoping will fail. But nonetheless, the broad vision of an increasingly AI-dominated workplace does bring with it a sense of trepidation.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Opinions expressed by Entrepreneur contributors are their own.
  • In a recent development, A large company was preparing to move a major customer segment onto a new service model.
  • According to recent reports, nobody approved it as final, and nobody said the tech giant was committed to that version.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Opinions expressed by Entrepreneur contributors are their own.

In a recent development, A large company was preparing to move a major customer segment onto a new service model. One part of the model depended on whether a third-party data feed would be available at the level of detail the company expected. The vendor hadn’t confirmed the final specification, so the program treated the feed as provisional.

According to recent reports, nobody approved it as final, and nobody said the tech giant was committed to that version. The program team simply needed a working basis for moving forward while the vendor finished its testing.

At the weekly program review, the current specification was sent forward to the teams that needed it. The cover note called it “provisional” and listed the vendor confirmation as still open.

Industry observers note that at the next review, the vendor still couldn’t confirm the final specification. The program kept the assumption open because there still wasn’t enough evidence to approve or reject it, while the work that depended on the current version continued.

Within two weeks, the provisional input had started shaping work across the program. Marketing had drafted customer communications using the expected level of detail. Finance had built the service cost estimate around the processing volume that specification would create.

Technology had completed part of the interface configuration, and Operations had started shaping support materials around the information employees expected to receive. None of those commitments looked decisive on its own.

Industry observers note that one team had already gone further. Technology had built a field-mapping routine that assumed the vendor feed would include several data elements still under review. The routine could be changed later, but doing so would require reopening testing that other work was already using.

That build step mattered because the interface team had also started testing how employees would use the information during a customer interaction. The screen layout, validation checks and exception handling all reflected the current feed structure. None of that work formally approved the assumption, but another part of the service was now being exercised against it.

It has been revealed that when the vendor finally confirmed that the feed would contain less detail than expected, the change hit several places at once. Marketing had to revise messages that no longer matched the service experience. Finance had to reopen the cost estimate because more manual handling would be required.

The organization had reached the consequences of a decision without ever making the decision itself.

Technology had to revisit the interface and repeat part of its testing, and Operations had to rework guidance that assumed employees would see information the feed wouldn’t provide.

It has been revealed that leaders expect a provisional item to remain movable until someone formally approves it. That expectation makes sense because the label indicates the matter is still open, yet the people doing the work still need a basis for moving forward.

In a recent development, one function prepares customer communication, another estimates cost, and another builds against the best information available. Each commitment is locally reasonable, and none of them settles the question.

Together, they change how much surrounding work has to move if the assumption changes.

This is where the “Broken Handoffs” execution leak appears. The program team hands over an input that’s openly provisional, and the receiving teams turn that input into work of their own. The handoff starts a series of separate commitments that no one reviews as one combined choice.

The sensible response is to make assumptions more visible. So, teams add labels for “confirmed, provisional and unresolved items.” Handoff templates call out dependencies, and open questions receive owners, dates and review points.

Recent findings suggest that those changes reduce ambiguity. In this program, the data-feed specification was identified as provisional in the review material, and the vendor confirmation remained visible as an open item. The teams still had work to do while the uncertainty remained unresolved.

According to recent reports, technology kept building the parts of the interface it could complete. Other teams continued their work from the latest available specification because waiting for certainty would have stopped parts of the program that could still move.

The more detailed handoff improved the description of the uncertainty without stopping the commitments growing around it.

That second review tested the assumption in more detail.

The vendor still hadn’t completed the work needed to confirm the final feed specification, so leadership asked whether enough evidence existed to approve the current version and concluded that it didn’t.

Industry observers note that keeping the assumption provisional was the right answer because the underlying question still wasn’t ready for a sound decision. The discussion then moved to what could continue safely while the program waited.

Technology noted it could keep building interface components unaffected by the missing detail. Finance could continue refining the cost view with a range, while customer messaging could move as long as the copy avoided specific promises about the data.

All of that was reasonable, and it also meant the organization continued adding commitments around an assumption that no one was yet able to decide.

By the time the vendor returned with the final specification, the program wasn’t revisiting one choice. It was dealing with the combined effect of choices made in different places, at different times and for different local reasons.

The usual controls work well when a decision exists. Leaders can ask who approved it, what evidence supported it, when it should be reviewed and whether the basis for it has changed.

It has been revealed that this situation leaves no single decision event to reopen. The assumption can stay correctly labeled as provisional, the review can correctly keep it open, and every team can act reasonably inside its own work.

According to recent reports, separate commitments gradually give the assumption the practical weight of a decision even though the organization never created one. By the time someone asks whether the business should still be operating on that assumption, the answer is already embedded in work spread across several teams.

A working assumption becomes dangerous when the organization no longer needs a decision for it to start behaving like one.

A large company was preparing to move a major customer segment onto a new service model. One part of the model depended on whether a third-party data feed would be available at the level of detail the company expected. The vendor hadn’t confirmed the final specification, so the program treated the feed as provisional.

Industry observers note that nobody approved it as final, and nobody remarked the firm was committed to that version. The program team simply needed a working basis for moving forward while the vendor finished its testing.

According to recent reports, at the weekly program review, the current specification was sent forward to the teams that needed it. The cover note called it “provisional” and listed the vendor confirmation as still open.

Microsoft’s final Outlook outage report details testing gaps and safeguards that backfired
