📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

by Todd Bishop on Nov 23, 2026 at 5:49 amNovember 23, 2026 at 6:01 am.

Sources indicate that microsoft Vice Chair and President Brad Smith offered a polite but pointed response to President Trump’s seemingly impromptu threat to tax U.S. companies that build data centers abroad: most of them have to be where their customers are.

Speaking on CBS News’ “Face the Nation” on Sunday morning, Smith said the president is “making an vital point,” and that there’s room to talk about keeping the training of the most advanced AI models in the U.S., much like the push to make more chips here.

But he said most data centers run everyday cloud services, such as streaming video, video games and business software, and need to be close to the people using them.

“You can’t support Helsinki from Fresh Jersey any more than you can keep the lights on in Helsinki from an electricity power plant in New Jersey,” he stated.

A tax on foreign data centers could have significant financial implications for Microsoft, which says it has more than 600 data centers in 34 countries.

Trump made the statement Friday at a White House press conference, saying companies would face a “tremendous tax” if they build data centers outside the U.S.

It has been revealed that his reason: “We’re not allowing data centers to go into other countries because China will take all of them, and we’re not allowing that to happen. And we’re going to put tremendous penalties on companies that try and do it.”.

.@POTUS: "Whoever wins SI, wins… We're not allowing data centers to go into other countries — because China will take all of them, and we're not allowing that to happen." pic.twitter.com/FiH1LfAQDu.

In a recent development, he gave no rate or timeline and acknowledged that he hadn’t told his own staff. “That’s a breaking story,” he said. “I haven’t even said that to my people. But I’m telling them now — they’re here.”.

Trump had just returned from the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit in Shenzhen, China, where he met with Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin.

His one example was an unnamed organization that wants to build in Finland. Google announced a €13 billion investment in Finland in September, covering data centers and clean energy projects. Margaret Brennan, host of the CBS program, said he might have meant a Chinese project.

Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent, who appeared earlier in the same CBS broadcast, said he hadn’t spoken with the president about the proposal, but added that Trump is “very concerned that we don’t do a substantial technology transfer offshore.”.

Smith also fielded questions on other topics in his “Face the Nation” appearance.

TikTok’s owner: Brennan asked about TikTok’s Chinese owner, ByteDance, which is in advanced talks to spend about $500 million more on Microsoft’s Azure cloud, mostly to use OpenAI’s models, The Information reported last week.

Rep. John Moolenaar, R-Mich., chair of the House Select Committee on the Chinese Communist Party, noted Microsoft should not sell AI tools to ByteDance, called it unacceptable for a Pentagon contractor, and asked the company for a briefing.

Smith noted that TikTok’s U.S. business is now a separate company, and said Microsoft expects to answer the committee’s questions on Capitol Hill.

White House ballroom: Microsoft committed $10 million to Trump’s ballroom project, according to an internal donor list reported by the Washington Post. Brennan asked why, and whether Microsoft is worried about scrutiny from a Democratic-controlled Congress.

Smith noted Microsoft takes the same approach with every administration, regardless of party. “We partner where we can. We stand apart when we should,” he said.

Industry observers note that he put the ballroom donation in the first category, and said the company “didn’t know, obviously,” that the project would involve tearing down the East Wing. In the second category, he pointed to lawsuits Microsoft has filed against the current administration, as it has against previous ones, to stand up for problems it considered crucial.

Industry observers note that outlook outage: Smith reiterated Microsoft’s apology for the Nov. 12 global Microsoft 365 and Outlook outage. He mentioned the outage wasn’t caused by AI or a cyberattack.

Speaking more broadly, he remarked much of the recent wave of tech failures can be seen as “AI ripple effects” — the result of AI making software bugs easier to find, which has companies racing to patch systems faster than they can test the fixes.

(GeekWire has covered that angle in depth, including the surge in AI-discovered bugs, Microsoft’s final outage report and Oren Etzioni’s column on the conspiracy theories.).

According to recent reports, smith remarked the patching race won’t be finished anytime soon. “The whole information infrastructure of the world is in effect being upgraded right now,” he said.

In the final stretch of 2026, some XRP Ledger protocol features await mainnet activation, with validator support and amendment voting as the final steps to bring new functionality to the XRPL network.

Sources indicate that in light of this, three amendments are racing against the 2026 calendar, with only a few votes left to reach a majority and enter the two-week activation period. These include SingleAssetVault, LendingProtocol and confidential transfers.

All three remain below the required validator approval threshold of over 80% support, making the final weeks of the year increasingly vital for their activation prospects.

With about five weeks left in 2026, activation remains possible this year, but additional validator support for each amendment must arrive soon enough and be sustained to complete the required two-week activation window.

In a recent development, the lending protocol allows on-chain fixed-term, uncollateralized loans from pooled funds in a Single Asset Vault. There are two amendments: LendingProtocolV1_1 and the original Lending Protocol amendment.

In a recent development, the focus is on LendingProtocolV1_1, which extends the Lending Protocol and SingleAssetVault amendments with a new closed-ended vault and cash-basis accounting. With the amendment, new loan brokers can only be created against closed-ended vaults.

LendingProtocolV1_1 has reached 70.59% support with 24 out of 34 validators voting yes, according to XRPScan data. It needs 28 votes to reach a majority, or more than 80% of 34 votes, meaning it has just four votes left.

A major privacy amendment for the XRP Ledger, confidential transfers, has 64.71% support and 22 of 34 validators voting yes. Confidential transfers, which rely on advanced cryptography (EC-ElGamal and ZKPs), offer institutional-grade privacy for Multi-Purpose Tokens (MPTs) and need six more yes votes to enter the activation window.

In a recent development, singleAssetVault creates a structure for aggregating assets from multiple depositors and is intended to be used with the on-chain Lending Protocol. It has gained 73.53% support so far with 25 out of 34 validators voting in favor. Reaching more than 80% of 34 votes requires 28 votes; thus, three votes remain for it to enter the activation window.

Since Grant Canary launched his company a decade ago, the technology he uses has shifted and pivoted but the goal has remained steadfast: restoring wild forestland.

It has been revealed that the Seattle startup began as DroneSeed, which mapped forests devastated by fires, then flew large drones to re-tree the landscape. It went on to purchase three companies that collect and cultivate conifer seeds and grow saplings for planting, and rebranded as Mast Reforestation.

According to recent reports, the organization recently shifted again, adding a newly introduced line of operations: taking scorched timber and burying it in clay-lined vaults where it won’t rot and release carbon. Biomass burial clears the woody debris — the most expensive step in forest restoration post wildfire — while also generating essential revenue by selling carbon credits. Proceeds from the sales help landowners “get their forest back,” Canary said, which benefits everyone.

Industry observers note that just as Canary has pursued unexpected paths to forest restoration, the sustainability leader also has unconventional solutions and sources of inspiration for tackling climate change. Keep reading to learn more. His quotes have been edited for clarity and length.

When did you realize you had to work in sustainability?

Sources indicate that high school. I had a really fantastic teacher my senior year, and they got me focused on my philosophical underpinnings. I’m a utilitarian — greatest good for the greatest number of people, is how I would define that — and so my worldview formed around that time. And climate change is the problem that all other problems report to.

What’s your biggest worry when it comes to solving climate change?

Industry observers note that humans aren’t great at long-term projection. We’re much more responsive to short-term, and I am concerned that by the time that it is short-term, which is now, that there is not enough political will to understand the implications of climate change and how that affects all of the problems.

What gives you the most hope for the planet?

Industry observers note that when I founded what would become Mast, there were not the technologies to replace the [fossil fuel] incumbents. That was 2016. The state of EVs versus internal combustion engine cars was not there yet. It’s getting there promptly. Solar was not necessarily the cheapest. Battery was still not there. Geothermal, we didn’t have that. Now we continue to have more and more of those tools to replace the incumbents. And by the way, the “incumbents” is the corporation, not the people working for those companies.

I very much want all of the better products and technologies. Yes, they’re sustainable, but they’re also just better. I want to brain drain all of the oil and gas companies and put them to work in geothermal.

If you could invent one sustainability solution overnight, what would it be?

In “Ready Player Two” [a sequel to “Ready Player One,” which Steven Spielberg turned into a movie], there is a technology that allows you to step into other humans’ lived experience and feel — and not just in video form, but in the smells, in the emotions, in the feelings, and basically live out other people’s lived experience.

Recent findings suggest that that ability to make empathy mass scale would be a massive game changer in humans having more empathy for each other and understanding the challenges and problems that others are dealing with globally. That would be the technology that would advance things significantly.

What’s one habit you’ve changed personally because of environmental concerns?

My personal infrastructure. I’m lucky enough to have bought a house a few years ago and upgraded to a heat pump; Span [electrical] panels, which sets us up for vehicle-to-grid, solar, batteries, other things; an EV; and then less glamorous but equally notable: insulation, both in the siding and in the windows and blinds. I’m sort of on my journey. We already have an electric cooktop, it’s not the amazing kind, and we have gas hot water heaters, so those are next up — and solar and batteries.

Coffee with any sustainability leader, past or present — who do you pick?

According to recent reports, I would change the question and say, who would I want to work for? There’s a ton to learn from someone by working for them, and I think my answer then is [New York City Mayor Zohran] Mamdani. Not a sustainability leader by default, but he has accomplished and built a political backing to do massive things that are ambitious, and from a sustainability lens, I would want to learn from that.

Industry observers note that in the climate space, when we got started, the problem was [a need for more sustainable] tools. It has moved down the supply chain into execution, it’s go-to-market, and that means political will.

What’s the most overhyped climate solution right now?

Sources indicate that AI. I use it. I enjoy it. I think it’s fun. But to say that it will solve the challenges of climate in the future are complete red herrings. AI is available to both sides. It is equally as effective at making gas extraction, oil extraction cheaper, faster, etc. as it is helping sustainable technologies get off the ground, and so I would say it is a neutral technology at best.

What’s an underrated solution that deserves more attention?

It has been revealed that nature as infrastructure. If people can’t get themselves to the place where they value forests for their aesthetics, for the health, for the community, for all of the other things, fine. Look at it on a spreadsheet and tell me how much it’s going to cost to replace several hundred thousand acres of forest with water treatment plants, water chiller plants, water purification plants, because that’s going to be a lot of tax dollars. And if we just let it burn, if we clear-cut it all to oblivion, that means that the city of Seattle’s water supply is not going to be as cold. It’s going to require a hell of a lot more purification, and there’s not going to be as much of it.

What impact do you hope your work has in 20 years?

Recent findings suggest that my hope is that we’ve established the funding source for reforestation with a carbon market. The carbon market is what pulls nature as infrastructure into a valued asset. It’s not an esoteric nice-to-have from a philosophical perspective, it is a valued asset that puts it into the human system of economics in a much bigger way. A carbon market is as massive an evolutionary step for humanity as the printing press, as banking, as generally accepted accounting principles.

Ripple’s dollar-pegged stablecoin, Ripple USD (RLUSD), has now entered the top five stablecoins by market cap, reaching a new all-time high in its circulating supply, a major milestone for the stablecoin less than two years after its launch. RLUSD went live in December 2024.

RLUSD has surpassed World Liberty Financial USD (USD1), Global Dollar (USDG) and PayPal USD (PYUSD) to become the fifth-largest stablecoin in the world, according to data from CoinMarketCap. Only Tether’s USDT, Circle’s USDC, Ethena’s USDe, and Dai (DAI) are ahead of it.

The milestone is proof of the rapid growth RLUSD has experienced in a competitive stablecoin market dominated by established players like Tether’s USDT and Circle’s USDC.

RLUSD’s total circulating supply across the XRP Ledger and Ethereum has reached a new high, with $2.85 billion in circulation, according to Ripple’s stablecoin tracker.

Industry observers note that ethereum commands $2.089 billion of this total figure, while $768 million in supply sits on the XRP Ledger. While Ethereum currently holds the larger share of RLUSD’s supply, XRPL has seen significant activity in RLUSD settlement volumes.

In March 2025, during a Bloomberg TV interview, Ripple CEO Brad Garlinghouse projected that RLUSD would enter the top five stablecoins; that projection has now been fulfilled.

It has been revealed that according to RWA Foundation, Ripple led weekly stablecoin growth, adding $75.4 million in the last seven days. This growth was reflected in RLUSD's market cap, allowing it to surpass World Liberty Financial USD to clinch the fifth spot in global stablecoin rankings.

Former Ripple executive Anthony Welfare highlighted this growth in a recent X post, saying, “RLUSD is the only major stablecoin growing right now.”.

Welfare noted that RLUSD supply is up nearly 20% in three weeks, rising from $2.42 billion to $2.9 billion, while USDT has fallen by $5 billion and USDC by $3 billion over the same period.

The XRP Ledger accounts for the majority of RLUSD settlements: in an analogy on X, Welfare noted that XRPL holds about 27% of RLUSD’s supply but processed 57% of its volume last week, amounting to $6.7 billion versus Ethereum, which recorded $5 billion.

5 Interesting Startup Deals You May Have Missed: Reflecting Sunlight From Space, Better Breathing And Smarter Garbage Trucks

💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, this is a monthly column that runs down five interesting startup funding deals that may have flown under the radar.
  • What if solar farms could keep generating electricity after sunset with a little help from mirrors orbiting Earth?
  • Industry observers note that those are two of the more unusual ideas that attracted startup investment in the past month.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, this is a monthly column that runs down five interesting startup funding deals that may have flown under the radar. Check out our previous entry here.

What if solar farms could keep generating electricity after sunset with a little help from mirrors orbiting Earth? Or researchers could send an experiment into space for less than the price of a car?

Industry observers note that those are two of the more unusual ideas that attracted startup investment in the past month. Our latest roundup also includes a firm bringing AI to the old-school business of garbage hauling, another rethinking how factories are programmed, and a consumer brand betting that better breathing could become a significant business. Let’s take a closer look.

Solar power has one rather obvious limitation: The sun goes down.

In a recent development, to that end, Reflect Orbital is working on a solution that sounds straight out of science fiction. The Hawthorne, California-based startup wants to put giant mirrors in orbit to redirect sunlight toward specific locations on Earth, potentially allowing solar farms to keep generating electricity longer after sunset.

The manufacturer recently announced $73.5 million in latest funding, bringing its total funding to more than $102 million, per Crunchbase. Existing investors Sequoia Capital, Lux Capital and Starship Ventures participated, alongside new backers including Buckley Ventures, Convective Capital, The Uncommon Group and Salesforce Ventures 1.

Industry observers note that reflect Orbital is developing lightweight, foldable reflectors that it notes can be rolled out aboard satellites and deployed in low Earth orbit. The firm envisions using them not only to extend solar power generation, but also to illuminate disaster zones for nighttime search-and-rescue operations or construction sites after dark.

The idea remains unproven in orbit, however. Reflect Orbital is targeting the second quarter of 2027 for its first demonstration mission, which has received FCC approval. The funding will help support those initial debuts, further development of its reflector technology, and commercial partnerships.

According to recent reports, the raise comes during a record year for space technology funding. By late August, investors had poured $20.3 billion into space- and satellite-related startups globally, per Crunchbase data, already comfortably exceeding previous annual records.

Nasal strips have been around for decades, but Intake Breathing Technology thinks there’s room for a serious upgrade.

The Santa Barbara, California-based consumer wellness organization recently confirmed a $62 million investment from Camino Partners, the investment platform founded by KIND Snacks entrepreneur Daniel Lubetzky.

In a recent development, intake makes a patented magnetic nasal dilator designed to open nasal passages and improve airflow. Rather than relying on a conventional adhesive strip stretched across the nose, its system uses adhesive tabs and a reusable magnetic band to pull the sides of the nose outward.

According to recent reports, the company markets its product to people looking to breathe more comfortably while sleeping, exercising or going about their daily routines. It indicates it has sold more than 100 million pairs of breathing tabs since 2023, with triple-digit revenue growth over the past three years.

Sources indicate that intake looks to use the latest capital to expand beyond its direct-to-consumer business and into more mainstream retail channels. That’s where Lubetzky’s experience building KIND into a household name could prove useful.

Its funding comes as venture investors show renewed enthusiasm for fitness and wellness. Startups in those categories raised more than $3.6 billion globally in the first half of 2026, putting the sector on pace for its strongest funding year since 2022, Crunchbase data shows.

Interestingly, much of this year’s investment into the sector has flowed to wearable devices and health platforms built around AI and data. Intake is a somewhat different bet: a relatively simple physical product that has apparently found a sizable audience without promising to reinvent healthcare through software.

Related Crunchbase query: Global Fitness- And Wellness-Related Startup Funding In 2026.

Taking out the trash isn’t exactly rocket science. But managing the businesses that collect it turns out to be surprisingly complicated.

San Francisco-based TrashLab Software recently raised $12 million in a growth funding round led by Ventana, with participation from existing investors Bienville Capital, Harlem Capital and CreativeCo.

The startup builds an AI-powered operating platform for waste-hauling businesses, an industry where many smaller operators still rely on spreadsheets, paper routes and clunky software to manage their fleets.

It has been revealed that trashLab indicates its platform combines dispatching, route planning, customer management, billing and payments. Its AI agent, called Haul-E, can answer customer calls and take orders, while cameras in garbage trucks can help document problems such as overflowing dumpsters, blocked containers or bins that weren’t put out for collection.

The organization states hundreds of waste haulers across the U.S. and Canada now use its software, and that more than 5 million tons of material have been managed through its platform.

Industry observers note that it’s not the only startup finding an AI opportunity in the waste industry. We recently covered Greyparrot, a London-based manufacturer using computer vision to identify and analyze waste moving through recycling facilities. While Greyparrot focuses on what happens after trash reaches a processing plant, TrashLab is tackling the messy logistics of getting it there.

Related Crunchbase query: Global Venture Funding To Waste Management Startups In 2026.

Factory automation has come a long way, but programming the machines that run industrial production lines can still require specialized expertise and a lot of time.

Gardena, California-based Neuron Industries wants to make the process a lot simpler.

The startup recently declared a $10 million seed round co-led by FCVC and Obvious Ventures, with participation from Y Combinator, Thin Line Capital, Zee Prime Capital and Founder Factor.

Neuron is developing a new kind of industrial controller — the hardware that coordinates sensors, motors and other equipment in factories — alongside AI-powered software that lets engineers describe what they want a machine to do in ordinary language.

Recent findings suggest that its system generates control code that engineers can inspect, modify and test in simulation before deploying it to real equipment. The goal is to reduce the time and specialized programming knowledge needed to get upcoming production lines up and running.

It has been revealed that the startup says it has already demonstrated its technology on existing factory equipment, including replacing an aging controller on a wood-processing line with roughly three hours of engineering work and eight hours of downtime. It intends to release its Cortex AI Controller commercially in early 2027.

According to recent reports, the investment fits into a broader surge in funding for physical AI — technology that applies artificial intelligence to robots, autonomous vehicles, industrial equipment and other machines in the real world. Startups in those categories raised $47.4 billion globally across 521 deals in the first half of 2026, nearly 4x the amount invested in the second half of 2025, according to Crunchbase data.

Related Crunchbase query: Global Physical AI Venture Funding In 2026.

Sending an experiment into space has traditionally required years of preparation, specialized engineering expertise and a very substantial budget.

Austria-based Tumbleweed wants to bring the cost of entry down to as little as 15,000 euros.

The Vienna startup recently raised 6.9 million euros (roughly $8 million) in seed funding led by PactVC, with participation from Vanagon Ventures, Prototype Capital and EWOR, among other investors. The company describes it as the largest space-tech seed round raised in Austria to date.

Tumbleweed develops standardized containers, called Pods, that allow researchers and companies to conduct experiments in microgravity without building their own satellites or navigating the complex certification process required for space missions.

In a recent development, customers can place their experiments inside the pre-certified containers, which provide power and communications capabilities while in orbit. The startup handles the logistics of launching the payloads and transmitting experimental data back to Earth.

Industry observers note that unlike many space startups still working toward their first launch, Tumbleweed has already put hardware in orbit. Its inaugural Oasis Alpha satellite launched in July carrying experiments for four paying customers, including research into biological processes and space-resource technologies. The mission was fully booked a year before launch.

Tumbleweed says its newly introduced funding will help it carry out three more missions in 2027 and develop a next-generation spacecraft that would allow customers to bring physical samples back to Earth beginning in 2028.

It has been revealed that tumbleweed is part of a growing European space startup ecosystem, although funding remains concentrated elsewhere. As of late August, European companies had attracted about 10% of global space-tech venture investment in 2026, compared with the more than 60% going to U.S. startups, Crunchbase data demonstrates.

Related Crunchbase query: Space And Satellite Tech Startup Funding.

Amazon is buying Decart’s AI chip software for a reported $7.5B and bringing its founders aboard

💡 Key Takeaways
  • by Todd Bishop on Nov 23, 2026 at 8:25 amNovember 23, 2026 at 8:27 am.
  • Amazon confirmed Monday morning that it will acquire Decart’s AI optimization technology, known as the Decart Optimization Stack, and bring on the 3-year-old startup’s founders and team of AI researchers and engineers.
  • Sources indicate that amazon didn’t disclose financial terms.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

by Todd Bishop on Nov 23, 2026 at 8:25 amNovember 23, 2026 at 8:27 am.

Amazon confirmed Monday morning that it will acquire Decart’s AI optimization technology, known as the Decart Optimization Stack, and bring on the 3-year-old startup’s founders and team of AI researchers and engineers.

Sources indicate that amazon didn’t disclose financial terms. Amazon agreed to pay about $7.5 billion for the assets, Bloomberg reported, citing a person familiar with the matter. The deal is tied to performance targets over five years, Globes reported.

Recent findings suggest that the deal could boost Amazon’s push to compete with Nvidia, which sells most of the chips used for training and running AI models today. Amazon makes its own AI chips, called Trainium, and has signaled plans to start selling them directly to other companies, beyond its own AWS data centers.

“We believe we’re going to have a very significant business selling chips externally,” CEO Andy Jassy said on the manufacturer’s earnings call last month.

Amazon confirmed the deal the same day Nvidia’s board reinstated Jensen Huang as CEO, ending a leadership shakeup at the chipmaker that put CFO Colette Kress in the interim role.

Decart’s software is designed to get more performance out of each chip, one of the main selling points Amazon needs to win those external customers. Microsoft is building its own Maia chips, mainly for its own AI services, and Google has its TPUs.

Decart’s software has also run on chips from Nvidia and Google. Amazon didn’t say whether that will continue.

“Every leap forward in AI starts with getting more out of every chip,” stated Peter DeSantis, Amazon’s senior vice president of foundational AI models, custom silicon and quantum computing, in the blog post announcing the acquisition.

Industry observers note that decart’s three co-founders are joining Amazon: CEO Dean Leitersdorf, his brother Orian Leitersdorf and Moshe Shalev. Amazon isn’t buying Decart’s AI models, Bloomberg reported. Those include Lucy, which edits live video in real time, and Oasis, which generates interactive virtual worlds.

Sources indicate that the deal runs through Annapurna Labs, Amazon’s chip unit, and Decart’s technology will be used to improve performance on Amazon’s Trainium and Inferentia AI chips, according to Globes. The Israeli business publication reported that Annapurna co-founder Nafea Bshara led the negotiations for Amazon.

The founders, who own about 64% of Decart, have committed to stay at Amazon for five years and could receive about $4.8 billion collectively, Globes reported.

Amazon bought Annapurna, also founded in Israel, in 2015 for a reported $350 million. Its engineers went on to design Trainium and Amazon’s other custom chips.

Amazon and Decart have worked together since 2025. Decart was among the first customers on Trainium3, and Amazon said last December that Decart was running real-time video four times faster on Trainium at half the cost of GPUs.

In a recent development, the deal follows Amazon’s release last month of TorchNeuron, a tool that runs common AI code on Trainium with minimal changes. Both moves target the software advantage that has kept developers on Nvidia hardware, as GeekWire explained when the talks surfaced in October.

Decart drew interest from other major buyers before Amazon. Anthropic was in talks to acquire it for about $6 billion, Bloomberg reported in August, before it walked away in September. Nvidia held earlier acquisition talks, according to CTech, and invested in Decart’s $300 million funding round in May.

“From day one, our mission has been to redefine the boundaries of what AI can do and to make it dramatically more efficient along the way,” Dean Leitersdorf said in Amazon’s announcement. “Joining Amazon gives our team the scale, the customers, and the infrastructure to pursue that mission faster than we could on our own.”.

The deal is subject to regulatory clearance. Amazon didn’t say what happens to Decart’s AI models or to its existing customers, such as eBay, which is also an investor in the startup.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

AI-assisted summary, reviewed by NullTX editors.

Nanbeige4.3-33B matches Qwen3.8-27B at 20 on the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index but uses 158K output tokens per task against 110K. Here is what that costs locally.

Sources indicate that two models just posted the same score. One needed 158,000 output tokens per task to get there. The other needed 110,000.

Sources indicate that nanbeige4.3-33B, a dense 33-billion-parameter reasoning model from the foundation model team at BOSS Zhipin, scores 20 on the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index v5. According to Artificial Analysis's evaluation, published November 5, that matches Qwen3.8 27B at its xhigh reasoning setting. The model is open weights under Apache 2.0, accepts text only, and has a 524K-token context window.

It has been revealed that behind the tie sits a gap in effort. Artificial Analysis indicates Nanbeige used 158K output tokens per Intelligence Index task against 110K for Qwen3.8 27B, about 44% more. That weighted average covers answer and reasoning tokens across all nine v5 evaluations, including agentic tool-use turns. For anyone running these models, tokens translate into time, electricity or money, so the same score doesn't mean the same cost.

In a recent development, the Intelligence Index v5 combines nine evaluations, among them AA-Briefcase, AutomationBench-AA, Terminal-Bench 4.0, FrontierCode 2.0 and AA-Omniscience. A score of 20 puts Nanbeige well above the 6 of Muse Glimmer, a 30B model in the same comparison. Artificial Analysis also notes that Nanbeige sets a new Pareto-optimal point for Intelligence Index against total parameters, since both it and Qwen3.8 27B are dense models. A larger mixture-of-experts model like DeepSeek V4.1 Flash, by contrast, scores 33 while activating only 16B parameters per token.

The model card Nanbeige's lab published on Hugging Face describes the base model, positioned as the flagship teacher for the Nanbeige4.3 series. The lab claims it will distill agentic capabilities into smaller models, such as an upcoming 3B version. On base-model benchmarks, the card shows 66.9 on MMLU-Pro against 59.3 for Gemma4-31B-Base. Those figures belong to the base model and are separate from the reasoning model's Intelligence Index result.

The two models reach 20 by different routes. Nanbeige scores 30% on Terminal-Bench 4.0 against 6% for Qwen, and 16% on the CritPt v2 Hard Subset against 4%. It also edges Qwen on AutomationBench-AA, 53% to 48%.

According to recent reports, elsewhere, it falls behind. On AA-Briefcase v1.1 it scores 1162 Elo against 1391, on FrontierCode 2.0 11% against 15%, and on HLE-Diamond 7% against 15%. The knowledge test tells the most distinctive story. On AA-Omniscience v1.1, Nanbeige scores -4 against Qwen's -6, with an 18% hallucination rate against 29%. Yet it answers only 29% of questions against 43%, declines 71% of them and gets 12% correct against 17%.

For general question answering, Qwen's higher accuracy is the better result.

Output tokens aren't a vanity metric. A reasoning model writes out its thinking as tokens, and every one costs decode time. If both models ran at the same speed on the same hardware, Nanbeige would take about 44% longer to finish a typical task.

It has been revealed that local decoding adds a second factor. Generation is usually limited by memory bandwidth, because each fresh token requires reading the model's weights, and a 33B dense model reads about 20% more weight data per token than a 27B dense model. Assuming the same quantization and the same memory-bound hardware, those two effects compound to roughly 1.7 times the wall-clock time per task. That figure is a back-of-the-envelope calculation, not a measured result.

Nor is there a hosted alternative to soften the blow. Artificial Analysis lists no confirmed public first-party or third-party APIs for Nanbeige, so unlike Qwen, which is sold per token through Alibaba's API, the cost is the hardware you run it on and the time it takes.

Artificial Analysis describes the model as small enough to run locally on a laptop, which holds true with a caveat. The weights are published in BF16, which at 33 billion parameters means roughly 66 GB, far beyond almost any laptop. At 8-bit, the weights fall to about 33 GB, and at 4-bit to about 17 GB, plus memory for the context cache. A machine with 24 GB of unified memory or more can plausibly hold a 4-bit build, though a long context will push it.

Recent findings suggest that the vendor's own quickstart points the other way. The card's SGLang and vLLM examples both set tensor parallelism across four GPUs, which suggests the reference deployment is a multi-GPU server. Its Transformers example also enables trust_remote_code=True, which runs code from the repository. Reading that code first is the safer move, as is serving the model through vLLM or SGLang instead.

Quantization changes the model, too. The Intelligence Index numbers come from Artificial Analysis's own runs, so a 4-bit local build may score somewhat lower, or generate different token counts, than the version they evaluated.

It has been revealed that this release is a clean example of why a headline score isn't enough. Nanbeige delivers Qwen-level results at 33B, with strengths in terminal tasks and physics reasoning and a more cautious answering style. The price for those strengths is length.

Sources indicate that anyone choosing between the two should run both on their own workload and record three numbers: the score on their tasks, output tokens per task and seconds per task on their hardware. For terminal-heavy, agentic work, Nanbeige's profile may justify the longer runs. For knowledge-heavy or latency-sensitive work, Qwen's shorter, more accurate answers look stronger.

Three signals are worth watching next: whether the 3B distilled version keeps the model's strengths, whether other labs report the same token behavior, and whether anyone publishes quantized local benchmarks. Until then, the simplest summary is also the most accurate: same score, different bill.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Bitcoin (BTC) fell as low as $55,081 on Nov. 21, its lowest price since September 2024, according to TradingView data. The cryptocurrency then bounced back and was trading at $60,583 on Sunday, after it opened November at $77,425.

Recent findings suggest that bitcoin has lost 21.6% so far in November 2026, according to CryptoRank. The last time Bitcoin had a worse month was June 2022, when the cryptocurrency lost 37.9%, according to the same data.

In a recent development, the four-year cycle theory ties Bitcoin's market cycles to halvings, and its supporters point to 2014, 2018 and 2022 as the years when each bear market went through its final sell-off. In this context, 2026 is the next year in that row, and the next Bitcoin halving is expected in April 2028. The previous three halvings took place in July 2016, May 2020 and April 2024.

Bitcoin set its record above $1,100 in late 2013. In February 2014, the Japanese exchange Mt. Gox, which handled most Bitcoin trading in 2013, filed for bankruptcy after it lost about 850,000 BTC. In November 2014, Bitcoin gained 11.6%, according to CryptoRank, but December of that year brought a 15.3% drop, and the bottom below $200 came in January 2015.

Sources indicate that in December 2017, Bitcoin reached a record near $20,000 on the back of the ICO boom, and during 2018, the ICO market dried up. In November 2018, the crypto market crashed after the Bitcoin Cash hard fork and the so-called hash war between the two camps of miners, and Bitcoin lost 36.4% that month. The cryptocurrency then lost another 6.4% in December 2018 and set its cycle low at about $3,200 in the middle of that month.

In a recent development, the 2021 record near $69,000 came in November 2021. In May 2022, the Terra ecosystem collapsed, and in July of that year, Celsius and Three Arrows Capital filed for bankruptcy. In November of that year, the FTX exchange went bankrupt. Bitcoin lost 16.1% in November 2022 and set its bear market bottom at around $15,500 on Nov. 21, 2022, four years to the day before the latest low. December of that year brought a 3.7% loss, and in January 2023, Bitcoin gained 39.9%.

In the current cycle, Bitcoin set its record above $126,000 in October 2025. In 2026, Bitcoin has lost value in six of the 11 months so far, according to CryptoRank. On Nov. 20, the cryptocurrency fell below $60,000 for the first time since July, and the decline continued the next day.

The latest drop comes amid a broad sell-off on Wall Street, where technology and AI stocks came under pressure, and amid expectations of further interest-rate hikes by the Federal Reserve.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Famous Bitcoin (BTC) advocate and investor Bill Miller IV said that it is much easier to value the world's largest cryptocurrency than AI investments, even though Bitcoin does not produce any cash flow.

He noted that this has to do with the expectations investors have when it comes to these two assets, specifically regarding their capacity to deliver future profits.

In a recent X post, Miller, who is the chairman and chief investment officer of Miller Value Partners, broke down why he thinks that it's easier to make an investment case for Bitcoin than for AI companies.

Recent findings suggest that "Bitcoin and AI owners have different expectations. The owners of AI expect companies will one day produce free cash flow. Bitcoin owners never did or will expect this," Miller said.

And the end result is that "the valuation case is still much easier for Bitcoin than AI.".

Simply put, when investors buy stocks in AI companies, there is an expectation that at some point these companies will deliver significant profits and free cash flow.

Free cash flow is the money a tech giant produces from its operations after capital expenditures. This is a significant metric for understanding the value of a company.

However, when it comes to AI companies, it can be difficult to assign a value because investors need to try to determine what kind of revenue these companies will generate, how much they will invest in infrastructure, and when these investments will start to deliver sufficient returns.

Miller has made it a point to push back against the argument that Bitcoin does not have value because it doesn't produce cash flow.

In a commentary from June 30, Miller explained that the traditional way of looking at intrinsic value, which revolves around future cash flows, doesn't really capture the potential of Bitcoin as a decentralized monetary network.

Instead, Miller mentioned that Bitcoin's value could be determined by comparing its potential role within the global financial system to that of gold.

It has been revealed that in his view, Bitcoin could theoretically reach about $1.4 million per coin if it achieved a valuation similar to gold's. At least, that's what he calculated at the time.

From dorm delivery robots to real‑world video games, UW students show off inventions

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • by Grace Kaste on Nov 23, 2026 at 3:29 pmNovember 23, 2026 at 3:29 pm.
  • Recent advancements in AI have cast a cloud over college students studying software engineering.
  • But at CSEED’s Buildspace Demo Day last week, 60 undergraduates in the University of Washington student club indicated that AI hasn’t dampened their drive to create.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

by Grace Kaste on Nov 23, 2026 at 3:29 pmNovember 23, 2026 at 3:29 pm.

Recent advancements in AI have cast a cloud over college students studying software engineering. Jobs seem to be disappearing every day, while coursework can be done by chatbots.

But at CSEED’s Buildspace Demo Day last week, 60 undergraduates in the University of Washington student club indicated that AI hasn’t dampened their drive to create. If anything, it’s allowing them to build things they wouldn’t have been able to before.

It has been revealed that “We’re seeing projects that normal college students would not be expected to make,” club co-president Leonard Paya remarked. “As AI becomes more advanced, you can see how fast they scale up their knowledge and execute on things that are truly amazing.”.

Recent findings suggest that CSEED, founded a few years ago and already one of UW’s largest clubs, supports aspiring software designers and engineers. It’s funded by the Paul G. Allen School of Computer Science & Engineering, as well as venture capital firms such as AI House, Madrona and Pack Ventures. Its members have gone on to join startup incubators including Y Combinator, Z Fellows and Founders Inc.

Industry observers note that twice a year, CSEED accepts applications for its Buildspace cohort, a program for students with hardware, software or design pitches. Over six weeks, the cohort meets up for build sessions, and they also receive mentorship, supplies and AI credits. Demo Day on Nov. 17 at the UW’s Gates Center marked the conclusion of the sixth Buildspace cohort, with 30 inventions presented to 150 audience members.

“We’ve brought together curious and ambitious students from all backgrounds,” vice president Amy Lu mentioned. “CSEED gives them the community to turn their ideas into reality.”.

One of the most technically advanced ideas presented was DubDash, a fully autonomous robot for delivering food orders from the dining hall to dorms.

It has been revealed that “The best part of this is that these people were all freshmen who hadn’t yet taken robotics classes,” Paya said. “Who would have thought that four freshmen could make a fully fledged robot in six weeks?”.

It has been revealed that according to junior and Buildspace co-director Talal Kheiry, that’s a testament to AI. Buildspace members receive AI credits, which Kheiry remarked have changed everything.

“AI helps guide them through the gritty parts of the project, so they can just focus on the creative parts without worrying about the technical stuff,” Kheiry noted.

Sources indicate that other inventions offered a glimpse into what’s on students’ minds these days. From notification-silencing focus apps to social connectors and mental health education platforms, nearly half of them had to do with curbing the effects of social media.

“Social media isn’t social anymore,” Junaid Akhtar told the audience as he and his three team members presented. “It’s just a place to see media. Our goal is to make social media bring people together again.”.

Industry observers note that his team’s presentation was the audience’s favorite: a satirical pitch for a platform they call FeedPicks, which creates live ranked prediction markets of friends’ social media feeds. Their demo won an award for “best energy” at the end of the night.

It has been revealed that other inventions sought to get owners off their screens altogether. Joe Chae, a freshman at the Allen School, presented Pidgin, a Tinder-style app that helps users who want to practice each other’s languages to meet up in real life.

“I came to UW hoping to meet some Korean international students here and learn to speak Korean with my relatives, but I didn’t meet anyone,” Chae stated. “So I thought, what if I made an app that could help me find someone who speaks Korean natively and wants to learn English?”.

Also focused on the real world was Sasha Bogatirev’s Hadden Cybernetics. Bogatirev built a wearable gaming console that takes in information from a user’s environment and turns it into a game.

“The person has to pay attention to their surroundings,” Bogatirev stated. “The idea is to prompt the imagination as much as possible for someone to experience another world.”.

His prototype used the ESP32-S3 microcontroller to render the visuals onto wearable glasses. An nRF chip on the wristband takes in scripted gestures, which he trained to turn a player’s gestures into shields, lightning strikes and fireballs. Next, he plans to add haptics using hardware supplied by CSEED.

Recent findings suggest that andrew Edwards also built a video game accessory: cStar, which is an open source, low-cost console that can play a game on any TV screen by loading it onto an SD card and popping it into a 3D-printed box. Inside that box is a microcontroller like you’d find inside a stopwatch or a microwave, unlike the highly complicated circuitry used by an Xbox or PlayStation.

“We were able to squeeze HDMI video out of the microcontroller, which allows us to show 2D and 3D graphics on a home television set,” Edwards said. “Since the games are based on standard SD cards, a curious programmer can just write software on the computer, stick it onto an SD card, put it in the console and you’re ready to play.”.

Other notable inventions presented at Demo Day:.

This cohort was their largest and most competitive yet. Next up, under the guidance of club advisor and Allen School professor Kurtis Heimerl, CSEED is looking to expand. They’ve started hosting build sessions every Saturday that are open to non-students.

Recent findings suggest that to do that, they’ll need to fundraise. According to CSEED co-president Benya Vahdat, they’ve already used up their Allen School allotment for the year, and they’re now in the process of raising money from donors. They recently incorporated as CSEED Foundation and received nonprofit status in Washington state.

“We want to grow this mentality of building, and maybe expand across campuses not just in Washington but across the country,” Vahdat stated. “Maybe even globally.”.

Freshworks alums raise $53M to take on Salesforce, HubSpot with AI-native CRM

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (870 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: TechCrunch

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Dreamteam, a startup founded by former Freshworks executives, has raised $53 million to challenge Salesforce and HubSpot with its AI-native CRM, betting that AI can finally shake up a market where established players have so far proved difficult to dislodge.
  • Recent findings suggest that the funding comprises seed and Series A rounds, led by Together Fund and Accel respectively, with participation from Premji Invest.
  • In a recent development, traditional CRMs depend on salespeople to manually record customer interactions and keep deal information up to date.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Dreamteam, a startup founded by former Freshworks executives, has raised $53 million to challenge Salesforce and HubSpot with its AI-native CRM, betting that AI can finally shake up a market where established players have so far proved difficult to dislodge.

Recent findings suggest that the funding comprises seed and Series A rounds, led by Together Fund and Accel respectively, with participation from Premji Invest. The San Francisco-based startup declined to disclose the size of each round or its valuation.

In a recent development, traditional CRMs depend on salespeople to manually record customer interactions and keep deal information up to date. That often leaves businesses with incomplete or outdated information. Dreamteam aims to eliminate much of that work by automatically capturing context from sources including emails and customer conversations. It also uses AI agents to handle tasks such as follow-ups, meeting preparation, and pipeline monitoring.

Industry observers note that dreamteam co-founder and CEO Anand Venkatraman (pictured above, right) told TechCrunch that he had repeatedly encountered problems with traditional CRM platforms over more than 25 years in enterprise software, including at Salesforce and Freshworks. Salespeople spent considerable time updating records, yet managers still struggled to get a reliable picture of their business. “In all these years, I have never come across an instance where I could click a button and get a forecast from the CRM,” he remarked.

That experience led Venkatraman to co-found Dreamteam in 2025 with Senthil Kanthaswamy (pictured above, center), who spent more than nine years at Freshworks, most recently as a product leader at Freshservice, and Ramesh Parthasarathy (pictured above, left), who previously worked on AI and platform engineering at Freshworks.

According to recent reports, at the heart of Dreamteam’s CRM is what it calls the Company Brain. This acts as virtual memory, pulling together information from emails, meetings, and other customer interactions to build a shared record of customer relationships. Four built-in AI agents use that information to research prospects, draft follow-up emails, flag potential risks to deals, and configure CRM workflows, with sales teams retaining control over what gets sent to customers.

Recent findings suggest that dreamteam has signed up more than 100 customers across 13 countries in the three months since it began actively selling its product, with most paying for the service, Venkatraman noted. The startup has also replaced established CRM platforms at several businesses, including Salesforce at healthcare tech giant DMS Health and HubSpot at other customers.

Sources indicate that the advertising sales team at media streaming firm Plex also chose Dreamteam over HubSpot and other AI-native CRM alternatives, Venkatraman told TechCrunch. Plex’s co-founder and chief product officer Scott Olechowski noted Dreamteam’s ability to integrate with AI tools already used across the company was a “game changer.”.

It has been revealed that replacing established CRM platforms at scale may prove more difficult. In a blog post earlier this year, venture capital firm Andreessen Horowitz (a16z) argued that while AI could transform how businesses manage customer relationships, existing CRMs are likely to remain the systems where customer records are stored, with a new generation of AI-powered tools capturing much of the value by working on top of them.

Venkatraman acknowledged that Salesforce and HubSpot are unlikely to disappear anytime soon, but noted that their entrenched positions do not guarantee they will dominate the next generation of CRM software.

“We see this as an electric-car moment for systems of record,” he said, adding that AI requires a fundamental rethink of how CRMs are built — not simply adding latest features to existing platforms.

Recent findings suggest that kanthaswamy believes startups have a window of two to five years to gain ground before established CRM providers can fully adapt to AI. Rebuilding software around a fundamentally different architecture takes time, he stated, giving newer companies an opportunity to attract customers while incumbents work to overhaul their existing products.

Dreamteam also looks to expand beyond sales into other parts of the customer lifecycle, including onboarding, customer support, and upselling. The startup already has a feature called Magic Apps that allows users to create custom applications and dashboards within the CRM using natural-language instructions, without writing code.

Currently, Dreamteam employs more than 35 people, with its engineering team based in Chennai and its go-to-market operations in the United States. Kanthaswamy said the startup aims to reach eight figures in annual revenue by the end of 2027, though he declined to disclose the startup’s current revenue.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • Recent findings suggest that forty-six attorneys general have joined a Fresh York-led antitrust investigation of Facebook, officials declared this morning, raising the stakes in a sweeping bipartisan probe that could result in massive changes to the firm’s business practices.
  • In a recent development, limited partners or LPs  — the pension funds, the university endowments, the family offices that largely provide venture firms with their spending money — are receiving a lot of attention from venture capitalists, some of it unwanted.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that softBank founder Masayoshi Son vowed tonight to “double down” on its investment in WeWork as he confirmed aims for a $9.5 billion rescue package that will provide up to $1.7 billion to WeWork cofounder Adam Neumann in exchange for cutting most ties with the company and will give SoftBank an 80 percent stake in the business. In a statement tonight in New York, SoftBank said it would “accelerate” WeWork’s path to profitability and positive free cash flow. More here in the Financial Times.

Recent findings suggest that forty-six attorneys general have joined a Fresh York-led antitrust investigation of Facebook, officials declared this morning, raising the stakes in a sweeping bipartisan probe that could result in massive changes to the firm’s business practices. The Washington Post has more here.

In a recent development, limited partners or LPs  — the pension funds, the university endowments, the family offices that largely provide venture firms with their spending money — are receiving a lot of attention from venture capitalists, some of it unwanted. VCs have begun knocking down their doors with requests for fresh capital commitments so they’ll have money to invest if the market cools down.

In a recent development, the problem is, many of these LPs are already over-allocated. LPs traditionally invest in many asset classes, such as public equities, and they allocate a small percentage of their portfolio to venture capital. Suddenly, they’re finding they’ve forked over more than they’d intended to VCs.

There are several reasons for this situation. First, VCs are returning to them ever faster for more capital  — sometimes in less than two years’ time  — because they are in vesting at such a furious pace.

It has been revealed that compounding the problem, not all LPs have received returns from their VC investments that they can recycle into new venture capital allocations. In some cases, this capital is still tied up in startups that are raising much more money than in the past and staying private longer. “We have some large exposures to blue chip names where IPOs have been rumored to be coming for a long time already, and now it’s maybe 2021, maybe 2022,” says one manager who asked not to be named. In other cases where startups have gone public, falling prices have prompted VCs to hang on to their shares instead of distribute them.

The result is that LPs are having to cut back on the number of managers they can fund, and that could mean bad news for venture capitalists and startups alike. These LPs don’t have much choice. As the LP explains it, “We have a pretty structured allocation process, and we’re really trying to be creative,” she claims. One venture manager who reappeared too promptly for more money was  “easy to walk away from,” says this person. “Others, we’re having to do financial backflips for them to remain strong partners.” Either way, this LP adds, “We can’t add any newly introduced relationships right now,” meaning new venture teams in particular are out of luck. “When [VCs] shorten their fundraising cycle by nine months to a year, you can only squeeze the balloon so much.”.

In a recent development, softBank’s $100 billion “Vision Fund” is one big reason LPs find themselves in their current predicament. From the moment SoftBank began waving money around several years ago, it released a vicious cycle. According to Chris Douvos, whose investment firm, Ahoy Capital, owns stakes in such venture funds as True Ventures and First Round Capital, “When Andreessen Horowitz hit the scene a decade ago, they changed the tempo of investing and everyone got more aggressive in their dealmaking as a response. Then SoftBank entered the picture in a big way, and it was like a16z on steroids.”.

Sources indicate that blueground, a six-year-old, New York-based startup providing turnkey flexible rental apartments, has raised $50 million in Series B funding, roughly six months after raising $20 million in Series A funding. Industry observers note that AHEAD OF THE fall, I knew I was going to need a sickening boot that could just fall in line with my entire wardrobe. I don’t spend much on clothes, because, well, I wear-test them for a living, but when it comes to shopping for footwear I’ve been guilty of dropping more bread than I’d like to admit. There are times I don’t mind dishing out a little cash for a well-made shoe, especially if that means I’ll have it for years to come. One style that was calling my name that I couldn’t resist was Our Legacy’s Camion Boot.

Industry observers note that if you’ve spent any time scrolling through men’s fashion content on Instagram or TikTok, chances are you’ve come across it. Even actor Paul Mescal has been spotted wearing the boot during a press tour for “Hamnet” in London. The sleek leather ankle-high boot has become something of a cult favorite among stylish guys, thanks to its distinctive square toe and minimalist design, which helps make any simple outfit look 10 times cooler. Whether I’m wearing baggy jeans or relaxed trousers, The Camion Boot adds a certain je ne sais quoi that my cowboy or lace-up boots can’t replicate. And by no means does the boot feel squishy like your favorite pair of sneakers, but the Vibram rubber outsole keeps my feet comfortable on days when I'm standing and walking around for hours.

It has been revealed that for those unfamiliar, Our Legacy is a Swedish fashion label founded in Stockholm in 2005. Over the past two decades, the brand has built a loyal following for taking menswear staples and remixing them with unique proportions, fabrics, and details. The Camion Boot is one of its most recognizable designs, decorated with an inside zip closure and a metal branded tab. It feels timeless without looking boring. Even though it’s easy on the eyes, its $700-plus price tag is tough on the wallet. Luckily, you don’t have to cough up designer money to get the look. Below, I’ve gathered a list of affordable alternatives to the Our Legacy Camion Boot that deliver the same vibe for a fraction of the price.

If you’re looking for a boot that captures the sleek appeal of Our Legacy’s Camion without spending a small fortune, Florsheim’s Medford is a strong contender. The leather upper has a subtle burnished finish that delivers a slightly worn-in look, as the clean silhouette makes it easy to dress up or down. I’d pair the brown version with black denim and a chunky sweater for dinner followed by a night out. It also looks sharp with dressy pants and tailored trousers, so you can get plenty of mileage out of it at the office.

Inside, there’s a fully cushioned, removable footbed made with OrthoLite rebound foam, which helps absorb impact and provides a little extra bounce underfoot. This comes in handy if you’re spending hours on your feet. The leather is also designed to feel comfortable from the jump, so you shouldn’t have to suffer through a lengthy break-in period. And while I wouldn’t treat these like rain boots, the leather construction makes them a practical choice for everyday wear, especially with proper care. You don’t have to settle for a black colorway either—it comes in a few different brown shades as well.

Recent findings suggest that zara offers a squared-off toe that is unapologetically bold, giving the boot that exaggerated, fashion-forward shape that makes Our Legacy’s Camion so recognizable. I’d argue the toe is even more pronounced here, which isn’t necessarily a bad thing if you want your footwear to stand out more. I’d style these with relaxed jeans that fall just over the shaft or wide-leg trousers to really lean into the silhouette.

According to recent reports, the biggest difference comes down to the material. Unlike the Camion, Zara’s version is made from polyurethane, a synthetic material that mimics the appearance of leather, so it’s a budget-friendly pick. It’s generally easy to wipe clean, but it won’t develop the same natural patina as genuine leather and can eventually peel or crack with repeated wear.

Steve Madden’s Ronco might be the closest style to the Camion boot as far as design is concerned. It nailed the features from the stitched detailing across the upper right down to the substantial rubber sole. The latter is worth pointing out because it gives the boot a similar sturdy, grounded appearance, while the 1.5-inch heel adds just enough height without going overboard. Sure, the rounded toe isn’t quite as boxy as the Camion’s signature square shape, but the overall silhouette comes pretty darn close. And at a fraction of the price, it’s hard not to appreciate the resemblance.

According to recent reports, I’m especially drawn to the brown leather version, which has a rich, burnished finish that shifts between lighter and darker shades, giving it a slightly weathered, vintage effect. It has a lot more depth than your standard brown boot. I’d pair these with relaxed denim and a chunky sweater for an easy apple-picking look, or throw them on with tailored trousers and a leather jacket for something a little sharper. There’s also a black option if you prefer to keep things simple.

Banana Republic takes a different approach with this Italian leather Chelsea-style boot. The silhouette is sleek and understated, but what really caught my attention is the leather’s distressed finish. It has that subtly weathered, almost cracked appearance you’d normally expect from a well-loved pair of boots, except the detail is already built into the design. It gives the shoe a vintage feel without looking like something that’s been sitting in the back of your closet for a decade. I also appreciate that this pair doesn’t try too hard to replicate the Camion. Instead, it offers a more classic interpretation that feels right at home with the rest of my wardrobe. I’d wear it with pleated trousers and a button-down for the office, then swap in straight-leg jeans and a crewneck for a day of shopping.

Camper has a knack for taking classic footwear and giving it a slightly unexpected twist, which perfectly describes the Dean Boot. The black-and-burgundy color combination immediately caught my attention because it’s subtle enough to wear with anything, but there’s also a richness to the pebbled leather texture that makes it more interesting than your standard black ankle boot. I’d pair these with relaxed black trousers or dark denim and let the boots bring a little personality to the outfit.

Recent findings suggest that the upper combines calfskin leather with recycled PET, which is plastic recycled from materials like water bottles, and latex for added flexibility. Underfoot, there’s a removable OrthoLite footbed for cushioning and an XL Extralight EVA outsole, a lightweight foam-based material designed to absorb impact without weighing you down. I also appreciate the pull tab, which makes slipping them on a little easier, especially since there’s no traditional side zipper. Plus, the defined heel and outsole design offer some stability for walking, though actual traction will depend on the surface.

I’ve owned my Frye boots for about a year now, and they’ve more than earned their place in my footwear rotation. They’re so versatile, I can wear them with a suit one day and jeans, a T-shirt, and leather jacket the next. The design is minimal with a premium leather upper and stitching around the edge that adds to the sturdy construction. Comfort-wise, I didn’t have to deal with that annoying break-in period that often comes with leather boots.

After a year of wear, the leather has started developing some natural creases, but I look at it like it adds character. There’s enough wiggle room in the toe box that my feet don’t feel cramped. The inner side zipper is another detail I’ve come to appreciate, especially when I’m taking them off after a long day. I’ve put these through their paces on city streets and even worn them in the rain. I found the leather has dried rapidly after getting wet, and the grip has felt secure underfoot. Sure, they’re not cheap, but considering how well they’ve held up and how often I wear them, I’d say I’ve already gotten my money’s worth.

In a recent development, if you’re a guy who gets suited up more often than not, Suitsupply’s leather boot deserves a spot on your radar. It’s the dressiest option on this list, with a smooth, semi-matte leather, which catches just enough light to look sharp without being overly shiny. It also has a fine, tight grain, which gives the surface a supple finish. I’d wear these with a charcoal suit or tailored black trousers and a crisp button-down, for a holiday party. But I would also style them with dark denim and a cashmere sweater. The side zipper makes getting dressed a little less of a production in the morning. The leather sole adds to that dress-shoe appeal, although I’d be a little more cautious wearing these on slick pavement.

Now, these are the most expensive boots on this list, but because they’re made in Italy using Blake-stitched construction, a technique that stitches the upper directly to the sole for a slimmer, more flexible profile than you’d typically get with bulkier boot construction. You can expect some natural creasing after a few wears, particularly where your foot bends, but that doesn’t mean the leather is cracking.

To keep it from drying out, Suitsupply recommends applying shoe polish at least once a month, or more frequently if you’re wearing them daily. This helps maintain the color and adds some protection against moisture. I’d also work in a leather conditioner whenever the material starts feeling dry to help prevent actual cracking. It’s a little extra maintenance, sure, but worthwhile if you’re investing this much in a pair of boots.

Five Forged Receipts Drained $304.5K From Ankr's Ethereum Bridge Using a 0.0044 ankrETH Deposit

📅 10 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1061 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Nulltx

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • SlowMist says five forged receipts with valid signatures let an attacker drain about $304,500 from Ankr's Ethereum bridge using one old Optimism deposit.
  • Industry observers note that on November 9, an attacker drained about $304,500 from Ankr's Ethereum cross-chain bridge.
  • All five carried valid signatures from the bridge's trusted consensus signer.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

AI-assisted summary, reviewed by NullTX editors.

SlowMist says five forged receipts with valid signatures let an attacker drain about $304,500 from Ankr's Ethereum bridge using one old Optimism deposit. Here is how the check failed.Every one of the five receipts was signed by the bridge's own trusted signer. Every one pointed to a deposit that had already been paid out.

Industry observers note that on November 9, an attacker drained about $304,500 from Ankr's Ethereum cross-chain bridge. According to SlowMist's alert, the attacker built five forged receipts that all referenced a single legitimate Optimism transaction, changing the recipient, the token and the withdrawal amount in each one.

All five carried valid signatures from the bridge's trusted consensus signer.

The reused transaction was tiny: a deposit of about 0.0044 ankrETH made on Optimism on November 3, which SlowMist's analysis states had already been redeemed on Ethereum the same day. Six days later, that one settled deposit was cited five times. The incident is recorded in the SlowMist Hacked database.Blockaid flagged the exploit as it unfolded, at about 08:42 UTC, with roughly $292,000 already gone. SlowMist followed at 09:14 UTC with the higher $304,500 estimate and an explanation of the forged receipts. Ankr paused withdrawals, and no recovery blueprint has been confirmed.

According to recent reports, the design is common across lock-and-release bridges. A user deposits on the source chain, and an off-chain set of signers watches for that deposit and signs a receipt describing it. The destination contract, in this case Ankr's Ethereum bridge contract, checks that the receipt carries a valid signature and then releases the funds.That setup makes the signers the source of truth. The contract can't see Optimism, so it leans on the signature to prove the deposit happened. The weak point sits in the gap between "the signer signed this" and "this really happened." A contract that treats the first as proof of the second inherits every mistake the signing process makes.

Industry observers note that the Ethereum transactions show the attacker extracted about 82.91 ankrETH, 515,206 ankrPOL and 7.98 million ANKR tokens. Blockaid described the five withdraw calls as using the tiny Optimism deposit to unlock the bridge's locked inventory and send it to a new wallet.The mix of assets tells its own story. Each forged receipt named a different token and amount, which suggests the attacker picked targets based on what the bridge held. That fits receipts built entirely by the attacker, apart from the one real transaction reference. Anyone wanting to trace them can open the bridge contract's transaction list on Etherscan and filter for the five `withdraw` calls on November 9.

According to recent reports, the most important fact is still missing. SlowMist says the origin of the unauthorized signatures is under investigation, and it hasn't confirmed whether the signers were compromised.A valid signature on a forged receipt has a short list of explanations. A signing key, or the service holding it, could have been accessed. A signing service could have been tricked into signing attacker-supplied data. Or the signing logic itself could have a flaw that produces signatures for receipts it shouldn't. Each one points to a different fix: a stolen key means rotating signers, a manipulated service means tightening input validation off-chain, and a logic flaw means rewriting the signing rules.Whichever it turns out to be, the on-chain contract and the off-chain signer both failed to ask the same question. Either one verifying the source event would likely have stopped the attack, and neither did.

Recent findings suggest that the lessons are narrow and practical. Replay protection should key on the immutable identity of the source event, not on the receipt's contents, and a source event should be consumable exactly once. The destination contract should confirm that the receipt's recipient, token and amount match what the source-chain event actually recorded, using a proof or an independent verifier instead of trusting the signer alone.Signer infrastructure needs its own scrutiny. Threshold schemes, hardware-backed keys and strict limits on what a signing service will sign all shrink the damage from a single failure. Rate limits and per-withdrawal caps help as well. A bridge that can release its entire locked inventory in five calls has no brake once a signature check is defeated.Trust in a bridge comes in layers, and one layer rarely holds up alone. Customers with funds in Ankr's bridge should watch for the project's post-mortem and its blueprint for restoring withdrawals. For developers, the question to put to their own code is a blunt one: if a signer signs something false, what stops the contract from believing it?

#190536. Latest Update: After dodging death, battery startup Our Next Energy is now going public

📅 16 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1461 w)
