Latest Update: After dodging death, battery startup Our Next Energy is now going public

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1461 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: TechCrunch

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It’s never been easy to run a battery startup in the U.S.
  • Our Next Energy (ONE) had some close calls, but soon it will go public via SPAC, the company exclusively told TechCrunch.
  • ONE claims it is valued at $600 million pre-money, and it expects the merger with Wen Acquisition Corp.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It’s never been easy to run a battery startup in the U.S. There have been more failures than successes over the last 20 years, and whipsawing federal policy has caused more than a few battery companies to shut shop.

Not all of them die, though. Our Next Energy (ONE) had some close calls, but soon it will go public via SPAC, the company exclusively told TechCrunch.

ONE claims it is valued at $600 million pre-money, and it expects the merger with Wen Acquisition Corp. will bring $400 million in gross proceeds assuming no redemptions. The combined company will trade on the Nasdaq under the ticker “ONEE,” and the pro forma implied equity value is $1 billion.

Industry observers note that over the years, ONE has raised $483 million, according to PitchBook, and at one point was valued at $1.3 billion. It has also received tens of millions of dollars in incentives tied to investments and job creation in Michigan.

Industry observers note that ONE is the brainchild of former Ford and Apple engineer Mujeeb Ijaz, who designed a way for electric vehicles to draw power from two batteries of different chemistries. In ONE’s first setup, it paired lithium-iron-phosphate (LFP) and with a manganese-rich chemistry, which would let each chemistry play to its strengths: LFP could be used day in, day out, while the more fragile but energy-dense, manganese-rich one would work for long, infrequent road trips. An initial prototype traveled over 600 miles on a single charge.

In a recent development, but the EV market didn’t take off as rapidly as anticipated, and automakers wanted to buy at lower prices (usually from China). Both of those reasons helped sink ONE’s first attempt at a Series C in late 2023. The startup had to lay off a chunk of its staff, and eventually vacated its lease for a planned $1.6 billion factory in Michigan.

The rough patch led to Ijaz’s ouster as CEO in December 2023, only to have him return to the position in March 2025 after a new round of funding closed. (His brother’s investment firm co-led the round.).

According to recent reports, part of the critique aimed at ONE during Ijaz’s first tenure as CEO was that the firm spent too much time developing fresh products instead of focusing on one or two, as most startups tend to do. When Ijaz came back to the helm last year, he noted that ONE would leave the automotive market and focus on grid-scale batteries.

Recent findings suggest that ONE isn’t alone in pivoting away from vehicle batteries. American automakers, which had similarly rosy views of EV adoption, also bet big on battery factories and supply chains. When sales didn’t pop in the U.S. like they have in China or Europe, they had to find an outlet for that capacity, and the grid started looking like the obvious target once it started groaning under the weight of AI data centers. Both Ford and GM have confirmed their own energy storage products.

Many upcoming grid-scale batteries use LFP, which is safer and cheaper than those used in most EVs in the U.S., and Ijaz saw an opportunity for ONE there as well. “We go back to the origins of LFP in this country and even to some of the factories that are in China,” he remarked. Indeed, just over a decade ago Ijaz led the automotive division at A123 Systems, the company that first commercialized the chemistry.

Soon, Ijaz saw other opportunities for ONE’s batteries, including defense and locomotives.

In a recent development, the defense play isn’t surprising. Nearly every battery firm I talk with these days mentions defense, in part because it’s a market that Chinese companies can’t play in. Building an American supply chain means that a company can sell batteries at a premium, shielded as they are from Chinese competition. It’s a higher-margin market, though much smaller than EVs.

My recent conversation with Ijaz last week was the first time I’d heard a company pitch rail companies as potential customers, though. Ijaz mentioned ONE is “finding a lot of traction in” that market. The company has built a hybrid locomotive that uses a 2.8 megawatt-hour battery, and another he calls a micro-hybrid, which uses a smaller battery to start the diesel engine faster, similar to a stop-start system on a fossil fuel car or truck.

“Our customers are seeing a 50% improvement in diesel fuel consumption, which is a big deal,” Ijaz noted.

Recent findings suggest that currently, ONE has three business lines, which could be a sign of its old culture creeping back into the picture. But Ijaz stated the addition of defense and rail were driven by the bottom line: Grid-scale battery customers are also “very much like automotive customers, where they were willing to buy from China as long as the price was low enough,” he said.

“Believe me, I would have loved to have made that grid business into the single business of the organization. But the customers would look and then be taken away to a Chinese option because of the pricing, and the tariffs also leading them to that conclusion,” Ijaz remarked. “And so we decided that we needed a more durable market, and we looked for who in the customer base valued an American battery company.”.

According to recent reports, today, ONE operates a pack assembly plant in Novi, Michigan, which can put together packs from cells at a rate of 3 gigawatt-hours per year. The plant uses cells from China-based and non-China-based suppliers, as well as ONE’s own cells from a smaller factory nearby, which is at the moment being upgraded to make 50 megawatt-hours of batteries per year.

Recent findings suggest that in its investor pitch, which TechCrunch has reviewed, ONE distills its business lines into defense and rail. Drones and submarines make up the majority of what ONE sees as a $16.2 billion market. Defense-focused data centers get lumped in there, too, contributing $4.1 billion to the defense business. (That appears to be the main outlet for grid-scale batteries.) The other line, which serves the rail industry, is expected to be worth $28.2 billion.

Both markets are sizable, but they pale in comparison to the EV sector, which is worth about $73 billion today, and could grow to $200 billion by the end of the decade, according to Grand View Research. This year, ONE expects to bring in $30 million in revenue, and hopes to make double that next year. The company said it has $200 million in binding, multi-year contracts with railroads and defense contractors.

Recent findings suggest that ONE hasn’t closed the door on the automotive industry, Ijaz said. “Automotive still is a race to the bottom on margins,” he said. “As time goes on, if we win an automotive contract for any purpose, we’ll take a look at it, but not at any cost.”.

It has been revealed that ONE’s pitch centers on the so-called foreign entity of concern (FEOC) restrictions: The U.S. government can’t buy batteries made in China or those made using minerals from China-controlled supply chains, so ONE will target them first.

But it’s a pitch that many battery companies are making today. Whether investors buy into ONE’s vision will depend on if they think the tech giant has parted with its tumultuous past and found a focus. It will need both to succeed in the increasingly cutthroat battery industry.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • Sources indicate that many Microsoft business customers are still wading through the session slide decks and “Book of News” collection of product and strategy announcements from Microsoft’s Ignite confab last week.
  • Microsoft’s curated Ignite keynote and session spotlights were, unsurprisingly, dedicated to Microsoft AI in all its guises — Copilot, the Microsoft IQ intelligence platforms and Agent 365.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

by Mary Jo Foley on Nov 24, 2026 at 6:44 amNovember 24, 2026 at 6:44 am.

Sources indicate that many Microsoft business customers are still wading through the session slide decks and “Book of News” collection of product and strategy announcements from Microsoft’s Ignite confab last week. But not all the newly introduced goodies announced there (or simultaneous with this year’s Microsoft Ignite show, which kicked off Nov. 17) might have made it onto everyone’s radar.

Microsoft’s curated Ignite keynote and session spotlights were, unsurprisingly, dedicated to Microsoft AI in all its guises — Copilot, the Microsoft IQ intelligence platforms and Agent 365. But there was some other important news last week that Microsoft customers could find equally, if not more, interesting and useful.

Among my picks for the “make sure you didn’t miss this” list:.

Recent findings suggest that copilot without the M365 subscription prerequisite arrives next week: Despite a LOT of talk about Copilot, “a new OS for work,” Microsoft didn’t mention anything at all during Ignite about a new purchasing option for Copilot that is set to go live on Dec. 1. Starting then, Microsoft will offer a version of Copilot to small business and enterprise customers without the current prerequisite of having a certain paid Microsoft 365 strategy.

For a flat fee of $21 per user per month for small businesses and $30 per user per month for enterprise customers (before discounts), owners will be able to buy this new standalone Copilot offering, as Microsoft quietly unveiled back in October on its Partner Center site.

Presently, to buy Copilot, business customers need to have purchased a qualifying Microsoft 365 subscription proposal before they shell out even more money for Copilot. Because of this requirement, Microsoft isn’t competitive price-wise when pitted against OpenAI’s ChatGPT or Anthropic’s Claude entry-level business tiers.

The newly introduced offer is for new customers buying through any of Microsoft’s channels, including its Cloud Solution Provider program, across commercial, education, government and nonprofit sectors.

Recent findings suggest that I’ve got a lot of questions about this newly introduced offer, including where Copilot chats are stored and how/if customers will get some kind of access to the Microsoft IQ technology that underlies Copilot and is positioned as its secret sauce if they don’t have a Microsoft 365 subscription. I’ve asked Microsoft, but no word back so far.

Azure Linux 4.0 is now ready for prime time: Declared on the same day Ignite kicked off (but without a mention during the conference), Microsoft’s own commercial Linux distribution, Azure Linux 4.0, is now generally available.

Industry observers note that the 4.0 release is interesting for a few reasons. First, it is the first release of Azure Linux — formerly known as Common Base Linux (CBL)-Mariner — designed as a general-purpose server OS for customer virtual machines, and it is based on the Fedora Linux stack. Checking off the requisite AI box, Azure Linux 4.0 is “purpose-built for cloud native and AI workloads,” as Microsoft stated back in May.

Microsoft officials have said two-thirds of customer cores in Azure run Linux (not Windows Server). Microsoft has acknowledged the platforms running Microsoft 365, GitHub and OpenAI’s ChatGPT “all sit on Linux foundations.”.

Microsoft has supported a wide variety of Linux distributions on Azure for years but never made its own available for commercial use by customers and partners until now.

Windows Server 2028 is in the works: Yes, another on-premises version of Windows Server is coming. Christened Windows Server 2028, the next release, likely to debut in late 2027, is now in public preview.

Microsoft mentioned Server 2028 in its Book of News and in passing in some sessions, but it was not positioned as a top-tier announcement.

The 2028 release includes some expected and a few surprise features, such as making 32-bit app support an optional component rather than installing it by default. That change, along with a hardened Server Core configuration included by default, is designed to improve the security of the platform from the get-go. But they may present potential backward-compatibility risks.

Microsoft is positioning Server 2028 similarly to the way it has been pushing Windows client lately: as a way to run AI workloads more cheaply because they can run locally. The “unmetered intelligence” pitch strikes again.

According to recent reports, sure, Microsoft can’t make every announcement a centerpiece in a two-plus-hour (waah!) opening keynote. But sometimes, hidden gems deserve their moments in the sun. Or pouring rain ….

A couple of years ago, the cofounder and CEO of a blood-testing organization was publicly taken to task for implying in articles and professional profiles that he has a PhD when in reality, he’d left a prestigious graduate group three years after enrolling, without a degree.

Recent findings suggest that the CEO is hardly alone in intentionally or otherwise sowing confusion around his credentials, however. Over the years, we’ve mistakenly believed that a number of founders have obtained specific college degrees based on their LinkedIn bio, only to learn offline that they enrolled for some period of time in a particular program that they didn’t complete.

It happened most recently with the cofounder of a startup who one would might surmise based on his LinkedIn profile has a master’s degree from Harvard but does not. We also misunderstood the CEO of a robotics tech giant to have a PhD based on her LinkedIn. It was our fault; it mentioned under the credit that she’d left to start a company. But anyone scanning the site might have come to the same wrong conclusion. (We pointed this out to her team, and mention of the PhD was deleted.).

In a higher-profile case, James Damore, the fired Google engineer who authored that infamous memo about the manufacturer’s diversity practices and whose LinkedIn page cited under “Education” a “PhD, Systems Biology,” removed mention of those doctoral studies after Wired confirmed with Harvard that he was enrolled in the program but didn’t complete the doctorate.

Sources indicate that damore tried to defend his own LinkedIn profile, tweeting at the time, “I never told anyone I have a PhD. LinkedIn can’t distinguish between being in the PhD program and having a PhD (I forgot to upgrade it).”.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

by Lisa Stiffler on Nov 24, 2026 at 9:47 amNovember 24, 2026 at 9:47 am.

It has been revealed that senseNet, a startup providing wildfire detection and intelligence, on Tuesday declared a $43 million financing package. The Vancouver, B.C.-based manufacturer says the funding will support its expansion across the U.S. and internationally.

Industry observers note that the startup uses a suite of technologies for the rapid detection of wildfires, including environmental sensors, AI-enabled cameras, satellite data, drone technology and predictive analytics. Its monitoring footprint covers 450 million acres in a dozen countries.

SenseNet says its technology has provided early alerts for more than 10,000 fires, in some cases hours before the first 911 calls.

“Wildfire protection is no longer just about detecting a fire as rapidly as possible. It’s about understanding what’s happening, what could happen next, and giving the right people the information they need to act,” Hamed Noori, co-founder and CEO of SenseNet, said in a statement.

Recent findings suggest that noori released SenseNet in 2019 with Chief Technology Officer Shahab Bahrami. Both hold doctorates in electrical and computer engineering from the University of British Columbia.

The Series B round was led by Idealist Capital, with participation from Fusion Fund, Stormbreaker Ventures, Thin Line Capital, National Bank of Canada and The Sitka Foundation.

Industry observers note that the financing includes purchases of newly issued shares, which put money into SenseNet; secondary share sales, which pay existing shareholders; and debt. SenseNet did not disclose how much of the $43 million falls into each category.

The startup previously raised $12.78 million and has 30 employees, according to PitchBook.

SenseNet competes with companies including OroraTech, Dryad and Pano AI, whose cameras, software and alerting services are used by Washington’s Department of Natural Resources to detect wildfires. The companies are developing their technology as warming temperatures and drier conditions increase wildfire risks.

Breaking: Island is a upcoming screen-time app that turns staying off your phone into a game

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (929 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: TechCrunch

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that A newly introduced startup is taking a different approach to helping people manage their screen time.
  • This carrot-instead-of-stick approach was dreamed up by entrepreneurs Ashish Selvaraj (CEO) and Ethan Pronev (CTO), who met while studying at the University of Waterloo, then went on to work at companies that included Jane Street, Citadel Securities, Databricks, and Microsoft.
  • Later, they quit their jobs to join the startup accelerator Y Combinator, where they first tried out other ideas in areas like B2B and software-as-a-service, but weren’t finding the right fit.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that A newly introduced startup is taking a different approach to helping people manage their screen time. Instead of blocking apps or restricting the phone’s use after a set period, an app called Island encourages you to meet your screen time goals by way of a farming simulator game. Yes, a game! Island works by rewarding you when you’re disciplined enough to meet your goals with a “credit score” that increases your farm’s production, unlocking new crops, animals, and other content.

This carrot-instead-of-stick approach was dreamed up by entrepreneurs Ashish Selvaraj (CEO) and Ethan Pronev (CTO), who met while studying at the University of Waterloo, then went on to work at companies that included Jane Street, Citadel Securities, Databricks, and Microsoft.

Later, they quit their jobs to join the startup accelerator Y Combinator, where they first tried out other ideas in areas like B2B and software-as-a-service, but weren’t finding the right fit.

Island ended up being their fifth pivot, and the first the founders actually found themselves enjoying.

“Once we were in YC, I think there’s a massive mindset — I think in [San Francisco], in general — of, ‘selling shovels.’ Everyone wants to ‘sell shovels’ to other companies, and around us, that’s just what was going on,” explains Selvaraj, speaking about the concept that many successful startups sell the tools, infrastructure, or services to others following whatever the current market boom or trend may be.

It has been revealed that “So all the ideas we had — we tried these things — but we found that we weren’t passionate about it. Like idea after idea seemed like ultimately the product was just a dashboard with some kind of different backend,” he added. “It felt like we quit our jobs … just to do something that was a variation of that.”.

With Island, the team gets to tap into their creativity, having drawn the pixel art themselves.

It has been revealed that “A lot of people do use [AI] models to generate the art, but we felt that it had a certain character when we drew it ourselves,” he told TechCrunch. “I feel like with Claude getting so good, there’s a tendency to give away every task to Claude. But ultimately it feels like there’s something else that comes out when you do it yourself, especially in something like art,” Selvaraj stated.

Recent findings suggest that what’s more, the app does appear to be successful in helping owners meet their goals, the startup’s early data shows. After early testing and an October launch, the team claims that the majority of its users (82%) will end their screen time right at the limit they’ve set. Many more are ending their screen time when they get the “15 minutes left” warning.

Sources indicate that island could appeal to those who have given up on other screen time apps out of frustration because the app doesn’t actually lock you out of apps or your phone. That’s something that can end up being more disruptive, especially when you’re in the middle of doing something, like posting, sharing, commenting, or chatting, among other things. Instead, Island taps into people’ own self-discipline and their desire to see their island flourish to encourage screen time breaks.

The idea to encourage users to keep their goals by offering some other type of in-app reward system isn’t entirely novel. Last year, Hank Green’s screen time app Focus Friend went viral for its experience, which involved a little friend that could only knit items that, in turn, allowed you to get points used to decorate your room when you were focused on your non-distracting apps.

Industry observers note that similar ideas have been used in self-care apps and habit-trackers like Finch, Amaru, Belly, Flora, Urso, and others. But Island expands this concept from being focused on helping out a virtual friend or pet to one that’s more of a game — and one where you can experience the consequences without “having to torture your pet,” notes Selvaraj.

Recent findings suggest that island also allows users to add friends and visit each other’s islands, compete in group challenges, and keep each other accountable by tying your island together with one friend of your choosing. In the latter scenario, if either friend goes over their limit, both of their islands will suffer.

The startup notes Island has proven to be fairly “sticky” with a 51% daily active customers-to-monthly active users ratio, and a day 30 retention rate of 49%, meaning 49% of users were still active on the app on the 30th day since the app was installed.

The app is right now free to use, with a $39.99 per year subscription that allows you to set individual limits on different apps, instead of just an overall daily screen time limit. The manufacturer hasn’t raised additional seed funding outside of YC, but aims to begin marketing the app on social media for the rest of the year.

Renowned financial guru and Rich Dad Poor Dad author Robert Kiyosaki has offered compelling insight into the reasons behind his buying spree of Bitcoin (BTC) and Ethereum (ETH) despite the current crypto market crash.

Kiyosaki, who is an esteemed investor, predicts that a financial crisis could be on the horizon, and it might be even worse than the 2008 market crash. He believes that crypto assets and other hard assets are an effective hedge against the repercussions of government-induced overborrowing and money printing.

The financial guru's latest X post explains his rationale behind investing in Bitcoin, Ethereum, gold, silver, real estate, and oil instead of traditional financial assets.

"Why I am buying real (no ETFs) gold, silver, Bitcoin, and Ethereum," Kiyosaki noted in his latest post.

In a recent development, he attributed his views to the Federal Reserve, the U.S. Treasury and the colossal debt obligations of the U.S.

According to Kiyosaki, the government's inability to curb spending will lead to massive money printing in the future. This might erode the purchasing power of the U.S. dollar.

"The MAJOR PRINT is about to begin," Kiyosaki warned.

This is the core reason for his investments in Bitcoin and Ethereum. He believes that these assets will rise in value when the government is forced to aggressively print money in response to escalating financial issues.

Industry observers note that moreover, he believes that holding these crypto assets directly would be better than investing in exchange-traded funds (ETFs). However, he did not offer a reason for his opposition to ETFs in his post.

Furthermore, Kiyosaki stated that the next financial crisis could be much bigger than the global financial crisis of 2008.

"This crash we are just now sliding into is much bigger than 2008. Possibly a global depression," he commented.

He also mentioned that his gold, silver, Bitcoin and Ethereum holdings could make him one of the ultra-rich if his predictions come true.

However, Kiyosaki mentioned some figures that were not entirely accurate. For instance, he stated that the U.S. national debt stood at $49 trillion. But according to Treasury data, the national debt was about $40.7 trillion in November 2026. Also, his claim that the U.S. is printing $1 trillion every 90 days conflates government debt with money printing.

Although Kiyosaki is a strong believer in Bitcoin, he recently advised investors not to buy Bitcoin immediately amid the digital asset's current price slump.

On Nov. 20, the Rich Dad Poor Dad author cautioned against catching a 'falling knife.'.

"Never grab a falling knife." This means that investors should wait for the market crash to end before buying.

"I started buying bitcoin around $20k after the market crashed last time," Kiyosaki recalled.

"Will wait for Bitcoin bottom again," he added.

#190526. Uncommon Thinkers: Saf Rabah wants to make it easier to build housing, one permit at a time

📅 24 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 9m • 📚 Deep Dive (1785 w)

Uncommon Thinkers: Saf Rabah wants to make it easier to build housing, one permit at a time

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1785 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Geekwire

⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • by Grace Kaste on Nov 24, 2026 at 9:50 amNovember 24, 2026 at 1:22 pm.
  • Recent findings suggest that editor’s note: This series profiles five Seattle-area “Uncommon Thinkers,” who will be recognized Dec.
  • When startup founder Safouen (Saf) Rabah decided to get in on the AI boom, he didn’t start by coding or by training any models.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

by Grace Kaste on Nov 24, 2026 at 9:50 amNovember 24, 2026 at 1:22 pm.

Recent findings suggest that editor’s note: This series profiles five Seattle-area “Uncommon Thinkers,” who will be recognized Dec. 10 at the GeekWire Gala in partnership with Greater Seattle Partners.

When startup founder Safouen (Saf) Rabah decided to get in on the AI boom, he didn’t start by coding or by training any models. He got in touch with urban planners at Bellevue City Hall, and together they combed through nearly 300 land use permit applications to find common mistakes and bottlenecks.

Industry observers note that bellevue began using Rabah’s platform, Govstream.AI, in the summer of 2025, starting with an AI assistant for city staff. In a test using past applications, about three times as many were judged complete with Govstream’s tool. Rabah claims that change alone has the potential to alter the housing stock of the city.

It has been revealed that “Why can’t we build more housing? All the macro economic reasons, inflation, material costs, labor, land scarcity, are all exacerbated by the slow permitting process,” Rabah said. “That’s what we want to change.”.

So, how did Rabah, a B2B software engineer by training, find his way to land use permitting?

Rabah hadn’t heard of the government technology sector, aka GovTech, until mid-career, but looking back, the signs were all there. He was born in Sfax, Tunisia, and grew up in Tunis. Throughout his childhood, he dreamed of running for office.

“I come from a small developing country, so there’s always this idea of, what could a small developing country become? How can it prosper and grow?” Rabah mentioned. “Building has always been a big part of what I imagined myself doing.”.

As a teenager in the 1980s, he attended a USAID-funded boarding school in Tunis. The school was part of Cold War efforts to expand American soft power around the Middle East; classes were conducted in English and many of the students went on to university in North America.

In a recent development, “The school had the first Macintosh lab in all of Africa,” Rabah mentioned. “I can still picture the USAID logo on the back of each computer.”.

Rabah got a scholarship to University of British Columbia, where he studied electrical engineering while running what he calls his “first entrepreneurial venture”: a service that built and hosted websites for small businesses.

That led to a job at a startup called Pivotal, a customer relationship management platform where Rabah led a team responsible for e-business applications. After Pivotal went public, Rabah left for a job at TELUS, one of Canada’s “big three” telecommunications corporations, but quickly felt frustrated by the dynamics at such a large tech giant.

It has been revealed that “Even though I worked on nascent products, it was very, very bureaucratic,” Rabah mentioned. “There were committees, a hundred thousand employees. I missed building things.”.

Rabah began to look for a upcoming job that would not only allow him to build but also to make a difference.

“Being an immigrant, it’s always tempting to stay content with having a good job, good status,” Rabah noted. “But I’ve always enjoyed the ‘what if?’ mindset, the clean slate. It’s this way today, but could we imagine it to be something different?”.

That vision led him to Socrata, which in 2010 was just a nascent government technology startup.

“I really connected with the founder,” Rabah said. “It had a really cool mission, it combined the ‘do-well’ with ‘do-good.’”.

It has been revealed that socrata was one of the first platforms to host data portals for local governments and federal agencies, allowing citizens to access and map public data sets. Many U.S. cities, including Seattle, still use Socrata’s software today to publish information including crime logs, permits, and budgets.

“We were a massive part of pioneering the open data movement,” Rabah said. “At one point almost every major city was our customer, and half the states.”.

Socrata was acquired by Tyler Technologies in 2018, and Rabah stayed on until 2024.

“The funny part is today we use that data quite a lot in our work because one of the most popular data sets that any city publishes is its permit data,” Rabah mentioned. “We’ve even built a connector between Socrata and Govstream.”.

But once Socrata was acquired, Rabah began to feel the same way he had at TELUS: boxed in by bureaucracy.

“Tyler was a really good firm, but it is a significant company,” Rabah stated. “Tech was getting repetitive, and I was thinking about leaving it altogether.”.

According to recent reports, “The thing that pushed me over the edge is that AI happened,” Rabah said. “It was one of those moments where once you start working with it, you really can’t help but think, ‘I can revisit virtually every assumption I’ve made over the last 20 years, every constraint.’”.

Immediately, he thought of his passion for building—building a startup, building a better country, and literally building a building.

Recent findings suggest that “I’ve been fascinated by the built environment since my Lego days: What makes some cities livable and others not?” Rabah said. “Then, living in Seattle, you see the lack of housing, affordability, and the homelessness problem we have, and you’re like, why can’t we build more housing? I started believing that these problems are in fact solvable if we simply speed things up and simplify things with AI.”.

In July of 2024, Rabah began working with his “design partner,” Bellevue’s Development Services Department, to learn more about common permitting problems.

It has been revealed that “We started with something visionary and high-level, but you can only get there if you understand the granular problems of the day-to-day,” Rabah stated. “So we talked with developers and builders and we talked with the people on the other side of the counter who are processing these permits and guiding these builders.”.

In a recent development, he learned that most permitting mistakes are avoidable, like applying for the wrong zone or forgetting to include a north arrow on an architectural plan. Those oversights can send an application back to square one while clogging up the permitting process for all other projects.

Industry observers note that “The wait time disproportionately affects lower margin projects,” Rabah said. “It really constrains the supply of housing, especially the housing we need more of, which is the more affordable kind.”.

Govstream’s AI assistants are designed to help first-time builders avoid those errors and make permitting faster for everyone. Rabah and his team began by building what they call an “intelligent intake” platform for a city permitting portal, which guided users through preparing to submit their applications.

It has been revealed that when Bellevue first tested Govstream’s intake tool on 276 past residential building permit applications, the city reported a completeness rate of 67%, compared with 22% when those applications were originally filed. According to the tech giant, the latest testing has yielded an 88% completeness rate.

More recently, they’ve begun to build out an AI assistant for the backend, which assists city permit techs with the initial review and reduces what Rabah calls “toil,” like answering unnecessary pre-application emails and tracking down missing documents.

Bellevue staff estimated that Govstream’s tools saved them 152 hours over one month this summer by helping them research and respond to pre-application inquiries.

According to recent reports, “For a developer, time is money, so the type of housing that can be built in Bellevue will become more affordable,” mentioned Jake Hesselgesser, Bellevue’s development services director. “This technology has a direct and material impact on the cost of housing.”.

Recent findings suggest that eventually, Govstream.AI will be an end-to-end service, assisting in later stages of the permitting process, too. But Rabah is emphatic that Govstream will not give AI the final say.

“We always put our AI systems in the role of assistants that suggest stuff, but never decide stuff,” Rabah said.

Rabah states Govstream uses preset rules, outside the AI model, to check whether a portion of the application is complete, whether a site needs a geotechnical report, or whether an architect is properly licensed. In Bellevue, city staff retain final authority.

Hesselgesser remarked that Rabah’s conservative approach to AI is what made the city of Bellevue want to work with his startup.

“Our core principle around Bellevue’s use of AI is to retain human decision making, and we wanted to ensure that we were aligned with a manufacturer with the same core value,” Hesselgesser said. “Saf took that holistic approach.”.

Around the office, Rabah has become known for his eagerness to build. According to Mariia Derevianko, head of marketing, he spends his weekends building out a product or an idea in order to workshop it with the team.

Industry observers note that “He’s very hands-on with the product, with design, marketing, all of the aspects,” Derevianko remarked. “He never waits for the engineers to build something.”.

Most recently, he built a lead tracker to research which cities Govstream should partner with, and previously, he vibe-coded one of the research assistants in the Govstream platform as a template for his software engineers.

Derevianko, who joined the team last year after Rabah poached her from AWS, said he’s also known for his kindness.

Industry observers note that “I originally didn’t want to join a start-up,” Derevianko noted. “I only said yes because I saw he is a genuinely good person who really cares about this project.”.

Govstream.AI has already won at least 12 contracts around the Puget Sound, including King County and the City of Everett, as well as cities across the country, such as Louisville, Kentucky.

Ultimately, Rabah has his eyes set on Seattle, where construction and development has been on the decline. Last December, the city council passed permanent “middle housing” rules to upzone residential neighborhoods and encourage the construction of ADUs, all of which will need a permit.

In a recent development, seattle tested a competing AI tool from CivCheck in 2025. In June, city staff recommended a pilot that would let applicants check their submissions for completeness before filing.

According to recent reports, “We need affordable housing in Seattle,” Rabah mentioned. “We would really, really love to help our home city streamline permitting and remove it as a barrier.”.

In founding Govstream.AI, Rabah has found the job he has been looking for: one in which he can build things without the bureaucracy of a large firm, all while “doing good.”.

According to recent reports, “This has become my obsession,” Rabah noted. “I can point to things in a city and say, maybe Govstream was a part of what allowed this project to get built.”.

Three months after introducing its product, AI cybersecurity startup Corma has raised a $125 million Series A round at a $1 billion valuation led by NEA, the organization mentioned. Corma offers AI models and agents trained for cybersecurity defense. It has now raised a total of $185 million from backers, including Sequoia Capital, Khosla Ventures, and Coatue.

The startup came out of stealth in August. Interest in its product skyrocketed after a series of security incidents sent chief information security officers scrambling on October 21 when a critical flaw was found in PHP, a popular web programming language. Another flaw was found in Node.js, the open source JavaScript runtime environment. Popular open source tool LiteLLM, a proxy for routing requests to multiple LLM providers, also disclosed a security incident. Other incidents were disclosed that day, too. The day showcased the kind of onslaught on security that AI has enabled.

Corma isn’t the only tech giant using AI to play defense. Other examples include Kevin Mandia’s newly introduced startup Armadin, as well as Anthropic, OpenAI, Microsoft, and other established players, and too many other startups to count. Still, it’s a young market and a necessary one. Corma claims it stands out from the crowd by being a frontier AI research lab focused on protection.

  • It has been revealed that karpelès’ warning comes as Pump.fun has set a Nov.
  • Sources indicate that but to maintain their current accounts, Pump.fun is asking users to import their private keys.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that former Mt. Gox CEO Mark Karpelès has strongly warned consumers of Solana-based memecoin launchpad Pump.fun about potential major security risks associated with the new wallet migration process, which could put users' private keys at great risk.

It has been revealed that karpelès’ warning comes as Pump.fun has set a Nov. 30 deadline to stop allowing external wallet logins to its website. The platform is moving to email and social logins, which will enable users to access their accounts via Google, Apple and GitHub.

Sources indicate that but to maintain their current accounts, Pump.fun is asking users to import their private keys. This is what Karpelès thinks could compromise the security of their crypto assets.

In a recent X post, Karpelès said he studied Pump.fun's JavaScript code to understand the nature of the upcoming migration process.

The analysis has raised questions about the security of customers’ private keys, despite the platform's claims.

“At best, it's a misnomer to refer to it as 'end-to-end encryption,'” said Karpelès.

According to Karpelès, users' private keys are first encrypted in their browsers before being sent through Pump.fun’s servers to the platform’s wallet infrastructure provider, Privy.

It has been revealed that also, Pump.fun's backend provides the public key used for encryption during migration. Consumers’ browsers have no way to check whether the public key is authentic, according to Karpelès.

The possibility of a security breach involving Privy’s infrastructure is another major concern.

“Your money also now relies on Privy never getting hacked,” Karpelès warned.

One of the most vital aspects of Karpelès' warning is the need for migration in the first place.

He noted Pump.fun could use signature-based authentication without forcing users to expose their private keys.

Pump.fun already uses a "Sign in with Solana" message to prove ownership of a wallet, according to Karpelès.

So theoretically, customers can prove ownership of their wallets and execute transactions without having to import their private credentials into a upcoming system.

Bitcoin’s recent weakness has reinforced concerns about another leg down, with traders closely watching whether the token can hold its current support levels or extend its decline toward lower price targets.

Notably, he views the $53,000 region as a potential final liquidity sweep, where additional selling could force leveraged investors and traders out of their positions before the market finds a more durable bottom.

If Bitcoin reaches $49,000, SeffafNet believes the move could mark the end of the current correction and create an opportunity for a major reversal. Nevertheless, he stressed that the price target is not guaranteed, describing it as a scenario he is preparing for rather than a certainty.

He believes investors could make costly decisions if they panic during another sell-off, particularly if the decline occurs near the end of the broader market correction.

Additionally, analyst Crypto Patel maintains a bearish outlook, suggesting Bitcoin could experience a temporary recovery before resuming its downward movement.

According to recent reports, the pundit identified a potential relief rally toward the $71,504-$74,800 region, where a bearish order block and fair value gap could provide resistance. Such a move could offer temporary relief to traders following the recent decline without necessarily signaling a broader trend reversal.

According to recent reports, crypto Patel remarked Bitcoin’s higher time-frame bearish structure remains intact, although a breakdown has not yet been confirmed. He is watching for a candle close below $57,800, which would strengthen the case for additional downside.

Furthermore, if that level breaks, his broader downside targets extend between $50,000 and $35,000, placing his outlook below SeffafNet’s $49,000 bottom projection.

However, Crypto Patel would reconsider his bearish position if Bitcoin records a higher-time frame candle close above $87,400, the level he identified as the critical change-of-character threshold.

Despite Bitcoin’s weakness, Michael Van de Poppe sees a potentially encouraging development in Ethereum’s performance against Bitcoin.

The analyst noted that Bitcoin fell approximately 25% over the two weeks, while Ethereum’s performance against BTC remained relatively stable. He considers this resilience a sign of strength, particularly because altcoins typically suffer greater losses against Bitcoin during severe market downturns.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

And it’s Friday! [Throws frisbee into tree.].

Industry observers note that before we dive into the newsletter, one more bit of great news about our upcoming event (which we promise we’ll stop talking about soon): Michael Grimes, the star tech banker from Morgan Stanley at the center of Uber’s IPO (and Facebook IPO, and Slack’s and Spotify’s), has been persuaded to come and talk about direct listings, which we’re very excited about. If you’re as confused as we are about whether these make sense for more than a couple of companies each year (current status: we don’t think they do), you won’t want to miss this rare conversation with “Wall Street’s Silicon Valley whisperer.”.

It has been revealed that note that seats are almost gone. Giant thanks to NextWorld, the early-stage enterprise-focused firm that’s hosting all of us; to KCPR, the boutique tech PR and strategy firm; and to Carta, a platform that helps companies and VCs manage their cap tables, valuations, investments, and equity intends, for their support.

Ben Horowitz,  the co-founder of the venture firm Andreessen Horowitz, has a latest book coming out this coming Monday titled “What You Do is Who You Are,” that takes a look at how to create “culture” at a company.

It’s a word that’s thrown around a lot but that’s very hard to grasp, let alone implement in a sustainable way. Horowitz learned firsthand as a CEO how elusive it can be when he took stock of his tech giant, only to discover it was made up of “screamers who intimidated their people,” others who “neglected to give any feedback,” and at least one compulsive liar who excelled at sucking up to Horowitz and also making up stories from whole cloth.

Horowitz states creating culture was a missing part of his education, and in this fresh book — a follow-up to his best-selling “The Hard Thing About Hard Things” — he does his best to fill that gap for other CEOs, using his own experience, as well as lessons gleaned from historical figures Toussaint Louverture and Genghis Khan, along with Shaka Senghor, a contemporary who served time for murder and today is a criminal justice reform advocate.

Recent findings suggest that it’s an instructive and novel combination, and we suggest picking up the book, especially if you love history. In the meantime, we sat down recently with Horowitz to talk about its timing and whether some of the biggest cultural blow-ups in the startup industry — Uber and WeWork — could have been avoided. These excerpts have been edited for length and clarity. Note that we’ll have more of the conversation — including Horowitz’s thoughts about dual-class shares —  for readers of Extra Crunch on Monday.

You’ve just written a book about culture that’s coming out just as a lot of questions are being raised about culture because of WeWork. What happened there?

Sources indicate that [Cofounder Adam Neumann] had a certain kind of culture there. He had some holes — some great strengths and great holes. And sometimes that happens. When you’re really good at part of it, you can delude yourself into thinking that you’ve got everything you need when you have some massive incompleteness.

It has been revealed that adam is so amazing. Like, the way they got all the money and everything. And the vision was so spectacular. And everybody there believed it, and they recruited some phenomenal talent. But when you’re that optimistic, it does help to have something in the culture that notes [allows] people to bring you the bad news, like, if the accounting is all over the place or what have you.

As with Uber’s Travis Kalanick, whose culture also came under fire, Neumann operated in very plain sight. He wasn’t hiding who he was or what he was spending.

Right, everybody knew how Travis was running the manufacturer. Everyone in Silicon Valley knew, let alone everyone on the board. The culture was published. You can look up Uber’s values [from that period].

In a recent development, travis designed, I think, a really compelling culture, and believed in it, and published it. And the consequences of what he was missing were also super well-known. It’s only when board members think people are coming after them that [they take an interest in these things].

What are the biggest lessons in these two cases?

It has been revealed that I obviously know more about Uber [as a Lyft investor who follows the space]. In Uber’s case, it’s a very subtle thing. Travis had a really good code. But he had a bug in it.

Sources indicate that I think it was reported that, like, Travis encouraged bad behavior. I don’t think he did at all. I just think he didn’t make it clear that legal and ethical [considerations] were more important than competitiveness. As a result, when left to their own devices, in a distributed organization where there was a lot of distributed power, that combination had people doing things that were out of bounds.

Industry observers note that and he was making everybody so much money. And the manufacturer was growing so fast that, for the board members, I suspect they were like, ‘As long as it’s making money, I’m not going to worry about what happens next.’.

It has been revealed that to me, the unfair part is, like, they shouldn’t get any credit at the end. Whatever you’re blaming Travis for [you should blame them, too] because they didn’t see it, either. I think that’s a charitable way of putting it.

  • It has been revealed that the more than 1,900 startups on the The Crunchbase Unicorn Board have a combined valuation of roughly $9 trillion, based on their last reported valuations.
  • Most unicorns are estimated to have gained value, even as others have lost ground, our analysis shows.
  • Industry observers note that the majority of companies on the board are valued higher by the Current Valuations model than they were when they last raised funding.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that the more than 1,900 startups on the The Crunchbase Unicorn Board have a combined valuation of roughly $9 trillion, based on their last reported valuations. But Crunchbase’s newly introduced Current Valuation Model, which estimates how private-company values have changed since their last funding rounds, puts that figure closer to $11 trillion.

Most unicorns are estimated to have gained value, even as others have lost ground, our analysis shows. Among the biggest potential gainers are AI startups Thinking Machines Lab, whose estimated value has climbed from $12 billion to $40 billion, and Sierra, from nearly $16 billion to $31.5 billion.

Industry observers note that the majority of companies on the board are valued higher by the Current Valuations model than they were when they last raised funding. Only around 236 companies — roughly 12% of the board — are down by more than $100 million in value compared to their last reported valuations.

Industry observers note that the valuation model estimates that a select group of 24 companies have gained more than $10 billion in value since their most recent funding rounds. They include Mira Murati’s AI research lab Thinking Machines Lab, which was last valued at $12 billion in its 2025 seed funding but has a current valuation projected at $40 billion.

According to recent reports, similarly, Bret Taylor’s customer oriented AI agent builder Sierra was last valued at close to $16  billion in a May 2026 funding round. It is now estimated to be valued at $31.5 billion, per the Crunchbase model. (On Monday, Bloomberg reported that Sierra is raising a upcoming round at a roughly $30 billion valuation.).

Physical Intelligence, a company building AI for robotics, was valued at $5.6 billion in its Series B. Crunchbase’s Current Valuation model estimates its valuation now at $18.5 billion.

Another 53 companies are estimated to have current valuations that are $5 billion to just under $10 billion higher than those achieved in their most recent funding rounds. They include Unconventional AI, which is focused on energy efficiency for AI; Lila Sciences, which is building artificial intelligence for science; AI cloud company Vultr; AI research lab humans&; stablecoin payment platform Tempo; and Yann LeCun’s Advanced Machine Intelligence, which is modeling physical world intelligence.

Sources indicate that A total of 484 companies are estimated to have current valuations that are $1 billion to $5 billion higher than their most recent funding valuations. More than 1,100 companies have values that were flat or up to $1 billion higher than their most recent funding valuations.

Only around 236 companies are estimated to be below their most recent valuation, by more than $100 million. Collectively, their current valuations are down by $326 billion from their most recent fundings, Crunchbase estimates.

It has been revealed that the Crunchbase Unicorn Board reached its highest value in 2026 as three companies approached or exceeded $1 trillion valuations — unprecedented in the board’s history. The board peaked at $10 trillion in advance of the Anthropic IPO this past week. The firm’s public-market debut removed close to $1 trillion from the board. This followed another trillion-dollar exit from the board earlier this year, when SpaceX — last valued at $1.3 trillion in a secondary financing this year — before it went public in June at a value of $1.8 trillion.

According to recent reports, all told, the unicorn board this year is currently up by $1.5 trillion from its $7.5 trillion value at the end of 2025. With its closest rival now on the public markets, OpenAI is currently the most highly valued private manufacturer at an official valuation of $1.25 trillion.

Sources indicate that the unicorn board has picked up pace this year. Around 360 companies joined the board so far this year, the second highest count in a single year after 2021 when 621 companies joined.

A faster pace of newly introduced entrants and rising valuations have helped replenish the board, while current estimates suggest substantial additional value has accumulated between funding rounds.

Sources indicate that the next test is how closely these estimated values align with prices investors are willing to pay. Future funding rounds, secondary transactions, public listings and M&A will reveal how much of the board’s estimated $2 trillion uplift translates into realized value.

Sources indicate that current valuations are based on the upcoming Crunchbase Current Valuation Model, which prices companies using a proprietary machine learning model that starts with a company’s most recent post-money valuation and continuously estimates how its value has shifted since that funding event. The model covers roughly 230,000 funded private companies. Read more here.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

by Kurt Schlosser on Nov 24, 2026 at 9:58 amNovember 24, 2026 at 9:58 am.

Zin Boats made a splash with fast, pricey electric boats. But most of its business is now coming from what’s under the floor.

The Seattle startup has launched Zin Power, a newly introduced division that will supply its electric propulsion systems to other boat builders and to industries that rely on diesel engines, such as construction and mining.

The company also raised $5 million to scale up production and expanded its headquarters in the Interbay neighborhood to 11,000 square feet.

About 90% of the organization’s revenue comes from selling motors and batteries to customers in the marine and drone industries, founder and CEO Piotr Zin told GeekWire. A typical setup includes two motors and about 500 kilowatt-hours of battery storage.

“We noticed a steady demand for pleasure craft year over year, but at the same time a massive increase in propulsion sales,” Zin remarked.

Customers include StanCraft Wooden Boats, which teamed with Zin on the 340 Hammerhead E, an all-electric wooden runabout. StanCraft delivered the first one to a customer this summer.

According to recent reports, geekWire first checked out the company in early 2024, when it was relaunching after a pandemic shutdown with its Z2R, a 20-foot carbon fiber runabout. Later that year Zin showed off the Z11, a 37-foot electric tender designed to shuttle passengers to and from megayachts at more than 60 mph. The company said boats on the platform would cost $1.75 million to $3.75 million.

Industry observers note that the manufacturer also offers the Z7 Convertible, a 22-foot runabout with a removable roof that it pitches for fishing, surfing and cruising. The boat has a top speed of 40 mph and a range of more than 80 miles.

Sources indicate that zin Power grew out of the drivetrains engineered for those boats. Zin sees the marine track record as a selling point for other industries that need high torque, including construction, mining and remotely operated vehicles (ROVs).

“The ocean is one of the harshest environments there is, so the technology has already proven itself under about the toughest conditions it could face,” Zin stated.

In a recent development, many of those machines still run on diesel engines, a technology more than a century old. Zin stated operators are eager to switch to electric.

“What’s interesting is that economics is driving the shift, not regulation or image,” he said.

Recent findings suggest that electric systems cost up to 70% less to operate, according to Zin. He estimated that replacing a single 250-horsepower industrial diesel engine that runs eight hours a day could save as much as $1.5 million over 10 years.

The new funding will pay for more manufacturing capacity, a dedicated sales and engineering team to work with boat builders, and support for customers converting from diesel. Zin calls it a seed round, with a larger raise planned down the road. The firm has raised $6.5 million to date, including a $1.275 million seed round in early 2024.

Zin Boats has nine full-time employees and brings on about a dozen contractors as needed.

In a recent development, for now, each Zin Power system is built to order. The company’s motors range from 100 to 600 kilowatts and deliver up to 2,700 pound-feet of torque, and its systems can run fully electric or as hybrids. A proprietary control unit that Zin Power calls the “Magic Box” manages everything from charging and cooling to software and safety.

It has been revealed that “Our goal is to keep delivering what we’ve built while developing simpler, more advanced plug-and-play systems,” Zin remarked. “Eventually, we want a customer to be able to pull out a diesel engine and drop in a Zin Power system as a direct one-for-one replacement.”.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

“I was recently on a podcast and the host asked me what my lowest part of my career was,” Hank Green mused on a recent episode of his own podcast, Dear Hank & John.

That’s a tough question for anyone to answer, let alone someone who has spent about two decades regularly posting videos online for an increasingly broad audience.

“Really the low — the long low — was just watching as [the internet] went from being this lovely thing that a bunch of creatives were goofing around [on] to it being freaking everything, and mattering so much, and getting taken over by all tons of terrible vibes and algorithms selecting for outrage, and it being a huge degradation to the social order,” Green stated.

That’s bleak, but Green is at least trying to lead by example in showing that we don’t have to accept that the good parts of the internet are gone forever. The notoriously entrepreneurial vlogbrother has spun up a new manufacturer with Leslie Morgan: ClockwiseTV, a curated, ad-free educational video platform for children ages 8 to 12.

“[Hank] came to me last September like, ‘I have had this idea for a really long time, and it stems from the fact that my child, who’s nine, always is asking me for five more minutes on whatever device he’s on,’” Morgan, who has spent 20 years working on the business side of the creator economy, told TechCrunch. “I was like, I have that same problem… ‘How do you contain time, but also give the child agency?’”.

Clockwise’s answer to that question seems to be this: At the start of each viewing session, the parent and child decide how long they can watch, and the platform will recommend videos that will adhere to that time frame. If a kid is in the midst of a 30-minute session and has already watched two 10-minute videos, they’re not going to be suggested a 20-minute video when they only have 10 minutes left.

The startup is addressing a pretty widespread concern among parents, who are worried about more than simply negotiating with their children about how long they can use the iPad. According to a 2025 study by the Pew Research Center, about 51% of parents of children 12 or younger say their kid watches YouTube every day, among other video apps.

Recent findings suggest that youTube has a dedicated app for children under 13, YouTube Kids, which offers a wide range of parental controls, but the app can reportedly still serve children a wealth of low-quality AI slop. Other apps that don’t have a kids’ version can be even worse.

Clockwise indicates it is also solving that problem by hand-curating a library of educational videos from creators like Odd Animal Specimens, Draw with Jazza, and Nerdforge, as well as channels Green had a hand in creating, like Crash Course Kids and SciShow Kids.

“When you go into the app, there’s a dozen choices [of videos] that you can choose from to start,” Morgan, the startup’s CEO, remarked. “There’s search functionality as well, so you can say, ‘Hey, I’m really interested in math today,’ so you can look up Stand-up Maths and look at what’s available in that time frame.”.

Some of these creators cater to people of all ages, but Clockwise says its team manually reviews each video it uploads and edits it so that it’s ready for younger eyes. The team might remove anything from embedded product placement to what Morgan calls “spectacle power tool use.”.

It has been revealed that “Simone Giertz, who’s a maker creator, tends to curse a lot. But a lot of that content is great for kids,” Morgan explains. “She makes a skateboard for her three-legged dog, and if she drops an f-bomb, we’re going to cut it out so that it’s suitable for children.”.

Clockwise pays these creators an upfront fee to use their videos, then shares 25% of revenue based on watch time. Clockwise charges parents $6.99 per month or $69.99 per year to access the platform, which it promises will remain free of ads.

“Humans are checking [the videos] four times at least before it’s ever published into our app […] That will always stay,” Morgan said. “We’re not interested in using AI to wash down our content.”.

It has been revealed that so far, a few hundred parents have tested Clockwise with their children in beta. On Tuesday, the platform is opening to the public with apps made for iOS and Android smartphones and tablets.

The platform has not taken on any outside funding, and is funded by Green himself.

According to recent reports, “It was really important that he had full control,” Morgan mentioned. “He wanted to invest his own wealth into this. That was also really important because it is something he just believes in so wholeheartedly, as do I.”.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Revolution, the investment firm cofounded 14 years ago by entrepreneur-investor Steve Case, has closed its second Rise of the Rest seed fund with $150 million in capital commitments, just like the debut fund it revealed two years ago.

Industry observers note that rise of the Rest — which fund startups outside of the biggest U.S. tech hubs in an effort to foster innovation and momentum elsewhere — has rounded up some of the funding from institutional investors, presumably, but also from numerous very wealthy individuals.

According to Forbes, which is at the moment hosting a summit where Case confirmed the upcoming fund, some of the new fund’s backers include Jeff Bezos of Amazon, Sara Blakely of Spanx, hedge fund manager Ray Dalio, Under Armour cofounder Kevin Plank, former Tennessee governor Bill Haslam, and Apollo Global Management cofounder Joshua Harris.

Some of these investors backed the first fund, too, including Bezos and Dalio.

Very notably, Hillbilly Elegy author J.D. Vance, who ran the first fund with Case, has stepped back, and longtime Revolution investor David Hall will manage the second fund instead.

Certainly, that first fund kept its investors busy, with stakes in 125 companies. Barely a week passes without a startup announcing some funding from the Rise of the Rest team.

It has been revealed that ACV Auctions, a five-year-old, Buffalo, N.Y.-based online platform for franchise and used-car dealerships to buy and sell wholesale inventory through 20-minute auctions, is reportedly looking to raise $150 million in Series E funding at a post-money valuation north of $1 billion. Reuters has more here.

According to recent reports, weave, a seven-year-old, Lehi, Ut.-based developer of patient communications software focused on the dental and optometry market, has raised $70 million in Series D funding at a post-money valuation of $970 million. Tiger Global Management led the round, with participation from earlier backers Catalyst Investors, Bessemer Venture Partners, Crosslink Capital, Pelion Venture Partners and LeadEdge Capital. TechCrunch has more here.

1906, a two-year-old, Denver-based cannabis brand that makes a wide variety of edibles, has raised $18 million in funding led by Navy Capital. More here.

Aviatrix, a five-year-old, Palo Alto, Ca.-developer of software that allows companies to build hybrid clouds, raised $40 million in Series C funding. Earlier backer CRV led the round, joined by fellow insiders Formation 8, Ignition Partners, and Liberty Global Ventures. VentureBeat has more here.

Recent findings suggest that choco, an 18-month-old, mobile ordering platform for restaurants and their suppliers, has raised $33.5 million in Series A funding by Bessemer Venture Partners. The company has now raised $41 million to date. Other investors include Atlantic Labs, Target Global, Visionaries Club and Greyhound. TechCrunch has more here.

Recent findings suggest that duffel, a two-year-old, London-based startup that connects travel agencies with airline reservation systems, has raised $30 million in Series B funding led by Index Ventures, with participation from earlier backers Benchmark and Blossom Capital. 📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

by Kurt Schlosser on Nov 24, 2026 at 11:08 amNovember 24, 2026 at 11:09 am.

When Seattle’s Living Computers: Museum + Labs closed for good in 2024, it seemed like the end of the line for anyone who wanted to do more than just look at old computers.

But in a Tukwila business park 20 minutes south of downtown, a sizable collection of vintage computers is still alive — kept running by a few of the same people who once did the same for Paul Allen.

The Interim Computer Museum is a nonprofit that opened to the public in 2024 and has quietly grown into a hands-on showcase of dozens of machines, from early Apples and IBM PCs to hulking DEC systems that once filled university labs. At 4,400 square feet of public space, it’s nearly as big as Living Computers was before that museum expanded in 2016.

ICM is led by Stephen Jones, who calls himself the museum’s “caretaker.” Jones spent two decades helping track down and restore machines for Allen, first at PDP Planet, Allen’s private collection of vintage systems, then at Living Computers, where he was senior engineering manager.

When the late Microsoft co-founder’s estate wound down Living Computers, the majority of the collection went to the Mimms Museum of Technology and Art in Georgia, where Jones is also a curator. The machines in Tukwila are privately owned, and Jones has helped bankroll ICM with personal funds, with intends to eventually donate the collection to the nonprofit.

He chose not to reuse the Living Computers name, which ICM now holds, because “it has a finite past.” Instead, he wants to carry on “the spirit of the engineering focus.”.

It has been revealed that “Between Mimms and here, this is the legacy,” Jones stated. “We show the name and the connection to the past, but we’re doing latest things.”.

ICM occupies space in Seattle Exchange @ Southcenter, a sprawl of low-slung flex buildings off Strander Boulevard near Westfield Southcenter mall. Its neighbors include a car detailer, a pest control company, a welding shop, an embroiderer and an upholsterer.

Recent findings suggest that more than four decades ago, Seattle Computer Products operated just down Industry Drive. That’s where Tim Paterson wrote 86-DOS, the operating system Microsoft bought and turned into MS-DOS for IBM’s first PC.

According to recent reports, jones calls that proximity part of the “magic” of the location. The museum has a Gazelle computer that SCP built nearby, using boards that Jones said the organization hired high school students to assemble and test. Volunteers recently pulled data off its hard drive, which boots into MS-DOS 2.11 and still holds SCP’s own source code.

Allen’s fingerprints are everywhere. One display holds a 1971 letter from Hellmut Golde, director of the University of Washington’s Computer Science Laboratory, kicking Allen and his “friends from the Lakeside School” out of the lab. Among the offenses: tying up the teletypes to print “endless listings,” and taking an acoustic coupler from a professor’s office “without leaving at least a note.” Golde asked them to turn in their keys.

Recent findings suggest that the letter sits beside an Imlac PDS-1, the same type of graphics computer Golde scolded the teens for using without permission. More than five decades later, the letter is headed back to campus: ICM intends to display it, along with the Imlac, at UW’s 60th anniversary celebration for its computer science program in March.

Jones recalled that Allen insisted visitors to Living Computers get “the 10-minute experience” of loading an Altair 8800 from paper tape, just as he remembered it. The kit computer was the machine for which Allen and Bill Gates wrote Microsoft’s first product, and Allen wanted to reinforce “how far we’ve come and how difficult old computers were.” ICM has an Altair 8800 on display.

It has been revealed that around the corner is Miss Piggy, a DEC datasystem 570 that Microsoft used in the early 1980s to support the group that built Multiplan, Word and later Excel. It was also the email host for much of the organization, including Gates, who once had to print out an key message on its console printer when the system went down before a speaking engagement.

Recovered email reveals Allen pushing to get Piggy networked. “Paul Allen is very keen on doing this,” Henry Burgess wrote in 1982. Retired in 1986, the machine now runs again in Tukwila. It’s one of ICM’s most popular remote systems, and some fans come in just to write programs while sitting next to it.

In a recent development, other local ties include a PDP-7 that Boeing used to process flight data in the 1960s, and a Toad-1, a modern take on the PDP-10 built in the 1990s by Redmond’s XKL. Jones first got involved with Allen’s world through a 1997 Usenet post inviting PDP-10 enthusiasts onto a Toad. That machine became the cornerstone of PDP Planet.

In a 2024 video for Christie’s, Jones remarked what inspired Allen was “being able to recover old programs, mythical code, and get them running on hardware so that they can be studied.”.

In a recent development, asked what Allen would make of ICM, Jones didn’t hesitate. “I think he’d be happy,” he said.

On a monitor beside ICM’s PDP-6, a 1968 artificial intelligence program is having trouble.

“SORRY, I DON’T KNOW THE WORD ‘STEEPLE,'” it replies.

The program is SHRDLU, created by Terry Winograd at the MIT AI Lab. It let a user type plain-English commands to move blocks around a virtual world. Only the PDP-6’s front console and display survived, so ICM is rebuilding the machine as a “hybrid,” with the original hardware wired to an emulator.

It has been revealed that jones sees a lesson in that old error message. “You look at this and you think of how we use ChatGPT now,” he stated. “The cool thing about SHRDLU is that it can tell you ‘I don’t know.’ It doesn’t try to fabricate anything.”.

Recent findings suggest that ICM has its own ties to the modern AI world. An Anthropic employee is a member and strong supporter, and in October the museum brought six vintage computing stations to an Anthropic event, where the manufacturer’s Claude chatbot wrote programs for machines like the Commodore 64.

Back in Tukwila, Claude has become one of ICM’s most useful restoration tools. The team feeds it huge stacks of scanned documentation, such as the full set of schematics for a PDP-10. When a machine has a logic fault, they ask where to look, and Claude points them to a page in the maintenance manual or a likely bad module.

“That’s turned things that would take a couple of weeks to solve into a couple of days,” Jones said.

Industry observers note that AI can point the way, but the repairs remain hands-on work. When Miss Piggy wouldn’t run properly this year, former Living Computers engineer Josh Dersch stepped through the machine’s microcode one instruction at a time using a recreated DEC test board, until he found a single bad chip. A spare board brought it back.

Asked if it still takes a human to keep these machines running, Jones agreed — at least for now. If a humanoid robot with AI built in ever shows up to do the repairs, he joked, “then I sit at the front desk all day.”.

Nearly everything at ICM is meant to be touched, switched on and played with, and that can be intimidating. On machines with nothing but a text prompt, “you kind of have to know the commands in your head already,” Jones remarked.

Industry observers note that that’s by design. From the start, the idea was to challenge people “either by confronting them with their past or demonstrating how difficult it was,” Jones stated. His example: two friends, one with an Apple IIe and one with an IBM PC, whose computers “could never share” software. ICM continues that legacy, he said, “challenging the visitor to go beyond what they might feel comfortable with.”.

Sources indicate that volunteers have written cheat sheets to help newcomers, and Jones is encouraged when families come in and kids start typing BASIC programs. “That to me was the spirit of what PDP Planet and Living Computers was meant to be,” he said.

Very little is behind glass. Jones jokes that a Timex Sinclair 1000, which would wipe your painstakingly typed program if you bumped it, is “the only computer that deserves to be behind glass.” The goal, he noted, is to avoid “a boneyard that people walk through.”.

Other highlights include Galaxy Game, the first coin-operated video game, installed at Stanford in 1971 and now being restored, and a Thinking Machines CM-2 supercomputer, whose 40th anniversary ICM just celebrated with members of its original design team.

Industry observers note that for younger engineers raised on modern tools, Jones has a go-to move. He asks if they’ve used Linux, then walks them over to the PDP-7, the type of machine Unix was first written on more than 50 years ago. Many of the basic commands they type every day started there.

Sources indicate that that remote access helps explain why ICM has about 500 members and sponsors, even though only 81 members have visited in person this year. Memberships start at $36 a year. Along with a King County grant through 4Culture, they help cover rent, with personal funds from Jones filling the gap. The museum hopes to become self-sustaining within five years, and maybe someday buy its own building.

The museum’s name reflects the urgency. “We’re in this magic window right now, where the hardware can still run, we can still maintain it, you can replace parts,” Jones remarked. “But slowly we’re getting further and further away.”.

ICM is open Saturdays through Mondays from 10 a.m. to 4 p.m. Admission is $9 for adults and free for those under 18. Last May, the museum revived Vintage Computer Festival Pacific Northwest, which had been canceled in March 2020. The event drew 981 people, and it returns May 1–2 at the Tukwila Community Center.

Among the machines on the floor is MIT-AI, a DECsystem-2020 that once served as the ARPANET host for MIT’s Artificial Intelligence Lab. As Living Computers shut down in 2024, Christopher Zach, who sold the machine to Allen, told GeekWire he was ready to drive a U-Haul to Seattle to rescue it.

When a friend of Zach’s stopped by ICM’s booth at WorldCon and asked about “Chris’s computer,” Jones had a simple message to pass along: “Please just tell him it’s safe.”.

💡 Key Takeaways

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Science Corporation, the medical technology startup founded by former Neuralink president Max Hodak in 2021, raised a $400 million Series D, the firm stated in a blog post.

Sources indicate that investors in the fresh round valued the tech giant at $3.5 billion, a person familiar with the deal told TechCrunch. Those backers included Khosla Ventures, the Ackman Oxman Institute, Tenet Healthcare, 885 Capital, Y Combinator, and PLC Neurotech.

Hodak, who talked his way into a graduate neuroscience lab as a college student and has pursued biotechnology ever since, co-founded Science to leverage new technologies to understand and interact with the brain.

Science’s first product is PRIMA, a wearable and implantable chip that helps people with age-related macular degeneration recover some vision. The device is approved in Europe and available in Germany, as well as being trialed for new conditions.

Hodak announced that the device is now being trialed for patients with another blindness-causing condition, Stargardt disease, while onstage at TechCrunch Disrupt.

Industry observers note that with the funding, the firm aims to bring the device to the United States through the FDA’s Humanitarian Device Exemption, which lets experimental medical technology be used to treat rare conditions. Science has convinced the FDA that advanced macular degeneration in both eyes is uncommon enough to let them seek approval to use the device on people in the U.S.

Still, the startup’s big ambition and founding purpose is connecting directly to the human brain through a bio-hybrid sensor built from a combination of cultured neurons and silicon. The firm is at the moment designing initial human trials of the device with Yale neurosurgery professor Murat Günel, who told TechCrunch it could offer potential treatments for Parkinson’s disease, among other brain injuries and illnesses.

Among other things, Musk posted "Everyday is Zeroday" and replied with fire and laughing emojis to CZ's earlier warning about phishing links.

CZ then asked Musk to stop, calling it a "bad time to troll," and reminded him that Binance's $500 million investment in Twitter in 2022 has become a stake in SpaceX worth more than $1 billion.
